areas.title: Oxidative stress biology & antioxidant supplements
areas.summary: Reactive oxygen species are normal signalling molecules at low levels (oxidative eustress) and damaging only in excess (distress). Defence is dominated by enzymes such as peroxiredoxins, glutathione peroxidases and the Nrf2-controlled glutathione system, not by dietary scavengers. Large RCTs show high-dose antioxidant supplements (beta-carotene, vitamin E, cocktails) do not prevent disease and some cause harm. Plant compounds most likely help through mild Nrf2/hormetic signalling and gut effects, and ORAC-type 'antioxidant capacity' numbers are meaningless for health.

areas.title: Foods, drinks & dietary patterns
areas.summary: How specific foods, drinks and eating patterns change systemic oxidative stress in humans. The biggest dietary levers are not 'antioxidant superfoods' but avoiding chronic overfeeding, large high-glycemic and high-fat meal spikes, alcohol, processed meat and high-heat dry cooking, inside a Mediterranean-style pattern. Among individual foods, high-phenolic extra-virgin olive oil, cruciferous foods that actually deliver sulforaphane (sprouts, seed powder with active myrosinase, raw or mustard-dressed broccoli), filtered coffee, blueberries, cocoa flavanols and brewed green tea have the best human evidence. Polyphenol milligrams and ORAC scores do not predict benefit: these compounds work through different routes (Nrf2 electrophile signalling, gut-microbial metabolites, endothelial nitric oxide, blunting NADPH oxidase), most show thresholds and plateaus, and very few human trials measure validated oxidative-damage markers.

areas.title: Exercise, lifestyle & environment
areas.summary: Lifestyle and environment drive more of the body's oxidative load than any supplement. Not smoking, losing excess visceral fat, staying fit, keeping blood sugar in range and limiting alcohol produce the largest, best-documented drops in validated markers such as urinary F2-isoprostanes. Exercise works by hormesis: each session briefly raises ROS, which trains the body's own antioxidant systems, and megadose vitamin C/E can blunt that signal. Sleep, air quality, sun protection and gum health matter at a smaller scale, while hydrogen water, grounding, ozone therapy and IV glutathione lack credible evidence.

areas.title: Sperm health & DNA fragmentation
areas.summary: Sperm are unusually exposed to oxidative damage: their membranes are packed with oxidisable fatty acids, they have almost no cytoplasm for antioxidant enzymes, and they cannot repair oxidised DNA themselves, so the egg has to. High sperm DNA fragmentation (SDF) is linked to slower natural conception, roughly double the miscarriage risk and lower IVF/ICSI success. The biggest proven levers are treating a clinical varicocele, stopping smoking, avoiding testicular heat and exogenous testosterone, and ejaculating every 1-2 days; diet, weight and exercise help modestly. Over-the-counter 'male fertility' antioxidants have mostly failed in large, well-run trials (MOXI, FAZST), so they are a low priority, and megadoses may do harm.

areas.title: Egg (oocyte) quality & oxidative stress
areas.summary: Egg quality depends above all on age: chromosome errors driven by cohesin loss and declining mitochondrial function rise steeply after the mid-30s, and no lifestyle change or supplement has been shown to reverse that in humans. Within that limit, the biggest controllable factors are not smoking, avoiding obesity and heavy drinking, taking folic acid, and eating a Mediterranean-style diet in the ~3 months of follicle growth before conception or IVF. Antioxidant supplements, including CoQ10 and melatonin, have at best low-quality evidence for women, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF.

entries.headline: A pattern of supplemental folic acid, B12 and vitamin D plus low-pesticide produce, whole grains, dairy, soy and seafood was associated with 53% higher odds of IVF live birth per SD of adherence (top vs bottom quartile: +28 percentage points).

dose.effective: Folic acid supplement (>= 400-800 ug/day), adequate B12 and vitamin D, whole grains, dairy, soy foods, seafood instead of other meats, and lower-pesticide-residue fruit and vegetables.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of a score from a validated food-frequency questionnaire.
dose.timeframe: Diet in the year before treatment was measured.
dose.notes: Not related to estradiol, oocyte counts or endometrial thickness; associated with less clinical pregnancy loss.

entries.mechanism: Likely via one-carbon metabolism (folate/B12), vitamin D signalling and lower pesticide exposure rather than a direct antioxidant effect.
entries.interactions: Contains [folic-acid] and [vitamin-d]; overlaps with [mediterranean-diet] and [omega3-fish].
entries.caveats: Derived and tested in the same single US cohort (357 women) by the same group, which risks overfitting; needs independent replication or an RCT.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth odds per SD adherence
Live birth, top vs bottom quartile

entries.title: "Profertility" diet pattern (EARTH study)

entries.headline: Acute alcohol raised urinary isoprostanes in a time- and dose-dependent way in healthy volunteers, tracking blood alcohol; red-wine polyphenols do not cancel this.

dose.effective: Less is better for oxidative stress; there is no antioxidant reason to drink.
dose.studied_range: Acute doses in a randomized placebo-controlled study; patients with alcoholic liver disease.
dose.too_much: Dose-dependent; heavy and binge drinking worst.
dose.timeframe: Hours.
dose.notes: Covered in more depth in the lifestyle section.

entries.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism by CYP2E1 generates ROS; acetaldehyde depletes glutathione; raised NADH/NAD+ alters mitochondrial redox; iron mobilisation.
entries.interactions: Negates the polyphenol benefit of [red-wine-resveratrol].
entries.caveats: Small acute study; chronic moderate intake data are confounded.
entries.title: Alcohol (dietary)

entries.headline: Alcohol raises lipid-peroxidation markers even at moderate intake (4 drinks/day of red wine raised urinary 8-iso-PGF2a versus the same wine without alcohol); there is no antioxidant benefit from drinking.

dose.effective: Less is better. If drinking, stay at or below ~100 g alcohol/week (about 7 US standard drinks or 12 UK units), spread out, with alcohol-free days; avoid binges.
dose.studied_range: Experimental: 41 g/day (4 drinks) red wine for 4 weeks; acute dosing in volunteers; cohorts across 0 to >350 g/week.
dose.too_much: Mortality rose above ~100 g/week; heavy and binge drinking drive CYP2E1 induction and liver injury.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostane rise within 4 weeks of daily moderate drinking; acute rise after single doses.
dose.notes: The polyphenols in red wine did not offset the alcohol; dealcoholized wine performed better.

entries.mechanism: Ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and, with chronic use, by induced CYP2E1, which leaks superoxide and H2O2. Acetaldehyde forms protein/DNA adducts and depletes glutathione; a high NADH/NAD+ ratio, iron mobilization and gut-derived endotoxin activating Kupffer-cell NADPH oxidase add to the load.
entries.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking]. Can worsen [short-sleep] quality, [sleep-apnea] and [weight-loss] (alcohol is calorie-dense).
entries.caveats: The 'red wine is an antioxidant' story is not supported by biomarker data. Observational 'J-curves' for heart disease are confounded.
entries.title: Alcohol

entries.headline: Daily or heavy drinking lowers semen quality (about 33% lower concentration above 40 units/week); occasional light drinking shows little effect.

dose.effective: Keep intake at or below about 5 units (UK units, ~8 g alcohol each) per week while trying to conceive; avoid daily drinking.
dose.studied_range: From 0 to over 40 units/week in 1221 young Danish men; 15 cross-sectional studies (16,395 men).
dose.too_much: Adverse associations appear above ~5 units/week and are strongest above 25 units/week.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Binge drinking was not independently linked to semen in the Danish study, but heavy episodes are best avoided.

entries.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism generates acetaldehyde and ROS (CYP2E1), lowers testosterone, raises estrogen and depletes antioxidants such as glutathione.
entries.interactions: Often clustered with [tobacco-smoking] and [excess-adiposity].
entries.caveats: Direct SDF data are scarce; most evidence is on conventional parameters and is cross-sectional.
entries.title: Alcohol

entries.headline: Heavier drinking lowers fertility, but under about 7 drinks a week effects on conception are small or undetectable; one IVF cohort saw 16% lower live birth at 4 or more drinks a week.

dose.effective: Ideally none while trying; if drinking, keep well under 4 drinks/week before and during IVF.
dose.studied_range: 0 to >= 14 servings/week; light <= 12.5 g ethanol/day vs >12.5 g/day.
dose.too_much: >= 4 drinks/week associated with lower IVF live birth (OR 0.84); >12.5 g/day (about one drink/day) with ~23% lower fecundability; ASRM: >2 drinks/day best avoided.
dose.timeframe: Preconception months; stop entirely once pregnancy is possible (fetal safety).
dose.notes: Data do not separate binge from regular drinking; binge drinking in the fertile window is probably worse.

entries.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism generates acetaldehyde and ROS (CYP2E1), disturbs estrogen and LH signalling, and depletes antioxidant reserves.
entries.interactions: Effects combine across partners in IVF (both drinking >= 4/week: OR 0.79).
entries.caveats: Studies conflict: a large Danish cohort found no effect below 14/week, and the EARTH IVF cohort found no effect of <= 12 g/day. The pregnancy-safety case for abstinence is stronger than the egg-quality case.
entries.title: Alcohol

entries.headline: A systematic review reports some positive effects on oocyte maturation, embryo grade and endometriosis pain, but the trials are small and no live-birth benefit has been shown.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: Small trials, often combined with inositol or other agents.
dose.notes: Mostly from Italian combination-product studies.

entries.mechanism: Mitochondrial enzyme cofactor and redox-cycling antioxidant that regenerates glutathione, vitamins C and E.
entries.interactions: Usually given with [myo-inositol].
entries.caveats: Evidence base is too weak to recommend.
entries.title: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA)

factors.name: Antioxidant supplements in general (for the female partner)

entries.headline: The Cochrane review of 63 trials found only low- to very-low-quality evidence that antioxidants help subfertile women, several included trials have since been retracted, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF.

dose.effective: No antioxidant product or dose is proven to raise live birth in women.
dose.studied_range: Trials of NAC, melatonin, L-arginine, myo-inositol, carnitine, selenium, vitamins C/E/D, B complex, CoQ10 and omega-3, usually for 1-3 cycles.
dose.too_much: No clear harms in pooled data (miscarriage OR 1.13, GI effects OR 1.55, both NS), but in animals blocking ROS impairs ovulation, so more is not better.
dose.timeframe: Trials typically 1-3 months.
dose.notes: Cochrane's headline OR for live birth (1.81) rests on very-low-quality, small, often unregistered trials; treat it as unreliable. A 2026 editorial note lists 7 retracted and 2 'concern' trials in the review.

entries.mechanism: Direct scavengers cannot reach the mitochondrial sites where oocyte ROS are generated at meaningful concentrations, and ROS are required for LH-triggered ovulation; the 'antioxidant paradox' applies.
entries.interactions: Specific agents are listed separately: [coq10], [melatonin], [myo-inositol], [n-acetylcysteine], [vitamin-c-e-combined], [l-carnitine], [alpha-lipoic-acid], [isolated-polyphenol-supplements], [nmn-nad]. Antioxidants for the male partner are a different question.
entries.caveats: Supplement marketing for 'egg quality' far outruns the evidence. Spending on lifestyle basics and folic acid is better supported.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, antioxidants vs control (very low quality)

entries.title: Antioxidant supplements in general (for the female partner)

entries.headline: One tiny trial (30 men) found 16 mg/day astaxanthin lowered seminal ROS and reported more pregnancies; never replicated at scale.

dose.effective: 16 mg/day for 3 months (studied dose).
dose.studied_range: 16 mg/day, 3 months.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

entries.mechanism: Carotenoid that spans lipid bilayers and quenches singlet oxygen and lipid peroxyl radicals.
entries.interactions: Similar role to [tomatoes-lycopene].
entries.caveats: 11 vs 19 analysed men; pregnancy result very fragile; industry-supplied product.
entries.title: Astaxanthin

entries.headline: At 20-30 mg/day, beta-carotene raised lung cancer by 18-28% and total mortality by 8-17% in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers. No benefit for anyone, and USPSTF recommends against it.

dose.effective: None as a supplement. Food carotenoids (carrots, leafy greens, sweet potato) are a different matter.
dose.studied_range: 6 mg/day (SU.VI.MAX mix) to 20-30 mg/day (ATBC, CARET, HPS)
dose.too_much: 20-30 mg/day: lung cancer RR 1.16-1.28, stomach cancer RR 1.34; harm concentrated in smokers and asbestos workers.
dose.timeframe: Excess lung cancer appeared within the 4-8 year trial periods
dose.notes: CARET combined it with 25,000 IU retinol; Cochrane also found dose-related mortality with vitamin A. Smokers should avoid all beta-carotene and vitamin A supplements.

entries.mechanism: At pharmacological doses in a smoke-oxidised lung, beta-carotene lowers lung retinoic acid and RARβ signalling, and raises AP-1/cyclin D1 proliferation signals. In ferrets, a ~30 mg/day-equivalent dose caused squamous metaplasia and a ~6 mg/day-equivalent dose did not. This is a clear example of dose- and context-dependent pro-oxidant harm.
entries.interactions: The harm is amplified by [tobacco-smoking] and asbestos exposure. Part of [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail] and HPS regimens.
entries.caveats: Observational studies linked high blood beta-carotene to lower cancer risk, probably because it marks high fruit and vegetable intake. Supplements reversed this. Multivitamins with small amounts (a few mg) have not shown this harm.
entries.title: Beta-carotene supplements

entries.headline: Black tea's catechins are largely converted to theaflavins and thearubigins; in the same smoker trial where green tea cut 8-OHdG, black tea had no effect.

dose.effective: No oxidative-stress benefit shown; normal intake (2-4 cups) is fine.
dose.studied_range: 4 cups/day for 4 months.
dose.notes: Folin values for black tea are similar to green tea, but the compounds differ.

entries.mechanism: Theaflavins/thearubigins and catechins, extensively metabolised by gut bacteria.
entries.interactions: Reduces non-heme iron absorption when taken with meals.
entries.caveats: Cohort associations with cardiovascular outcomes exist but are confounded.
entries.title: Black tea

entries.headline: As rich in polyphenols as blueberries (mostly cyanidin-3-glucoside and ellagitannins), but the only human feeding trial measured fat oxidation and insulin sensitivity, not oxidative stress; benefits are inferred from other anthocyanin foods.

dose.effective: A 150 g serving is a reasonable berry portion by analogy with blueberry trials; 600 g/day was used in the one controlled feeding study.
dose.studied_range: 600 g/day for 7 days (1500 mg flavonoids/day).
dose.timeframe: Days to weeks.
dose.notes: Ellagitannins are converted by gut bacteria to urolithins, and people differ in whether they produce them.

entries.mechanism: Anthocyanin and ellagitannin metabolites (gut-derived phenolic acids, urolithins) acting on endothelium and inflammation.
entries.interactions: Interchangeable with [blueberries] and [berries-other] as a berry serving; little reason to think combining berries beyond ~1 cup/day adds much for oxidative stress.
entries.caveats: No RCT on oxidative-stress markers. In a 600 g/day feeding study blackberries lowered 24-h respiratory quotient and insulin AUC in overweight men.
entries.title: Blackberries

entries.headline: One cup (150 g) a day improved endothelial function over 6 months in metabolic syndrome, while half a cup did nothing; several trials show lower oxidized LDL, monocyte ROS or DNA oxidation.

dose.effective: 150 g fresh (1 cup) daily, or ~22-25 g freeze-dried powder.
dose.studied_range: 75-350 g fresh-equivalent/day for 6 weeks to 6 months; acute doses of 319-1791 mg blueberry polyphenols.
dose.timeframe: Acute FMD rise at 1-2 h and 6 h; chronic effects by 6-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Acute FMD rose with dose up to ~766 mg blueberry polyphenols and then plateaued. Frozen wild blueberries count. Juice with added sugar is not equivalent.

entries.mechanism: Anthocyanins are poorly absorbed intact; benefits track circulating phenolic metabolites (many made by gut bacteria) that lower neutrophil NADPH oxidase activity and improve nitric-oxide-dependent vasodilation. Not direct radical scavenging in plasma.
entries.interactions: Within-class saturation: little extra acute benefit above ~766 mg polyphenols per serving, so megadoses of berry extract are unlikely to add much. Mechanistically complementary to [broccoli-sprouts] (Nrf2) and [extra-virgin-olive-oil].
entries.caveats: Trials are small (n=18-115) and often industry-funded; oxidative-marker results are inconsistent across the 45 human studies reviewed, while vascular function results are the most consistent. A 75 g/day dose was ineffective. Insulin resistance, blood pressure and plasma thiols did not change in the 6-month trial.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, chromatography (highbush, sum of compounds)
FMD gain with 150 g/day for 6 months

entries.title: Blueberries

entries.headline: Seeds are the most concentrated glucoraphanin source, and taken whole (not extracted) their own myrosinase makes sulforaphane 3-4x more bioavailable than glucoraphanin-only preparations; outcome trials with seed powder itself are scarce.

dose.effective: Doses delivering roughly 50-230 µmol glucoraphanin were used in bioavailability studies; aim for a dose that, given ~30-40% conversion with active myrosinase, supplies tens of µmol sulforaphane (comparable to the effective Qidong beverage dose).
dose.studied_range: 50-230 µmol glucoraphanin per dose in pharmacokinetic studies.
dose.too_much: Not established; bitterness and GI upset at high intakes. Product potency varies widely.
dose.timeframe: Sulforaphane metabolites peak within hours; plasma half-life ~2.5 h, so effects are pulsatile with daily dosing.
dose.notes: Mix ground seed into cool or room-temperature food or water and let it sit a few minutes before eating; do not cook it (heat kills myrosinase). Adding seed powder to cooked broccoli works on the same principle as [mustard-seed-myrosinase].

entries.mechanism: Same Nrf2/KEAP1 electrophile mechanism as sprouts; seed powder supplies both substrate (glucoraphanin) and enzyme (myrosinase).
entries.interactions: Directly redundant with [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements] for the Nrf2 effect; see the saturation discussion. Complements polyphenol foods.
entries.caveats: Bioavailability data come from small volunteer groups. No trial has shown that seed powder lowers validated oxidative-damage markers (F2-isoprostanes, 8-oxo-dG) in healthy people.

key_numbers.label: Bioavailability with active plant myrosinase vs glucoraphanin alone
Glucoraphanin-only supplement, conversion to urinary metabolites

entries.title: Broccoli seed powder (with active myrosinase)

entries.headline: The richest whole-food source of glucoraphanin plus active myrosinase; daily intake reliably delivers sulforaphane and induces Nrf2-driven detoxication in human trials, but direct proof of lower oxidative damage in healthy people is thin.

dose.effective: About 30-40 g fresh sprouts daily (a small handful) in food trials; detoxication trials used beverages giving ~600 µmol glucoraphanin + 40 µmol sulforaphane per day, and the lowest clearly effective dose produced ~25 µmol urinary sulforaphane metabolites per day.
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day for 10 weeks; 40 g single servings; up to 200 g sprouts as homogenate (dose escalation); beverages 400-600 µmol glucoraphanin/day for 2-12 weeks.
dose.too_much: No toxicity at trial doses; a 12-week beverage trial found no effect on thyroid hormones or thyroid autoimmunity. Very high doses cause bitterness and GI upset.
dose.timeframe: Enzyme induction within a day; detox biomarker changes within 1-2 weeks and sustained for 12 weeks without tolerance.
dose.notes: Chew thoroughly: chewing intact sprouts raised sulforaphane metabolite excretion vs swallowing whole. Sprouts gave ~3x more absorbed sulforaphane than a myrosinase-treated extract at the same nominal dose. Conversion of glucoraphanin by gut bacteria alone varies 1% to >40% between people.

entries.mechanism: Myrosinase released on chewing hydrolyses glucoraphanin to sulforaphane, an electrophilic isothiocyanate that modifies KEAP1 cysteines, freeing Nrf2 to induce glutathione synthesis, GSTs, NQO1 and HO-1. This is an indirect, catalytic antioxidant effect (enzymes are not consumed), not radical scavenging.
entries.interactions: Partly redundant with [broccoli-seed-powder], [sulforaphane-supplements] and other strong Nrf2 inducers: human dose-response data show a threshold (Qidong benzene trial: only the full dose worked) but no established plateau; stacking several strong doses on the same day likely gives diminishing returns for the Nrf2-specific effect. Not redundant with polyphenol foods ([blueberries], [coffee], [cocoa-flavanols]) that act mainly on endothelium, NADPH oxidase and gut. Eating mature [broccoli-mature] still adds fiber, vitamin C, folate and lutein that sprouts and seed powder do not replace.
entries.caveats: Most oxidative-stress positives come from small trials (e.g. broccoli sprout powder in type 2 diabetes lowered MDA and oxidized LDL, but the sulforaphane dose was taken from manufacturer claims, which later assays did not confirm). A 4-week sulforaphane trial in COPD (25 and 150 µmol/day) found no Nrf2 target induction in lung cells and no change in oxidative markers. Benefits for hard outcomes are unproven.

Fresh sprouts vs myrosinase-treated extract, absorbed sulforaphane

entries.title: Broccoli sprouts (fresh, chewed)

entries.headline: Moderate coffee or tea does not clearly affect semen quality; caffeinated soft drinks and energy drinks look worse.

dose.effective: Up to about 2-3 cups of coffee per day appears fine.
dose.studied_range: 28 observational studies, nearly 20,000 men.
dose.too_much: Avoid large intakes from colas and energy drinks.
dose.notes: Some studies linked caffeine to sperm aneuploidy and DNA breaks, but findings are inconsistent.

entries.mechanism: Coffee polyphenols are antioxidant; caffeine effects on sperm DNA are uncertain.
entries.interactions: Separate from [refined-sugar-high-glycemic].
entries.caveats: Observational and inconsistent; residual confounding by smoking.
entries.title: Coffee and caffeine

entries.headline: Moderate caffeine (under ~200 mg/day) shows little or no effect on conceiving or IVF success; the clearer risk is miscarriage once pregnant, rising about 7% per 100 mg/day.

dose.effective: Keep under 200 mg/day (about 1-2 cups of brewed coffee) while trying and in pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: <50 to >700 mg/day.
dose.too_much: > 500 mg/day linked to lower fertility (ASRM); in pregnancy, 350-699 mg/day RR 1.40 and >= 700 mg/day RR 1.72 for pregnancy loss.
dose.timeframe: Matters most from conception onward.
dose.notes: Keep fertility and miscarriage data separate: preconception intake was not associated with miscarriage in a large Danish cohort; early-pregnancy intake was.

entries.mechanism: Adenosine-receptor antagonism; effects on ovulation and tubal function are speculative. Not primarily an oxidative-stress factor.
entries.interactions: Coffee and tea are also polyphenol sources; there is no evidence that this offsets or adds to the caffeine effect on fertility. For general (non-pregnancy) oxidative-stress effects of coffee, see [coffee].
entries.caveats: Observational and confounded by pregnancy nausea (women with healthier pregnancies feel sick and drink less coffee). Male caffeine intake >= 300 mg/day was associated with lower fecundability in one cohort.

key_numbers.label: Miscarriage risk per +100 mg/day in pregnancy

entries.title: Caffeine (high intake)

entries.headline: In CALERIE, the only long-term RCT of calorie restriction in healthy non-obese adults, prescribed 25% CR for 2 years lowered urinary F2-isoprostanes by 13-27% vs ad libitum controls.

dose.effective: A sustained moderate deficit; CALERIE participants achieved about half the prescribed 25% restriction.
dose.studied_range: 25% CR for 6 months to 2 years.
dose.too_much: Malnutrition, low bone density and loss of lean mass if extreme; not for underweight people, pregnancy or eating disorders.
dose.timeframe: Reduction present at 12 months and sustained at 24 months; DNA damage reduced at 6 months.
dose.notes: In overweight people, weight loss itself drives much of the effect.

entries.mechanism: Lower mitochondrial ROS production per unit of energy, lower insulin and IGF-1 signalling, less adipose inflammation, hormetic upregulation of defences.
entries.interactions: Opposite of [overfeeding].
entries.caveats: Long-term adherence is hard; most people will benefit from avoiding surplus rather than strict CR.
entries.title: Calorie restriction

entries.headline: Regular cannabis use is associated with more sperm DNA fragmentation and chromosome abnormalities in small studies.

dose.effective: Stop regular use at least 3 months before trying.
dose.studied_range: Regular users vs non-users in 54 infertile men.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Smoking cannabis also delivers combustion oxidants similar to tobacco.

entries.mechanism: THC acts on endocannabinoid receptors in the testis and sperm, disturbing the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, spermatogenesis and mitochondrial function.
entries.interactions: Often co-used with tobacco [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Exploratory, small, retrospective data; confounding by tobacco is likely.
entries.title: Cannabis

factors.name: Carrots and carotenoid-rich vegetables (vs beta-carotene pills)

entries.headline: Carotenoid-rich foods are associated with lower oxidative DNA and lipid damage, but isolated beta-carotene supplements increased lung cancer and mortality in smokers (CARET), a textbook antioxidant paradox.

dose.effective: Regular orange/yellow and green vegetables eaten with some fat; a medium carrot (~60 g) provides ~5 mg beta-carotene.
dose.studied_range: Food: cohort and feeding studies. Supplements: 30 mg beta-carotene + 25,000 IU retinol daily (CARET).
dose.too_much: Beta-carotene supplements in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers: lung cancer RR 1.28, all-cause death RR 1.17. Beta-carotene supplements raised mortality in Cochrane analysis.
dose.notes: Absorption needs dietary fat: salads with full-fat dressing delivered much more carotenoid than reduced-fat or fat-free versions.

entries.mechanism: Carotenoids quench singlet oxygen and lipid peroxyl radicals in membranes and lipoproteins; at high doses in high-oxygen, smoke-exposed lungs beta-carotene can act as a pro-oxidant.
entries.interactions: Absorption improved by [extra-virgin-olive-oil], avocado.
entries.caveats: Food associations are observational. The supplement results are the reason not to translate food carotenoid data into pills.
entries.title: Carrots and carotenoid-rich vegetables (vs beta-carotene pills)

entries.headline: Gonadotoxic chemotherapy and ovarian radiation destroy the egg reserve directly; less than 2 Gy is estimated to kill half of human oocytes.

dose.effective: Fertility-preservation counselling before treatment; egg or embryo freezing is standard care.
dose.too_much: Oocyte LD50 estimated at < 2 Gy; chemotherapy risk depends on drug (e.g. cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin), cumulative dose and age.
dose.timeframe: Primordial-follicle oocytes die within 12-24 h of gonadotoxic drug exposure, so preservation must happen before treatment.
dose.notes: GnRH agonists may be offered (e.g. breast cancer) but are not a substitute for proven preservation methods.

entries.mechanism: DNA double-strand breaks in primordial-follicle oocytes trigger apoptosis; radiation generates ROS and direct DNA damage.
entries.interactions: No antioxidant has been shown to protect human ovaries from chemotherapy.
entries.caveats: This is a medical-referral factor, not a lifestyle one.
entries.title: Chemotherapy and pelvic radiation

entries.headline: Activated neutrophils and macrophages are a major regulated source of oxidants, and ROS and NF-kB amplify each other, so persistent inflammation keeps oxidative stress high.

dose.effective: Treat the source (adiposity, smoking, infection, autoimmune or periodontal disease).
dose.timeframe: Not specified in these studies
dose.notes: Antioxidant supplements have not reduced inflammatory cardiovascular outcomes in large trials.

entries.mechanism: NOX2 and myeloperoxidase in phagocytes generate superoxide, H2O2 and hypochlorous acid that damage endothelium and tissue. ROS modulate NF-kB activation, and NF-kB targets regulate ROS production.
entries.interactions: Fed by [excess-adiposity], [tobacco-smoking] and [glycemic-control]. Nrf2 activation can counter NF-kB-driven inflammation.
entries.caveats: Inflammation is also protective acutely. The target is chronic, unresolved inflammation.
entries.title: Chronic low-grade inflammation

entries.headline: A palpable varicocele is the single largest common driver of high SDF, adding roughly 10-14 percentage points on average.

dose.effective: Clinical (palpable, grade 1-3) varicocele found on physical exam; ultrasound-only (subclinical) varicoceles matter much less.
dose.studied_range: Present in roughly 40% of infertile men; meta-analyses compare men with vs without varicocele.
dose.too_much: Higher grades and bilateral varicoceles tend to do more damage, but the grade-SDF relationship is inconsistent.
dose.timeframe: Damage accumulates over years; after repair SDF falls over 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Ask a urologist for a scrotal exam if SDF is high, semen is abnormal or there is a dull ache or visible veins.

entries.mechanism: Venous pooling raises testicular temperature and causes hypoxia and reflux of adrenal/renal metabolites; this drives mitochondrial ROS, NADPH oxidase activity in leukocytes and lipid peroxidation, producing 8-OHdG and strand breaks in poorly protaminated sperm.
entries.interactions: Heat from [sauna] and [everyday-scrotal-heat] adds to the varicocele's thermal load. Smoking [tobacco-smoking] in varicocele patients compounds oxidative stress. The fix is [varicocele-repair], not supplements.
entries.caveats: Many men with varicocele are fertile; it is a problem mainly when semen or SDF is abnormal. Varicocele and SDF studies are mostly cross-sectional.
entries.title: Clinical varicocele (enlarged scrotal veins)

entries.headline: Cocoa flavanols reliably improve endothelial function (EFSA-authorised at 200 mg/day); in the 21,442-person COSMOS trial, 500 mg/day did not significantly cut total CVD events (HR 0.90) but reduced CVD death by 27% as a secondary outcome.

dose.effective: 200 mg cocoa flavanols/day: about 2.5 g high-flavanol cocoa powder or 10 g high-flavanol dark chocolate (EFSA).
dose.studied_range: 200-900 mg flavanols/day; COSMOS 500 mg/day (80 mg epicatechin) for a median 3.6 years.
dose.too_much: Chocolate brings sugar, fat and calories; extracts avoid these. Ordinary chocolate flavanol content varies widely and is rarely labelled.
dose.timeframe: FMD rises within hours; chronic improvement plateaued after ~2 weeks.
dose.notes: Epicatechin is the key active monomer; blood-pressure effects were larger above 50 mg epicatechin/day.

entries.mechanism: (-)-Epicatechin and its metabolites raise endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability and reduce NADPH-oxidase-driven superoxide in vessels; procyanidins are mostly degraded by gut bacteria to valerolactones.
entries.interactions: Shares flavan-3-ols with [green-tea], apples and grapes; FMD gains appear regardless of dose in meta-analysis, implying a plateau.
entries.caveats: Most vascular trials are short and many were funded by cocoa companies. COSMOS primary endpoint was null; the CVD-death finding is secondary. Direct oxidative-damage markers are seldom measured.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, Folin assay, cocoa powder

entries.title: Cocoa flavanols / high-flavanol dark chocolate

entries.headline: CoQ10 at 200-300 mg/day modestly raises sperm motility and concentration, but there is no evidence it raises pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: 200 mg/day (ubiquinone or ubiquinol) with a fat-containing meal for 3-6 months.
dose.studied_range: 200-300 mg/day for 3-6 months.
dose.too_much: Well tolerated; may interact with warfarin.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Men with low baseline motility and low seminal CoQ10 responded best.

entries.mechanism: Electron carrier in the mitochondrial electron transport chain and lipid-soluble antioxidant in sperm midpiece membranes.
entries.interactions: Common ingredient in [male-antioxidant-combination] products.
entries.caveats: Meta-analysis of 3 small RCTs; no live-birth data; SDF rarely measured.
entries.title: Coenzyme Q10

entries.headline: The best-studied 'egg quality' supplement: 600 mg/day for 60 days before IVF increased eggs retrieved (median 4 vs 2) and good embryos in young poor responders, and meta-analyses show higher clinical pregnancy (OR ~2.2-2.4) but no significant live-birth gain.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day (200 mg three times daily) for 60 days before IVF (Xu 2018 RCT).
dose.studied_range: 600 mg/day in the Xu RCT; pooled RCTs (5 trials, 449 women) used varying regimens.
dose.too_much: No harms reported in these trials.
dose.timeframe: At least 2 months before stimulation; ideally covering the ~3-month follicle-growth window.
dose.notes: Fat-soluble. Evidence is mainly in poor responders/low ovarian reserve; no good data in women with normal reserve.

entries.mechanism: CoQ10 carries electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and is a lipid-phase antioxidant. Ageing oocytes in mice and women express less of the CoQ-synthesis enzymes PDSS2 and COQ6; in mice CoQ10 restored oocyte mitochondrial function and reduced spindle defects.
entries.interactions: Mechanistically overlaps with [nmn-nad] (both target mitochondrial ageing). Often bundled with [melatonin] and [myo-inositol] in commercial products, which prevents attributing effects.
entries.caveats: Small trials; the Xu RCT was open-label without placebo and excluded 17 non-compliant women. ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF. Not shown to reduce aneuploidy in humans.

key_numbers.label: Cumulative live birth, CoQ10 vs control (NS)

entries.title: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol)

entries.headline: The biggest single polyphenol (chlorogenic acid) source in many Western diets; RCTs at 3-4 cups/day cut background DNA strand breaks by about a quarter and urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha by ~15%, and cohorts show the lowest mortality at 3-4 cups/day.

dose.effective: 3-4 cups (about 750 mL) per day of paper-filtered coffee.
dose.studied_range: 200-800 mL/day, from 8 hours to 4 weeks in intervention trials.
dose.too_much: Unfiltered coffee (French press, boiled, Turkish) raises LDL cholesterol through cafestol/kahweol; ~10 mg cafestol is in 2-3 cups of cafetiere coffee. Caffeine limits apply in pregnancy (see fertility sections).
dose.timeframe: DNA strand-break reduction detectable 2 h after the first cup; sustained at 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Paper filters retain the diterpenes. Decaffeinated coffee was also associated with lower mortality, so caffeine is not the whole story. Roast level shifts the compound mix (dark roast: less chlorogenic acid, more N-methylpyridinium).

entries.mechanism: Chlorogenic (caffeoylquinic) acids are partly absorbed in the small intestine and extensively metabolised by gut bacteria to dihydrocaffeic and ferulic acid derivatives; coffee also contains roast-derived compounds such as N-methylpyridinium. Trials show raised glutathione (consistent with induced antioxidant defences) and fewer DNA strand breaks rather than higher plasma 'antioxidant capacity'.
entries.interactions: Shares chlorogenic acids with [eggplant], [blueberries] and artichoke. Caffeine and fertility: covered elsewhere.
entries.caveats: Effects on plasma antioxidant capacity, antioxidant enzymes and lipid/protein damage are unclear across 26 intervention studies; the clearest signal is DNA protection and glutathione. Some positive trials were industry-sponsored. Pregnancy: high intake associated with low birth weight and pregnancy loss. When trying to conceive or pregnant, keep total caffeine under about 200 mg/day; see [caffeine-fertility].

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, chromatography (filter coffee, sum of compounds)
Reduction in spontaneous DNA strand breaks vs water (4 wk, 750 mL/day)
All-cause mortality RR at 3-4 cups/day vs none

entries.title: Coffee (paper-filtered)

entries.headline: Regular winter swimmers show higher baseline antioxidant enzymes (a hormesis signal), but human evidence for health benefits is small and inconsistent, and cold plunges right after strength training blunt muscle gains.

dose.effective: If you do it: brief immersions (seconds to a few minutes) in cold water, with acclimatization and never alone; keep it away from (at least several hours after) strength sessions.
dose.studied_range: Winter-swimming studies over a season; post-exercise CWI 10 min after each strength session for 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: Cold shock and arrhythmia risk on sudden immersion, especially with heart disease; hypothermia.
dose.timeframe: Antioxidant adaptations seen after a winter season.
dose.notes: Each plunge itself causes acute oxidative stress; adaptation follows repetition.

entries.mechanism: Cold triggers a catecholamine surge and increased metabolic rate (brown-fat thermogenesis), generating a transient ROS pulse that may up-regulate glutathione, SOD and catalase. Post-exercise cooling reduces blood flow and anabolic signalling.
entries.interactions: Blunts adaptations to [resistance-training] if done immediately after.
entries.caveats: Winter swimmers are a self-selected healthy group; most studies are small, single-sex and uncontrolled. Reviews rate many claimed benefits as resting on weak or anecdotal data.
entries.title: Cold-water immersion and winter swimming

entries.headline: Cochrane finds possible benefit only from small, biased trials; the best-designed RCT (MOXI) showed no improvement in semen, DNA fragmentation or live birth.

dose.effective: No dose has proven benefit for live birth. If used, choose a modest-dose product (roughly vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 IU, selenium 100-200 ug, zinc 15-25 mg, folate 400-1000 ug, CoQ10 100-200 mg, L-carnitine 1-2 g) for 3 months, not stacked products.
dose.studied_range: MOXI: vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 mg, selenium 0.2 mg, L-carnitine 1000 mg, zinc 20 mg, folic acid 1000 ug, lycopene 10 mg daily for 3-6 months. Cochrane: 20 different antioxidants in 90 RCTs.
dose.too_much: Stacking several products or megadoses risks reductive stress ([high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]); antioxidants cause more mild GI upset (OR 2.70).
dose.timeframe: Trials use 3-6 months.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: counsel that supplements are of questionable clinical utility. EAU: insufficient evidence for widespread empirical use. Yet in a global survey 85.6% of reproductive specialists prescribed them.

entries.mechanism: Intended to scavenge seminal ROS and support antioxidant enzymes; only helpful if a man actually has oxidative stress and a deficiency.
entries.interactions: Not a substitute for removing the source of ROS ([tobacco-smoking], [varicocele], [genital-tract-infection]). May blunt hormetic benefits of [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
entries.caveats: Cochrane 2022: live birth OR 1.43 but very low certainty and null when high-risk-of-bias trials are removed; MOXI live birth was 15% vs 24% with placebo (not significant, small). A 6-month RCT in men with DFI >=25% also found no DFI change. Supplements may help a subgroup with proven oxidative stress, but no validated test identifies them.

key_numbers.label: Live birth OR (all trials, very low certainty)

entries.title: Combination 'male fertility' antioxidant supplements

entries.headline: In obese hypertensive adults DASH lowered blood pressure by ~8/7 mmHg, raised plasma antioxidant capacity and prevented the F2-isoprostane rise during an experimental lipid infusion.

dose.effective: 8-10 servings/day of fruit and vegetables, low-fat dairy, whole grains, nuts and legumes, low sodium and sweets.
dose.studied_range: 4 weeks per diet in a 24-person crossover study.
dose.timeframe: 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Blood pressure benefits of DASH are well established in larger trials; oxidative data are small.

entries.mechanism: High potassium, fiber and plant polyphenols; reduced sodium lowers vascular NADPH oxidase activity.
entries.interactions: Overlaps heavily with [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Oxidative-stress data come from one small study.
entries.title: DASH diet

entries.headline: Cochrane (2024, moderate certainty): DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth in poor responders (OR 1.30, NS); testosterone pre-treatment looks more promising (OR 2.53). ESHRE does not recommend DHEA.

dose.effective: Not recommended. A typical trial dose was 75 mg/day before and during the IVF cycle.
dose.studied_range: 75 mg/day (Wiser 2010) and similar regimens.
dose.too_much: Androgenic side effects (acne, hair growth); a hormone, use only under medical supervision.
dose.timeframe: Started before the IVF cycle and continued during stimulation in trials.
dose.notes: Network meta-analysis showed higher clinical pregnancy with DHEA (OR 2.46), but the larger Cochrane pooled analysis with live birth as outcome did not.

entries.mechanism: Androgen precursor proposed to increase FSH sensitivity of small antral follicles; not an antioxidant.
entries.interactions: Compare [coq10] in the same poor-responder population.
entries.caveats: Early small trials (e.g. 33 women) overstated benefit.
entries.title: DHEA in poor responders

factors.name: Dietary fiber and the gut microbiome

entries.headline: Most dietary polyphenols reach the colon and only work after gut bacteria convert them, and people differ widely in this; a fiber intake of 25-29 g/day is linked to 15-30% lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease.

dose.effective: 25-29 g fiber/day or more from varied plants (whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts).
dose.studied_range: Cohorts (185 studies) and 58 RCTs.
dose.too_much: Increase gradually to limit bloating.
dose.timeframe: Microbiome shifts in days; outcomes long-term.
dose.notes: 'High' vs 'low excretor' and 'producer vs non-producer' metabotypes (urolithins, equol) explain part of why the same food works differently in different people.

entries.mechanism: Microbial catabolism turns anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols, chlorogenic acids and ellagitannins into smaller phenolic acids, valerolactones and urolithins that are absorbed and circulate for up to 48 h; fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids that support barrier integrity and lower inflammation.
entries.interactions: Determines how much benefit you get from [blueberries], [coffee], [cocoa-flavanols], [pomegranate], [walnuts-nuts], and how much glucoraphanin converts to sulforaphane ([sulforaphane-supplements]). Antibiotics abolish microbial glucoraphanin conversion.
entries.caveats: Mechanisms are well described; direct evidence that changing the microbiome lowers systemic oxidative stress in humans is limited.

key_numbers.label: Fiber intake with greatest risk reduction
Anthocyanin relative bioavailability incl. metabolites (13C tracer)

entries.title: Dietary fiber and the gut microbiome

entries.headline: Vaping causes less oxidative stress than smoking but more than not using anything: a single e-cigarette acutely raised 8-iso-PGF2a, and dual use is worse than smoking alone.

dose.effective: Best: use neither. For a smoker who cannot otherwise quit, a complete switch lowers toxicant exposure; dual use should be avoided.
dose.studied_range: Acute single-session crossover; large cross-sectional cohort (PATH); 24-week switching RCT.
dose.too_much: Dual use (vaping plus smoking) had 9% higher F2-isoprostanes than smoking only.
dose.timeframe: Acute effects within minutes; switching changes over weeks.
dose.notes: Long-term data are still limited.

entries.mechanism: Heated propylene glycol/glycerol forms carbonyls (formaldehyde, acrolein), and coils release metals; nicotine activates NOX2. Exposure to radicals is far lower than from combustion.
entries.interactions: Only reduces harm versus [tobacco-smoking] if it fully replaces cigarettes.
entries.caveats: Long-term independent data are limited; the acute study tested one session in healthy adults, and the cohort data are cross-sectional.
entries.title: E-cigarettes (vaping)

entries.headline: Eggplant skin's nasunin is a strong superoxide scavenger and iron chelator in test tubes, and the flesh is rich in chlorogenic acid, but there is no human evidence that eggplant lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: No human dose for oxidative stress exists; eat it as a normal vegetable with the skin on.
dose.studied_range: One RCT used 1.2 g/day eggplant powder for 12 weeks (blood pressure outcome, attributed to acetylcholine, not antioxidants).
dose.timeframe: Unknown.
dose.notes: Phenol-Explorer has only a Folin value (61 mg/100 g) for whole purple eggplant. Chlorogenic acid is the dominant phenolic (>65% of phenolic acids) but content varies widely by cultivar and fruit segment. Frying in oil soaks up a lot of fat.

entries.mechanism: In vitro: nasunin (delphinidin-3-(p-coumaroylrutinoside)-5-glucoside) scavenges superoxide and inhibits hydroxyl radical generation mainly by chelating ferrous iron; chlorogenic acid is metabolised much like coffee chlorogenic acids.
entries.interactions: Chlorogenic acid overlaps with [coffee], which supplies far more per serving.
entries.caveats: The nasunin data are from rat brain homogenate and ESR assays at micromolar concentrations that dietary anthocyanins do not reach intact in human tissues. A 12-week RCT of eggplant powder lowered blood pressure in stressed adults, but the authors attribute it to choline esters (acetylcholine), not antioxidants.
entries.title: Eggplant (skin: nasunin; flesh: chlorogenic acid)

entries.headline: Endometriosis is an inflammatory, pro-oxidant condition linked to fewer and less mature eggs and lower oocyte mitochondrial content, but women with endometrioma have similar IVF live birth rates (OR 0.98) once eggs are retrieved.

dose.effective: Specialist management; surgery for endometrioma before IVF did not improve live birth (OR 0.90) and may reduce ovarian reserve.
dose.notes: Discuss fertility preservation and surgery timing with a reproductive specialist.

entries.mechanism: Peritoneal and follicular inflammation, iron from repeated bleeding (free-iron Fenton chemistry) and granulosa-cell ROS impair follicle development and oocyte maturation.
entries.interactions: Antioxidant supplements have been tried, but none has convincing live-birth data ([female-antioxidant-supplements]).
entries.caveats: Evidence on egg quality is mostly from small biological studies; the main clinical effect is fewer oocytes and more cancelled cycles rather than lower live birth per transfer.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, endometrioma vs none

entries.title: Endometriosis

entries.headline: Fat mass tracks systemic oxidative stress. BMI was one of the strongest independent correlates of urinary F2-isoprostanes in 2,828 Framingham participants, through adipose NADPH oxidase and inflammation.

dose.effective: Reducing excess fat mass (see lifestyle area for specifics).
dose.timeframe: Not specified in these studies
dose.notes: Mechanistic and cross-sectional human evidence. Intervention data are covered by the lifestyle area.

entries.mechanism: In expanded adipose tissue, free fatty acids activate NADPH oxidase and antioxidant enzymes fall, raising ROS. This disrupts adipokines (lower adiponectin, higher IL-6, MCP-1 and PAI-1) and drives systemic low-grade inflammation through NF-kB. Nutrient excess also raises mitochondrial superoxide.
entries.interactions: Compounds [glycemic-control] and [chronic-inflammation]. Supplements do not offset it.
entries.caveats: Most human data are associations. The causal chain is supported by mouse NOX-inhibitor experiments.
entries.title: Excess body fat (especially visceral adiposity)

entries.headline: Obese men are more often infertile and have lower IVF live-birth rates; the BMI-SDF link is real but smaller and less consistent than for smoking or varicocele.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30, ideally 18.5-25; waist reduction matters more than the scale number.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories from <18.5 to >=40.
dose.too_much: Risk rises steeply above BMI 35-40 (odds of oligo/azoospermia 2.04 in morbid obesity). Impaired glucose tolerance was linked to +13.8 points SDF.
dose.timeframe: Lifestyle weight loss over 3-6 months has improved semen in trials.
dose.notes: Very underweight (BMI <18.5) also trends toward worse semen.

entries.mechanism: Excess adipose tissue raises aromatase activity (lower testosterone, higher estradiol), systemic inflammation and insulin resistance, increases scrotal fat and temperature, and raises seminal ROS.
entries.interactions: Improves with [weight-loss], [aerobic-exercise-moderate] and [mediterranean-diet]. Often co-occurs with poor sleep and sugary drinks.
entries.caveats: In the SDF meta-analysis only class I obesity showed a small, borderline increase (SMD 0.23). Confounding by diet, activity and diabetes is substantial.

key_numbers.label: Odds of infertility, obese vs normal weight
ART live birth per cycle, obese men

entries.title: Obesity and metabolic dysfunction

entries.headline: Obesity (BMI >= 30) is associated with about 15% lower IVF live birth (RR 0.85), worse with PCOS, and with an inflamed, lipid-rich follicular environment.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30 and ideally 18.5-24.9; in PCOS, even 5% weight loss improved hormones and cycles.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories 18.5-24.9 vs >= 30 kg/m2 in meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Underweight (BMI < 18.5) and very low energy availability also impair ovulation (see [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]).
dose.timeframe: Follicular environment reflects the preceding ~3 months.
dose.notes: Donor-egg data did not change the overall conclusion, suggesting both egg and uterine effects.

entries.mechanism: Higher follicular fluid insulin, triglycerides, lactate and CRP; lipid accumulation in oocytes causes ER stress, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and cumulus-cell apoptosis (lipotoxicity).
entries.interactions: Compounds [pcos] and [glycemic-control]. Weight-loss evidence is in [weight-loss]. Vigorous exercise was not harmful in women with BMI >= 25 ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).
entries.caveats: Associations are confounded by PCOS and metabolic disease. Weight-loss RCTs before IVF have not raised IVF live birth (see [weight-loss]).

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, BMI >= 30 vs normal

entries.title: Obesity (BMI 30 or higher)

entries.headline: Outside testosterone shuts down the brain's signal (LH/FSH) to the testes and can drop sperm counts to zero; recovery takes months to over a year.

dose.effective: Any exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid, including gels, injections and 'cycles'.
dose.studied_range: Androgen regimens used for male contraception reliably suppress sperm output.
dose.too_much: Long-term, high-dose and long-acting preparations recover slowest.
dose.timeframe: Median recovery to 20 million/mL about 3.4 months after contraceptive-style androgen use; after steroid abuse, often 6-12+ months, sometimes incomplete.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: do not prescribe testosterone to men who want current or future fertility. Do not stop abruptly without medical advice; urologists can use hCG, SERMs or aromatase inhibitors to restart production.

entries.mechanism: Negative feedback suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH; intratesticular testosterone collapses, halting spermatogenesis (endocrine, not primarily oxidative).
entries.interactions: Overrides any benefit from diet or supplements. Often combined with other harmful exposures in body-building (high-dose supplements, stimulants).
entries.caveats: Not an SDF factor in the usual sense: it mainly lowers sperm number, often to azoospermia. Included because it is the most common avoidable cause of severe male-factor infertility in young men.
entries.title: Exogenous testosterone (TRT) and anabolic-androgenic steroids

entries.headline: In the 200-man EUROLIVE RCT, oxidized LDL fell linearly with olive-oil phenolic content at 25 mL/day; EU law authorises an LDL-protection claim for oils supplying 5 mg hydroxytyrosol and derivatives per 20 g, and PREDIMED's EVOO arm cut major CVD events by ~30%.

dose.effective: 20-25 g (about 2 tablespoons) per day of a high-phenolic EVOO meeting >= 5 mg hydroxytyrosol + derivatives per 20 g.
dose.studied_range: 25 mL/day for 3 weeks (EUROLIVE); ~1 L/week per household in PREDIMED for years.
dose.too_much: Calories (about 120 kcal per tablespoon).
dose.timeframe: Measurable LDL changes within 3 weeks.
dose.notes: Use as the main culinary fat, raw on food or for moderate-heat cooking; phenolics decline with storage, light and heat. Refined olive oil has a fraction of the phenolics.

entries.mechanism: Hydroxytyrosol and its secoiridoid precursors (oleacein/3,4-DHPEA-EDA, oleuropein aglycone) bind to LDL and protect its lipids from oxidation; high oleic acid content makes membranes and LDL less oxidizable than PUFA-rich oils; modest Nrf2 and anti-inflammatory effects.
entries.interactions: Best evidence when it replaces butter, refined seed oils or [oxidized-frying-oils]. Improves carotenoid absorption from [tomatoes-lycopene] and [leafy-greens]. Core component of [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Short trials use LDL oxidation markers rather than outcomes; PREDIMED was re-analysed after randomisation irregularities (results held). Phenolic content varies enormously between oils and labels rarely state it.

entries.title: Extra-virgin olive oil (high-phenolic)

entries.headline: Age is by far the dominant, non-modifiable driver of egg quality: fecundity falls from about 32 and faster after 37, and the share of women with no chromosomally normal embryo rises from 2-6% (age 26-37) to 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.

dose.effective: Not modifiable. The practical lever is time: ACOG/ASRM advise expedited evaluation after 6 months of trying from age 35, and immediate evaluation over 40.
dose.studied_range: Aneuploidy data from embryos of women aged ~22-47; egg chromosome-segregation data from ages 9-43.
dose.timeframe: Gradual decline from the early 30s, steep after ~37; no lifestyle change reverses it.
dose.notes: Lifestyle can avoid adding damage on top of age, but no diet or supplement has been shown to restore the chromosomal quality of older eggs in humans. Egg freezing at a younger age and IVF with PGT-A or donor eggs are the only interventions that address age directly.

entries.mechanism: Eggs are arrested in meiosis for decades. Cohesin that holds sister chromatids together is laid down before birth and is not renewed, so it erodes with age, causing chromosome mis-segregation (aneuploidy). In parallel, oocyte mitochondria become less efficient (less ATP, more mtDNA instability), CoQ10-synthesis enzymes and NAD+ levels decline (animal data), and spindle assembly becomes error-prone.
entries.interactions: Age magnifies almost every other harm: [tobacco-smoking] and [excess-adiposity] effects are layered on a declining baseline. Diet associations such as [mediterranean-diet] were seen only in women under 35 in one cohort. Supplements aimed at mitochondria ([coq10], [nmn-nad]) target the age mechanism but have no human live-birth proof.
entries.caveats: Aneuploidy also rises slightly in the very young (U-curve), but this is a minor effect compared with the rise after the mid-30s. Ovarian reserve tests (AMH, antral follicle count) predict egg number and response to stimulation, not egg quality; a woman with high AMH at 42 still has age-typical aneuploidy rates. Claims that any supplement 'reverses egg ageing' are not supported by human data.

key_numbers.label: Age at which fecundity starts falling

entries.title: Female age (oocyte ageing)

factors.name: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)

entries.headline: A fever of 39-40 C for even 2 days can raise DNA fragmentation and cut sperm count for 2-3 months before recovering.

dose.effective: Body temperature around 38.5-40 C for 1 day or more.
dose.studied_range: Case report: 2 days at 39-40 C followed for 79 days.
dose.timeframe: DFI up 24-36% at days 15-37, back toward baseline by about day 79; plan semen tests or ART cycles at least ~3 months after a high fever if possible.
dose.notes: Fever control with paracetamol/acetaminophen is reasonable; there is no evidence that it prevents the sperm effect.

entries.mechanism: Whole-body hyperthermia warms the testes, impairing late spermatogenesis and chromatin protamination and increasing heat-shock and apoptotic signalling.
entries.interactions: Same mechanism as [sauna]. A semen test taken within 3 months of a fever may overstate long-term problems.
entries.caveats: Evidence is mostly case reports and small series; the effect is temporary.
entries.title: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)

entries.headline: The largest male supplement trial (FAZST, 2370 couples) found folic acid plus zinc did nothing for semen or live birth, and slightly raised DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Not recommended for male fertility.
dose.studied_range: 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg elemental zinc daily for 6 months.
dose.too_much: SDF 29.7% vs 27.2% with placebo (+2.4 points); more GI symptoms. Long-term zinc above ~40 mg/day can cause copper deficiency.
dose.timeframe: 6 months studied.
dose.notes: Correcting a genuine zinc or folate deficiency via diet is still sensible.

entries.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism and DNA methylation; zinc stabilises sperm chromatin and is an antioxidant enzyme cofactor. High doses did not help replete men.
entries.interactions: High-dose folate overlaps with [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail] concerns.
entries.caveats: Population was general infertility patients, not selected for deficiency.
entries.title: Folic acid + zinc

entries.headline: Folic acid is mandatory preconception care (400-800 ug/day prevents neural tube defects) and is also consistently associated with better fertility: 15% higher fecundability and 20 percentage points higher IVF live birth at > 800 ug/day supplemental folate.

dose.effective: 400-800 ug/day folic acid, started before conception (ideally 3 months ahead) and continued through early pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: Supplemental folate < 400 to > 800 ug/day (cohorts).
dose.too_much: Higher doses only on a clinician's advice for specific indications.
dose.timeframe: Before conception for neural tube protection; 3 months covers follicle development.
dose.notes: Usually taken as a prenatal multivitamin. Diet folate (leafy greens, legumes) is good but does not replace the supplement.

entries.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism: DNA synthesis and repair, methylation and homocysteine clearance. Elevated homocysteine in follicular fluid is linked to poorer embryo quality.
entries.interactions: Core of [profertility-diet]; may buffer the [outdoor-air-pollution] association in one cohort.
entries.caveats: Fertility benefits are observational; the neural-tube benefit is RCT-proven and reason enough to take it.
entries.title: Folic acid / folate

entries.headline: Ejaculating every 1-2 days keeps sperm fresher: each extra day of abstinence adds about 0.65 points of SDF, and a second sample 3 hours after the first cut SDF from 35% to 24%.

dose.effective: Ejaculate (intercourse or otherwise) every 1-2 days through the fertile window and beyond. For ART with high SDF, ask about a sample after 1 day or a second sample 1-4 hours after a first ejaculation.
dose.studied_range: Abstinence from 1-4 hours to 7+ days; 2-day cut-off in RCT meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Volume and total count fall with very frequent ejaculation, but for natural conception daily intercourse is not harmful.
dose.timeframe: Immediate: works on the next ejaculate.
dose.notes: Diagnostic labs usually specify 2-7 days of abstinence and SDF guidelines suggest 2-5 days before a test; follow the lab's instructions when testing, and use short abstinence for conception attempts and ART samples.

entries.mechanism: Shortens the time sperm sit in the epididymis, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS and stored sperm accumulate oxidative DNA damage.
entries.interactions: Cheapest and fastest lever; a non-invasive alternative to [testicular-sperm-icsi]. Works alongside slower changes that act on sperm production.
entries.caveats: One large meta-analysis of risk factors found no significant abstinence effect, and absolute reductions in healthy men are small (about 2-3 points). The biggest drops are in men with high baseline SDF or abnormal semen.

key_numbers.label: SDF increase per extra day of abstinence
SDF in second sample 3 h later

entries.title: Frequent ejaculation (short abstinence, 1-2 days)

entries.headline: Doubling produce from 5.8 to 12 servings/day for 2 weeks reduced lymphocyte 8-OHdG and urinary isoprostanes, but another controlled trial found 600 g/day had no effect on oxidative DNA damage in healthy non-smokers; cohorts show lower mortality up to ~800 g/day.

dose.effective: At least 5 servings (400-500 g)/day, ideally up to ~800 g, from diverse botanical families.
dose.studied_range: 600 g/day for 24 days; 12 servings/day for 14 days.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Diversity across plant families mattered in the positive trial; benefit was larger in people with low baseline carotenoids.

entries.mechanism: Many compounds acting through different routes (Nrf2 electrophiles, gut metabolites, vitamin C/carotenoids, nitrate, fiber, potassium).
entries.interactions: The null Danish trial suggests healthy people with adequate defences may already be near a ceiling for oxidative DNA damage.
entries.caveats: Oxidative-marker trials conflict; cohort benefits may partly reflect healthier lifestyles.

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality RR per 200 g/day fruit and vegetables

entries.title: High fruit and vegetable intake

entries.headline: Low-pesticide fruit and vegetables (2.8+ servings a day) are linked to much higher sperm counts; high-residue produce is not.

dose.effective: At least 3 servings/day; wash produce and favour lower-residue choices.
dose.studied_range: <1.1 to >=2.8 servings/day of low-to-moderate-residue produce.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Benefit is likely part of the overall dietary pattern.

entries.mechanism: Food-level vitamin C, folate, carotenoids and polyphenols support seminal antioxidant defences without the megadoses that cause reductive stress.
entries.interactions: See [pesticides] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Total fruit and vegetable intake was unrelated to semen in the same study; the finding depended on pesticide residue classification.

key_numbers.label: Higher total count, >=2.8 servings/day low-residue produce

entries.title: Fruit and vegetables

entries.headline: Garlic supplements lower blood pressure in hypertensives (about -8.7/-6.1 mmHg) and a meta-analysis of 12 small RCTs reports lower MDA and higher antioxidant enzymes, but these markers are weak and the trials low quality.

dose.effective: Culinary: 1-2 cloves/day crushed and left 10 min before cooking; supplement trials used aged garlic extract or powder.
dose.studied_range: 80-4000 mg/day garlic preparations for 2-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Supplements can increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Red onions are a major dietary source of quercetin (onion chromatography total ~140 mg/100 g in Phenol-Explorer).

entries.mechanism: Organosulfur compounds (allicin breakdown products, S-allylcysteine) activate Nrf2 and raise hydrogen sulfide signalling; onion quercetin.
entries.interactions: Another mild Nrf2 inducer; much weaker than sulforaphane.
entries.caveats: TAC and TBARS-type MDA are non-specific oxidative markers; effect sizes in the meta-analysis (Hedges' g up to 13.8) are implausibly large, a sign of small heterogeneous studies.

key_numbers.label: Onion (red), total polyphenols, chromatography (sum of compounds)

entries.title: Garlic and onions

entries.headline: Active infection (e.g. Chlamydia, Mycoplasma) and white cells in semen raise ROS and SDF; treating a proven infection can lower SDF by about a third.

dose.effective: Leukocytospermia is defined as >=1 million white cells/mL; even 0.2-1 million/mL has been linked to higher ROS and SDF.
dose.studied_range: Antibiotic courses guided by culture/PCR; follow-up about 4 months.
dose.timeframe: In one study SDF fell from 37.7% to 24.2% after ~3.8 months of treatment; pregnancy rates were higher in couples who tried after rather than during treatment.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: if round cells exceed 1 million/mL, distinguish white cells from immature germ cells before treating. Treat confirmed infection; do not give empiric antibiotics for every abnormal semen test.

entries.mechanism: Activated neutrophils and macrophages produce superoxide via NADPH oxidase (NOX2) at rates far above sperm, overwhelming seminal antioxidants and attacking sperm membranes and DNA.
entries.interactions: [febrile-illness] from the same infection adds thermal damage. Antioxidants are not a substitute for treating infection.
entries.caveats: A large meta-analysis found overall effects of Chlamydia and HPV on SDF negligible, so the strongest data are from symptomatic or culture-positive cases. Evidence comes from small observational studies.
entries.title: Genital tract infection and leukocytospermia

entries.headline: In older adults with low glutathione, glycine plus NAC restored glutathione, lowered F2-isoprostanes and in a 24-person RCT improved mitochondrial, metabolic and physical-function measures. The trials are small and mostly from one group.

dose.effective: Glycine 1.33 mmol/kg/day + cysteine 0.81 mmol/kg/day as NAC (roughly 100 mg/kg glycine + 130 mg/kg NAC; ~7 g + ~9 g/day at 70 kg)
dose.studied_range: Same weight-based dose for 2 weeks to 24 weeks
dose.too_much: Long-term safety beyond 24 weeks not established; same cancer caveat as NAC.
dose.timeframe: Changes reported at 16-24 weeks; benefits declined within 12 weeks of stopping
dose.notes: Relevant mainly to older adults; young adults already have normal glutathione synthesis.

entries.mechanism: Supplies both limiting precursors (cysteine and glycine) for glutathione synthesis, which is reduced with aging. This restores GSH concentration and synthesis rate and lowers oxidative damage.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [n-acetylcysteine]. Probably redundant in people with high protein intake and normal glutathione.
entries.caveats: Evidence comes from small open-label and placebo-controlled trials from a single research group, with no hard outcomes. The large doses are not those in typical over-the-counter products.
entries.title: Glycine + N-acetylcysteine (GlyNAC)

entries.headline: Four cups a day of decaffeinated green tea cut urinary 8-OHdG by 31% in heavy smokers over 4 months, and 4 cups/day lowered plasma MDA/HNE in metabolic syndrome; evidence in healthy non-smokers is weak.

dose.effective: About 4 cups (~1 L) per day of brewed green tea.
dose.studied_range: 4 cups/day for 8 weeks to 4 months.
dose.too_much: Brewed tea is considered safe at usual intakes (90-300 mg EGCG/day; heavy drinkers up to ~866 mg/day); rare idiosyncratic liver injury reported. See [green-tea-extract] for the supplement risk.
dose.timeframe: Weeks to months.
dose.notes: EGCG bioavailability is low and variable; plasma half-life ~3.4 h. Ring-fission valerolactone metabolites appear 3-15 h later.

entries.mechanism: Catechins (EGCG, EGC, EC) and their microbial valerolactone metabolites; at physiological doses mild Nrf2 signalling and effects on endothelium rather than plasma radical scavenging.
entries.interactions: Flavan-3-ols overlap with [cocoa-flavanols]. Tea with meals reduces non-heme iron absorption (relevant to [iron-excess] and to iron-deficient people).
entries.caveats: The smoker trial used decaf tea and showed no benefit for black tea. Smokers have high baseline oxidative damage, so the effect may not generalise.

key_numbers.label: Urinary 8-OHdG change in smokers (4 cups/day, 4 months)

entries.title: Green tea (brewed)

entries.headline: Claims that touching the ground supplies 'antioxidant electrons' have no credible mechanism and rest on small, mostly unblinded studies by proponents.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Walking barefoot outdoors is harmless and pleasant if you enjoy it.
dose.studied_range: Small studies of grounding mats/patches over nights to weeks.
dose.notes: No validated oxidative biomarker improvement in rigorous trials.

entries.mechanism: Proposed mechanism (free electrons neutralizing radicals) is not physiologically plausible: radical chemistry occurs inside cells and is buffered by enzymes and glutathione.
entries.interactions: None.
entries.caveats: The main review is by advocates; independent replication is lacking.
entries.title: Grounding / earthing

entries.headline: Chronic periodontitis is associated with lower systemic antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde, and periodontal treatment lowers oxidative markers.

dose.effective: Brush twice daily, clean between teeth daily, and get professional cleaning and periodontal treatment if gums bleed or recede.
dose.studied_range: Non-surgical periodontal therapy studies with >=6 weeks follow-up.
dose.timeframe: Markers improved within 6 weeks to months after treatment.
dose.notes: Smoking and diabetes strongly worsen periodontitis.

entries.mechanism: Chronic bacterial infection recruits neutrophils that release superoxide, hypochlorous acid and other oxidants locally, with spill-over systemic inflammation.
entries.interactions: Worsened by [tobacco-smoking] and poor [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Most data are from saliva and gum fluid; systemic effects are less consistent and few trials are randomized.
entries.title: Gum disease (periodontitis)

entries.headline: Toxic metals deplete glutathione and drive oxidative damage; even at normal background levels, urinary cadmium tracked oxidative DNA damage in non-smokers.

dose.effective: Do not smoke (the main cadmium source); test well water for arsenic; check old homes for lead paint and pipes; choose low-mercury fish (salmon, sardines) over high-mercury species (swordfish, king mackerel, shark).
dose.studied_range: Observational studies at background and occupational exposure levels.
dose.too_much: Occupational exposures and contaminated water are the main high-dose risks.
dose.timeframe: Body burdens of cadmium and lead decline slowly (years).
dose.notes: Chelation 'detox' for people without documented poisoning is not supported.

entries.mechanism: Cadmium, lead and arsenic bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inhibit antioxidant enzymes; redox-active metals (iron, copper) generate hydroxyl radical via Fenton chemistry; arsenic can generate H2O2.
entries.interactions: Cadmium exposure is largely from [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Spot-urine biomarker studies are prone to confounding: in one study the strongest metal associations were for essential selenium and copper.
entries.title: Heavy metals: lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury

entries.headline: Higher follicular-fluid mercury (above ~0.5 ug/L) and lead were associated with lower IVF live birth (lead RR 0.68) in a small study; cadmium exposure comes mainly from smoking.

dose.effective: Favour smaller, lower-mercury fish over large predatory fish (e.g. shark, swordfish); do not smoke (main cadmium source).
dose.studied_range: Follicular fluid Hg, Pb, Cd, As in 56 IVF patients.
dose.too_much: Follicular fluid Hg > ~0.51 ug/L associated with lower biochemical pregnancy and live birth.
dose.notes: Keep eating fish: the omega-3 benefit is real; choose low-mercury species.

entries.mechanism: Metals bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inactivate antioxidant enzymes; cadmium and lead can displace essential metals and promote Fenton-type ROS generation.
entries.interactions: Trades off against [omega3-fish] (fish is the main source of both); [tobacco-smoking] supplies cadmium.
entries.caveats: One small cohort; associations were non-linear and imprecise.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, higher follicular lead

entries.title: Heavy metals (mercury, lead, cadmium)

factors.name: Heavy vigorous exercise & low energy availability (women)

entries.headline: In lean women, 5 or more hours a week of vigorous exercise was associated with about 32% lower monthly chance of conception; exercising to exhaustion or on most days was linked to 2-3 times the odds of fertility problems.

dose.effective: If trying to conceive and lean, cap vigorous exercise below ~5 h/week and swap some for moderate activity; eat enough to keep regular cycles.
dose.studied_range: Vigorous activity 0 to >= 5 h/week (Danish cohort); frequency/intensity categories (Norwegian cohort).
dose.too_much: >= 5 h/week vigorous: FR 0.68 in lean women; exercising most days: 3.2-fold odds of fertility problems; exercising to exhaustion: 2.3-fold.
dose.timeframe: Cycle recovery after restoring energy balance can take months.
dose.notes: Missed or irregular periods in an active woman are a red flag for low energy availability (hypothalamic suppression).

entries.mechanism: Low energy availability suppresses GnRH pulsatility (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea), lowering estrogen and ovulation; this is an energy-signalling problem more than an oxidative one.
entries.interactions: No adverse association in women with BMI >= 25, for whom activity helps ([aerobic-exercise-moderate], [weight-loss]). Different from acute oxidative damage after ultra-endurance events ([overtraining-ultraendurance]); in general health, vigorous exercise in normal amounts is beneficial ([hiit-vigorous-exercise]).
entries.caveats: Observational and self-reported; vigorous exercise was not associated with worse IVF outcomes in the EARTH cohort.
entries.title: Very intense exercise and low energy availability (RED-S)

factors.name: Herbs and spices (oregano, rosemary, cloves, cinnamon, etc.)

entries.headline: Their biggest proven effect is in the pan: a polyphenol-rich spice mix cut malondialdehyde in cooked burgers by 71% and in the eaters' urine by 49%, and herb marinades cut heterocyclic amines in grilled steak by 57-88%.

dose.effective: Generous use in cooking, especially in meat dishes and marinades (about a tablespoon of dried herbs per meal); 14 g spice blend in a meal in one trial.
dose.studied_range: Single meals; marinating steaks 1 h before grilling at 204 °C.
dose.too_much: None established at culinary amounts.
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Per gram, dried cloves, oregano and other herbs top every polyphenol table, but servings are small.

entries.mechanism: Rosmarinic acid, carnosic acid and carnosol inhibit lipid oxidation and Maillard/HCA chemistry in food and in the stomach, so fewer oxidized lipids are absorbed; a spice blend also lowered postprandial insulin and triglycerides.
entries.interactions: Counteracts [high-temperature-cooking] and [processed-red-meat] oxidation products. Here direct scavenging is plausible because the reaction happens in the food and gut, where concentrations are high.
entries.caveats: Meal studies are tiny (n=6-11) and short.

key_numbers.label: MDA reduction in spiced vs plain burger meat
Urinary MDA reduction after spiced burger
Total HCA reduction, Caribbean herb marinade

entries.title: Herbs and spices (oregano, rosemary, cloves, cinnamon, etc.)

entries.headline: In type 2 diabetes, urinary 8-iso-PGF2α tracked glucose variability (r = 0.86) and post-meal glucose, not HbA1c. Hyperglycaemia drives mitochondrial superoxide and AGE formation.

dose.effective: Limit post-meal glucose excursions and keep glucose in the normal range (see food and lifestyle areas).
dose.timeframe: Acute: postprandial window (hours); chronic: years
dose.notes: Dietary AGEs from dry-heat cooking add to the endogenous load (10- to 100-fold more than uncooked).

entries.mechanism: Excess glucose makes the mitochondrial ETC overproduce superoxide, which activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways. AGEs bind RAGE, activating NOX and NF-kB. Postprandial hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia transiently raise oxidative stress and impair endothelial function.
entries.interactions: Compounds [excess-adiposity]. Antioxidants taken with a meal can attenuate postprandial oxidative stress, but this has not translated into supplement benefits.
entries.caveats: The Monnier study is small (21 patients). The extent to which glucose swings matter in non-diabetic people is less established.
entries.title: High blood glucose and post-meal glucose spikes

entries.headline: Type 2 diabetes was associated with ~75% higher urinary 8-iso-PGF2a, which tracked day-to-day glucose swings (r = 0.86) more than HbA1c; reducing glucose spikes is a meaningful lever.

dose.effective: Keep fasting glucose and HbA1c in the normal range (individualized targets with diabetes); limit post-meal spikes with fibre-rich whole foods, fewer refined carbohydrates, and a short walk after meals.
dose.studied_range: Case-control comparison using continuous glucose monitoring.
dose.too_much: Large post-meal excursions and sustained hyperglycemia.
dose.timeframe: Glucose swings respond within days; HbA1c over ~3 months.
dose.notes: Exercise and weight loss are the main non-drug tools.

entries.mechanism: High glucose overloads mitochondria, causing superoxide overproduction that activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways; AGE-RAGE binding further activates NADPH oxidase and NF-kB.
entries.interactions: Improved by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [resistance-training], [weight-loss] and [short-sleep] correction.
entries.caveats: Monnier 2006 was small (21 patients); the 'swings matter more than average glucose' idea is supported mechanistically but outcome trials targeting variability are limited.
entries.title: Blood-sugar control and diabetes
