entries.headline: Women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes have 24-36% lower fecundability; in mice, maternal diabetes damages oocyte mitochondria and raises egg aneuploidy.

dose.effective: Good glycaemic control before conception (managed with the diabetes team); weight loss and physical activity for insulin resistance.
dose.timeframe: Preconception optimisation over at least 3 months covers one full cycle of follicle growth.
dose.notes: Preconception glucose control is also critical for reducing birth-defect risk.

entries.mechanism: Hyperglycaemia increases mitochondrial superoxide and advanced glycation end-products; in diabetic mice oocytes show abnormal mitochondrial structure, lower ATP and TCA metabolites, spindle defects and aneuploidy, and the defective mitochondria are passed to the embryo.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [excess-adiposity] and [pcos].
entries.caveats: Oocyte mechanism data are from animals; human data are fecundability associations.
entries.title: Diabetes and insulin resistance

entries.headline: Pooled over 78 RCTs, antioxidant supplements did not lower mortality and slightly raised it in low-bias trials (RR 1.04). A 20,536-person trial of vitamin E + C + beta-carotene found no effect at all. Around exercise they block training benefits.

dose.effective: None.
dose.studied_range: e.g. vitamin E 600 mg + C 250 mg + beta-carotene 20 mg/day (HPS); vitamin C 1,000 mg + E 400 IU/day (exercise studies)
dose.too_much: Any dose at these levels: no benefit; beta-carotene, vitamin A and vitamin E components carry the documented harms.
dose.timeframe: Exercise-blunting effect within 4 weeks; mortality signal over years
dose.notes: Raising blood vitamin levels does not mean oxidative damage was reduced; HPS raised levels 'substantially' with zero outcome change.

entries.mechanism: Suppresses ROS signals needed for adaptation (insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis, endogenous antioxidant enzyme induction). In tumours, lowering ROS can release p53-dependent brakes and increase metastasis (mouse data). Endogenous enzymatic defences do not respond to extra dietary antioxidants once someone is replete.
entries.interactions: Antagonises the adaptive (hormetic) benefits of exercise. Contains [vitamin-e-supplement] and [beta-carotene-supplement] harms. Redundant with endogenous defences.
entries.caveats: Marketing often cites ORAC or 'total antioxidant capacity' values, which USDA abandoned in 2012 because they have no demonstrated in-vivo relevance.
entries.title: High-dose 'antioxidant formula' supplements (vitamin C + E + beta-carotene/A, etc.)

entries.headline: Too much antioxidant can loosen sperm chromatin: one study saw DFI fall 19% but decondensation rise 23%, and high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: Avoid taking several fertility products at once or doses well above the RDA (e.g. vitamin C >1 g, zinc >40 mg, folic acid >1 mg) without a specific indication.
dose.studied_range: Antioxidant vitamins with zinc and selenium for 90 days (human); dose-escalation of vitamin C, zinc, folate, carnitine (mice).
dose.too_much: This factor is the 'too much' end of [male-antioxidant-combination].
dose.timeframe: Over one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: FAZST's small SDF increase with 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg zinc is consistent with this concern.

entries.mechanism: Sperm chromatin compaction depends on oxidative formation of protamine disulphide bridges in the epididymis, and capacitation needs a controlled ROS burst. Excess reductants (especially vitamin C) can reduce these disulphide bonds and blunt physiological ROS signalling.
entries.interactions: Opposes the benefits sought from [male-antioxidant-combination] and [vitamin-c-e-combined]; also relevant to [l-carnitine].
entries.caveats: Human evidence is one small uncontrolled study plus indirect trial data; the mouse data may not transfer. Plausible but unproven.
entries.title: Megadose or stacked antioxidants ('reductive stress')

entries.headline: EFSA (2018) concluded that 800 mg EGCG/day or more from supplements significantly raises liver transaminases in RCTs; extracts also cause rare severe liver injury, especially in multi-ingredient products.

dose.effective: No oxidative-stress benefit beyond brewed tea has been shown.
dose.studied_range: Supplements supply 5-1000 mg EGCG/day.
dose.too_much: >= 800 mg EGCG/day as a supplement (EFSA). Multi-ingredient products caused more severe injury.
dose.timeframe: Liver injury latency averaged ~6 months for green-tea-only products and ~6 weeks for multi-ingredient ones.
dose.notes: Brewed tea at traditional intakes is considered safe.

entries.mechanism: At high concentrations EGCG becomes pro-oxidant (generating H2O2) and hepatotoxic; patient susceptibility factors appear important.
entries.interactions: Do not combine with other hepatotoxic supplements.
entries.caveats: Absolute risk is low given wide use, but the dose threshold is clear from trials.

key_numbers.label: Typical EGCG from brewed green tea

entries.title: High-dose green tea extract (EGCG pills)

factors.name: High-dose vitamin C/E taken during training

entries.headline: Gram-level vitamin C plus vitamin E during training blunted molecular adaptations (insulin sensitivity in one trial, mitochondrial markers, lean mass in older men), though meta-analysis finds no clear loss of VO2max or strength.

dose.effective: Avoid routine supplementation at >=500-1000 mg vitamin C plus >=235 mg (~400 IU) vitamin E per day during training blocks; get antioxidants from food.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 500-1000 mg/day vitamin C, 235-400 IU vitamin E, for 4-12 weeks.
dose.too_much: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E/day removed the insulin-sensitivity gain from 4 weeks of training in Ristow 2009.
dose.timeframe: Effects appeared within 4-12 weeks of training.
dose.notes: Food-level intakes (fruit, vegetables) have not been shown to cause this. Correcting a true deficiency is different.

entries.mechanism: Exercise ROS are the signal that activates Nrf2, PGC-1alpha and insulin-signalling adaptations. Flooding the system with reducing agents blunts that signal, reducing induction of SOD, GPx and mitochondrial biogenesis.
entries.interactions: Directly undermines [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [resistance-training].
entries.caveats: Findings are mixed: Yfanti 2011 found no effect on insulin sensitivity, and the Clifford 2020 meta-analysis of 18 small RCTs found no significant loss of VO2max, endurance, lean mass or strength. Practical stance: no benefit, possible harm, so skip megadoses.
entries.title: High-dose vitamin C/E taken during training

entries.headline: Dry heat (grilling, broiling, roasting, frying) raises food AGEs 10-100-fold; a high-AGE meal cut flow-mediated dilation by 36% vs 21% for the same meal cooked gently, and a year on a low-AGE diet improved insulin resistance and oxidative stress markers.

dose.effective: Favour moist heat (stewing, poaching, steaming), lower temperatures and shorter times; marinate meat in acidic, herb-rich mixtures.
dose.studied_range: Single meals (15,100 vs 2,750 kU AGE); 1-year low-AGE diet in 138 obese adults with metabolic syndrome; 12 dietary AGE RCTs (293 people).
dose.too_much: Charred, well-done meat is the main HCA/PAH source.
dose.timeframe: Vascular effects within 2 h of a meal; metabolic effects over months.
dose.notes: Acidic ingredients (lemon juice, vinegar) and moist heat significantly reduced new AGE formation. Animal foods high in fat and protein are most AGE-prone; vegetables, fruit and whole grains stay low even when cooked.

entries.mechanism: Maillard reactions form AGEs (e.g. CML) that engage RAGE and activate NADPH oxidase and NF-kB; meat creatine + sugars + amino acids form heterocyclic amines; fat dripping on flames forms PAHs.
entries.interactions: Pairs with [processed-red-meat]; reduced by [herbs-spices] marinades; compounded by [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] (endogenous AGE formation).
entries.caveats: Many dietary-AGE trials come from one research group; measurement of food AGEs by ELISA is debated. The systematic review rated evidence as limited by trial quality.

key_numbers.label: FMD fall after high-AGE meal (vs 20.9% low-AGE)

entries.title: High-temperature dry cooking (AGEs, HCAs, PAHs)

entries.headline: Cycling 5 or more hours a week is linked to lower sperm concentration; moderate cycling is not a concern.

dose.effective: Under about 5 hours/week is fine; above that, use a well-fitted saddle, padded shorts and rest days.
dose.studied_range: Cycling >=5 h/week vs no regular exercise (2261 men); 16 weeks of intensive road training (24 cyclists).
dose.too_much: Intensive training raised seminal inflammatory cytokines, with some semen changes persisting 30 days after stopping.
dose.timeframe: Recovery may need more than 30 days; plan ~3 months.
dose.notes: Combine with general exercise advice ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).

entries.mechanism: Perineal pressure, scrotal heat and friction, plus inflammation and oxidative stress from very high training loads.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [everyday-scrotal-heat].
entries.caveats: Observational; the training study comes from a group with several retracted papers.

key_numbers.label: Odds of low concentration, cycling >=5 h/week

entries.title: High-volume cycling

entries.headline: Being dehydrated increased muscle H2O2 after resistance exercise in one small study; there is no evidence that drinking extra water beyond thirst lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Drink to thirst; aim for pale-yellow urine; replace fluids lost in heavy sweating.
dose.studied_range: One crossover study with 24 h fluid restriction.
dose.too_much: Overdrinking (hyponatremia) is a risk in endurance events.
dose.notes: 'Alkaline' or 'structured' water claims have no support.

entries.mechanism: Dehydration raises cell stress and may increase ROS production in exercising muscle.
entries.interactions: Relevant to [overtraining-ultraendurance] and [sauna].
entries.caveats: Evidence is a single small study; 'flushing out toxins' with water is not a real antioxidant mechanism.
entries.title: Hydration

entries.headline: Molecular hydrogen scavenges hydroxyl radicals in lab and animal studies, but human trials are small and show at most modest effects on lipids, not established oxidative-stress benefits.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Trials used ~0.5-1.5 L/day of hydrogen-rich water.
dose.studied_range: Pilot RCTs of weeks to 6 months.
dose.too_much: Appears safe.
dose.notes: Hydrogen escapes quickly from water once opened.

entries.mechanism: H2 reacts selectively with hydroxyl radical and peroxynitrite; may also signal via Nrf2. Doses from drinking water are tiny and transient.
entries.interactions: No known interactions.
entries.caveats: Most trials are small and come from a few research groups; the telomere result came from a 40-person pilot with many outcomes, and the lipid meta-analysis pooled only 7 small studies.
entries.title: Hydrogen-rich water / molecular hydrogen

factors.name: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking

entries.headline: Wood smoke at smoky-home levels raised airway oxidative stress in one chamber study but had no systemic effect in another; gas cooking is linked to childhood asthma, though the quality of that evidence is debated.

dose.effective: Use range hoods vented outdoors when cooking (especially on gas), keep wood stoves well-sealed and burning cleanly, avoid open fireplaces as daily heat, and ventilate.
dose.studied_range: Chamber studies: 3-4 h at 220-354 µg/m³ wood-smoke particles.
dose.too_much: Exposure in poorly vented homes with daily solid-fuel burning (much higher in low-income countries using biomass).
dose.timeframe: Airway markers changed within hours.
dose.notes: Electric or induction cooking removes the NO2 source.

entries.mechanism: Combustion particles and gases (NO2, aldehydes, PAHs) generate airway ROS and inflammation; NO2 is itself an oxidant.
entries.interactions: Similar pathways to [outdoor-air-pollution]; mitigated by [hepa-air-purifier] for particles.
entries.caveats: Controlled wood-smoke studies are small and inconsistent. The gas-stove literature is mostly cross-sectional; a 2013 meta-analysis found OR 1.32 for asthma while a 2023 review judged the evidence too low-quality for causal conclusions.
entries.title: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking

entries.headline: In randomized sham-controlled crossover trials, running HEPA purifiers cut indoor PM2.5 by about half and lowered oxidative and inflammatory markers (8-isoprostane, myeloperoxidase) and blood pressure within days.

dose.effective: Run a HEPA purifier sized for the room (check its clean-air delivery rate) continuously in the bedroom and main living space when outdoor or indoor PM2.5 is elevated, with windows closed.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 48 h to 1 week of real vs sham purification in dormitories with outdoor PM2.5 roughly 40-100 µg/m³.
dose.timeframe: Effects within 48 h to 1 week; they disappear when purification stops.
dose.notes: Benefits are largest where indoor air is polluted; in clean-air regions the gain is small.

entries.mechanism: Removes redox-active particles before they reach the lungs, reducing airway NADPH-oxidase activation, inflammatory cell activation and systemic lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: Counters [outdoor-air-pollution] and [indoor-combustion-smoke]; does not remove gases like NO2 unless the unit has activated carbon.
entries.caveats: Trials were short, in young healthy Chinese students exposed to high pollution; long-term clinical outcomes are not yet shown.
entries.title: Indoor HEPA air purification

entries.headline: Industrial trans fats raise LDL, lower HDL, promote systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, and carry a higher coronary risk per gram than any other fat.

dose.effective: As close to zero as possible from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts and controlled feeding studies.
dose.too_much: Any regular intake from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.timeframe: Years.
dose.notes: Now banned or restricted in many countries; still present in some imported or older products.

entries.mechanism: Altered lipoprotein metabolism and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), endothelial dysfunction.
entries.interactions: Often co-occurs with [oxidized-frying-oils] in fried fast food.
entries.caveats: The oxidative-stress component is one part of a broader cardiometabolic harm.
entries.title: Industrial trans fats

entries.headline: Early time-restricted feeding (6-hour window, dinner before 3 pm) lowered plasma 8-isoprostane ~14% vs a 12-hour schedule without weight loss in 8 men with prediabetes; an uncontrolled alternate-day trial reported large falls in oxidative markers with 8% weight loss.

dose.effective: Eating within an early daytime window, or alternate-day restriction, if sustainable.
dose.studied_range: 5-week supervised crossover (n=8); 8-week alternate-day (n=10).
dose.too_much: Not for pregnancy, diabetes on insulin/sulfonylureas without supervision, or eating disorders.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: In the eTRF trial the improvement came mostly from oxidative stress worsening on the control schedule.

entries.mechanism: Metabolic switching to ketones, circadian alignment of meals, reduced postprandial load, weight loss.
entries.interactions: Effects largely overlap with [calorie-restriction] when weight is lost.
entries.caveats: Very small trials; 8-isoprostane by ELISA is less reliable than mass-spectrometry methods.
entries.title: Intermittent fasting / time-restricted eating

entries.headline: IV glutathione is cleared from blood with a half-life of ~14 minutes; oral glutathione raised blood stores 17-35% in one 6-month RCT, but no trial shows clinical benefit for oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Not recommended. Oral trial used 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months; levels returned to baseline within a month of stopping.
dose.studied_range: IV: single 2 g/m² infusion pharmacokinetics; oral: 6-month RCT.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown; usual infusion risks apply to IV use.
dose.timeframe: IV effect gone within about an hour; oral effect builds over months and reverses within a month.
dose.notes: Cells make their own glutathione from cysteine, glycine and glutamate; exercise, sleep and not smoking support it.

entries.mechanism: Exogenous glutathione is broken down in plasma and by gamma-glutamyl transferase into amino acids; cells resynthesize glutathione internally.
entries.interactions: Lifestyle factors that preserve glutathione: avoiding [tobacco-smoking] and [alcohol], [short-sleep] correction.
entries.caveats: Biomarker increases do not equal health benefit; no outcome trials.
entries.title: Intravenous (IV) or oral glutathione

entries.headline: Carnitines improve sperm motility and morphology in small trials, with no demonstrable effect on pregnancy; very high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: 1-2 g/day L-carnitine (often with 0.5-1 g acetyl-L-carnitine) for 3-6 months.
dose.studied_range: 8 RCTs, mostly 2 g/day L-carnitine + 1 g acetyl-L-carnitine.
dose.too_much: In healthy mice, moderate-to-high carnitine doses caused severe sperm DNA fragmentation and lower pregnancy rates (reductive stress).
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Can cause fishy body odour and GI upset; raises TMAO.

entries.mechanism: Transports fatty acids into mitochondria for sperm energy; antioxidant properties in the epididymis.
entries.interactions: Included in MOXI (1 g), which was null. See [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Small, heterogeneous trials; pregnancy not improved.
entries.title: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine

entries.headline: Evidence for women is weak; the most-cited positive RCT (L-carnitine 3 g/day in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) has been retracted.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: 3 g/day in the retracted PCOS trial.
dose.notes: Male-factor evidence is separate and somewhat better.

entries.mechanism: Shuttles long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation, which oocytes use for energy.
entries.interactions: Included in [female-antioxidant-supplements] analyses.
entries.caveats: Retraction of the main trial removes the main human evidence.
entries.title: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine

factors.name: Laptops on the lap, tight underwear, long sitting, occupational heat

entries.headline: Everyday heat sources raise scrotal temperature 1-3 C; boxer wearers have about 25% higher sperm concentration, but direct SDF data are thin.

dose.effective: Laptop on a desk, not the lap; looser underwear (boxers); stand or walk for a few minutes every 30-60 min; heat protection or breaks for hot jobs (bakers, welders, drivers).
dose.studied_range: Laptop sessions of 60 min; scrotal temperature +1 C within 11-28 min.
dose.too_much: A laptop on closed thighs raised scrotal temperature 2.6-2.8 C in 60 min; lap pads did not prevent it.
dose.timeframe: Benefits, if any, would appear after one spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Sitting with legs apart reduces the rise. Heated car seats are plausible but unstudied for sperm.

entries.mechanism: Mild, repeated scrotal hyperthermia: same thermal pathway as saunas but smaller in size.
entries.interactions: Additive with [sauna] and [varicocele].
entries.caveats: Underwear and laptop data are cross-sectional or physiological (temperature) studies; the underwear association was partly explained by FSH. Occupational heat is a recognised risk but studies are older and confounded.

key_numbers.label: Scrotal temp rise, laptop on lap (60 min)
Higher sperm concentration in boxer wearers

entries.title: Laptops on the lap, tight underwear, long sitting, occupational heat

entries.headline: Nitrate-rich greens and beetroot lower systolic blood pressure by ~4 mmHg in short trials, and greens are the main dietary source of lutein; green leafy vegetables are among the produce most consistently linked to lower CVD and mortality.

dose.effective: 1-2 cups raw or 1/2-1 cup cooked daily.
dose.studied_range: Nitrate trials: 2 h to 15 days, dose-dependent BP effect.
dose.timeframe: Hours (nitrate) to weeks.
dose.notes: Nitrate effects on blood pressure were dose-dependent in meta-regression.

entries.mechanism: Nitrate -> nitrite -> nitric oxide supplements endothelial NO and can offset superoxide-driven NO loss; lutein and zeaxanthin protect membranes; folate.
entries.interactions: Nitrate and cocoa flavanols had additive effects on endothelial function at dietary amounts ([cocoa-flavanols]); pair greens with fat for carotenoid absorption ([extra-virgin-olive-oil]).
entries.caveats: Nitrate BP trials are short and small; oxidative-stress markers seldom measured.

key_numbers.label: Systolic BP change with inorganic nitrate/beetroot
Total polyphenols, chromatography, spinach (sum of compounds)

entries.title: Leafy greens (spinach, lettuce, rocket, chard)

entries.headline: Good for glycemic control and fiber intake, which indirectly limits postprandial oxidative stress, but direct human oxidative-stress data are scarce; their very high Folin 'polyphenol' scores are largely an assay artefact.

dose.effective: About 1/2-1 cup cooked most days as part of a high-fiber pattern.
dose.studied_range: Part of dietary-pattern trials.
dose.notes: Black beans: Folin 1391 mg/100 g but only 54 mg/100 g by chromatography; lentils: Folin 3697 vs 10 mg/100 g. Folin reacts with proteins, sugars and other reducing substances.

entries.mechanism: Low glycemic load, fermentable fiber (short-chain fatty acids), modest polyphenols in seed coats.
entries.interactions: Replacing refined starch or processed meat with legumes reduces [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] and [processed-red-meat] exposure.
entries.caveats: Mostly inferred from fiber and dietary-pattern data.
entries.title: Legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas)

factors.name: Losing excess body fat
aliases: Weight loss through diet and exercise (in men with obesity)
Weight loss when overweight or obese

entries.headline: Excess (especially visceral) fat is one of the strongest population drivers of oxidative stress; a 12-month diet-based weight-loss trial cut F2-isoprostanes by about 23%, and bariatric surgery lowers them further.

dose.effective: If BMI >=25 or waist is high, aim for 5-10% weight loss over 6-12 months via a sustained calorie deficit (e.g., ~500 kcal/day), ideally combined with exercise.
dose.studied_range: Duggan 2016: 12 months of reduced-calorie diet with or without exercise in women with BMI >25; CALERIE 2: prescribed 25% calorie restriction for 2 years in non-obese adults; sleeve gastrectomy in BMI >40.
dose.too_much: Very-low-calorie diets and rapid loss carry their own risks (gallstones, muscle loss) and need supervision.
dose.timeframe: Reductions visible by 6-12 months and scale with amount of weight lost.
dose.notes: Visceral fat matters more than subcutaneous fat. Calorie restriction lowered isoprostanes even in non-obese people.

entries.mechanism: Enlarged adipocytes and infiltrating macrophages produce ROS via NADPH oxidase, release free fatty acids that overload mitochondria, and secrete inflammatory cytokines. Obesity also causes insulin resistance and hyperglycemia. Weight loss reverses these sources.
entries.interactions: Works with [aerobic-exercise-moderate] (exercise adds fitness-related benefits); improves [glycemic-control] and [sleep-apnea].
entries.caveats: F2-isoprostanes vary with metabolic rate; one cohort found higher isoprostanes predicted less later weight gain, so interpret single measurements cautiously. Obesity is consistently linked to poorer sperm parameters (cross-link to fertility areas).
entries.title: Losing excess body fat (if overweight or obese)

entries.headline: Weight loss in obese men raises sperm concentration and motility and lowers DNA fragmentation (effect size about -0.7); lifestyle programmes beat bariatric surgery for semen.

dose.effective: Lose 5-15% of body weight over 3-6 months through diet plus exercise.
dose.studied_range: 12 studies, mean baseline BMI 45; residential programme with 15% median weight loss over 14 weeks.
dose.too_much: Rapid loss after bariatric surgery produced no clinically significant semen or DNA-damage improvement and may temporarily worsen semen; time conception carefully after surgery.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months; re-test semen after one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: GLP-1 drugs and metformin: too little sperm data to judge.

entries.mechanism: Reverses aromatase-driven hypogonadism, lowers inflammation and insulin resistance, and reduces scrotal heat, lowering seminal oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: Usually achieved via [mediterranean-diet] and [aerobic-exercise-moderate]; those may help independently of the weight lost.
entries.caveats: Mostly uncontrolled before-after studies in severely obese men; little live-birth data.

key_numbers.label: DFI effect size after weight loss

entries.title: Weight loss through diet and exercise (in men with obesity)

entries.headline: In overweight and obese women, diet-plus-exercise programmes increased natural pregnancy (RR 1.59) and ovulation, but two RCTs (LIFEstyle, Nordic trial) found that delaying fertility treatment for weight loss did not improve live birth from treatment.

dose.effective: 5-10% of body weight via a reduced-calorie diet plus aerobic exercise; >5% loss improved insulin and cycles in PCOS.
dose.studied_range: Mean losses 4.4 kg (LIFEstyle, 6 months) to 9.4 kg (12 weeks of 880 kcal/day low-calorie diet).
dose.too_much: Do not delay treatment for long in women over ~35: time lost costs egg quality ([maternal-age]).
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Weight loss increased spontaneous conceptions (10.5% vs 2.6% in the Nordic trial). Best for women not yet in IVF or with anovulation.

entries.mechanism: Lowers insulin and free androgens, raises SHBG, reduces follicular lipid and inflammatory load (lipotoxicity).
entries.interactions: Works with [aerobic-exercise-moderate] and [mediterranean-diet]; counteracts [excess-adiposity] and [pcos].
entries.caveats: LIFEstyle: 27.1% vs 35.2% healthy term singleton births, favouring prompt treatment, partly because the intervention arm delayed treatment by 6 months. Weight loss is still worthwhile for pregnancy health.

key_numbers.label: LIFEstyle healthy term birth, intervention vs prompt treatment
Nordic trial IVF live birth, weight loss vs IVF only

entries.title: Weight loss when overweight or obese

entries.headline: 200 g raw broccoli delivers about 3-10x more sulforaphane than fully cooked broccoli because cooking destroys myrosinase; glucoraphanin content of supermarket heads varies more than 100-fold.

dose.effective: ~200 g (2 cups) raw, chopped and chewed well, or lightly steamed; or cooked broccoli with a pinch of mustard powder.
dose.studied_range: 200 g single servings (pharmacokinetics); 250-400 g/day for 12 days to 12 weeks in metabolic studies.
dose.timeframe: Sulforaphane peaks 1.6 h after raw and ~6 h after cooked broccoli.
dose.notes: Raw: 32-37% of the potential isothiocyanate excreted; steamed/cooked: 3.4-10%. Mild heating (about 60 °C) can actually increase sulforaphane by inactivating epithiospecifier protein (which diverts glucoraphanin to an inactive nitrile), but 70 °C and above destroys myrosinase in florets. Frozen broccoli has been blanched and yields far less.

entries.mechanism: Nrf2 activation by sulforaphane; plus vitamin C, carotenoids (lutein), folate and fiber. Mature heads also contain indole glucosinolates, which sprouts largely lack.
entries.interactions: If you already take a strong sulforaphane dose ([broccoli-seed-powder], [broccoli-sprouts]), the extra Nrf2 boost from broccoli is probably smaller, but its vitamin C (89 mg/100 g), lutein and fiber are not duplicated. Add [mustard-seed-myrosinase] when eating it cooked.
entries.caveats: Rough arithmetic: supermarket heads averaged 0.38 µmol glucoraphanin/g, so 200 g holds ~76 µmol; raw, ~30% may reach urine as sulforaphane metabolites (~25 µmol), similar to the effective Qidong threshold. But heads ranged from <0.005 to 1.13 µmol/g, so any single head could be far lower.
entries.title: Mature broccoli (raw or lightly cooked)

entries.headline: Mind-body practices reliably lower cortisol and blood pressure modestly, but evidence that they reduce oxidative damage comes from small, weakly controlled trials.

dose.effective: If you enjoy it: ~20-45 min sessions, most days (yoga trials typically 2-5 sessions/week for 8-12 weeks).
dose.studied_range: Yoga/MBSR trials of 6-16 weeks.
dose.timeframe: 8-12 weeks in most trials.
dose.notes: Physical yoga also counts as light exercise.

entries.mechanism: Lower sympathetic and HPA-axis activity reduces cortisol and catecholamines; gene-expression studies show down-regulation of NF-kB inflammatory pathways.
entries.interactions: Addresses [psychological-stress]; can improve [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Oxidative-marker trials are small (e.g., 29 people), often lack active controls, and use crude markers like malondialdehyde. Grade honestly as limited.
entries.title: Meditation, mindfulness and yoga

entries.headline: In PREDIMED (7447 high-risk adults) a Mediterranean diet with EVOO or nuts cut major CVD events by ~30%; sub-studies found larger falls in urinary 8-oxo-dG, more oxidation-resistant LDL and borderline lower F2-isoprostanes vs a low-fat diet.

dose.effective: Daily EVOO as the main fat, vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts (about 30 g), fish weekly, little red/processed meat or sweets.
dose.studied_range: 4.8 years median (PREDIMED); 1-year oxidative sub-studies.
dose.timeframe: Oxidative markers improved at 1 year; CVD events diverged within a few years.
dose.notes: The wine component is optional and not needed for the benefits.

entries.mechanism: Combines olive phenolics (LDL protection), high produce and fiber (gut metabolites), lower glycemic load, fewer AGEs and processed meats, and better fatty-acid profile.
entries.interactions: Contains most of the beneficial foods here; individual 'superfoods' add little on top of it.
entries.caveats: PREDIMED was retracted and republished after randomisation irregularities; re-analysed results held. Oxidative endpoints were secondary and in subsamples.

key_numbers.label: LDL oxidative modifications, EVOO arm vs control

entries.title: Mediterranean diet

entries.headline: Men who eat a Mediterranean or 'prudent' diet have better counts and motility (about +24 million sperm, +8.8 points motility), but fertility outcomes are untested.

dose.effective: Daily: vegetables (3+ servings), fruit (2+), whole grains, legumes several times a week, nuts (30-60 g), olive oil as main fat; fish 2+ times a week; little processed meat, sweets or sugary drinks.
dose.studied_range: MedDietScore tertiles; observational studies in 2558 men plus 2 small RCTs.
dose.timeframe: About 3 months for sperm-level effects.
dose.notes: The pattern matters more than any single 'superfood'.

entries.mechanism: Supplies dietary antioxidants (vitamin E, carotenoids, polyphenols), omega-3 fats, folate and zinc at food-level doses; lowers inflammation and insulin resistance.
entries.interactions: Contains [walnuts-nuts], [omega3-fish], [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [tomatoes-lycopene]; displaces [processed-meat] and [refined-sugar-high-glycemic].
entries.caveats: Almost all data are cross-sectional or cohort studies; SDF itself is rarely measured; high heterogeneity (I2 ~80-90%).

key_numbers.label: Sperm count difference (high vs low adherence)
Odds of abnormal semen, lowest vs highest tertile

entries.title: Mediterranean / 'prudent' dietary pattern

entries.headline: Women in the lowest third of Mediterranean-diet adherence had much lower IVF live birth (26.6% vs 48.8%) in a Greek cohort of women under 35, but pooled evidence is inconsistent and no RCT has tested it.

dose.effective: Daily vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, olive oil and nuts; fish 2+ times/week; little processed meat, sweets and refined snacks.
dose.studied_range: MedDietScore 0-55 (tertiles <= 30 vs >= 36); EARTH quartiles.
dose.timeframe: Adopt at least 3 months before trying or IVF.
dose.notes: In the US EARTH cohort, benefit plateaued after the second quartile: the gain comes from avoiding a poor diet rather than perfect adherence.

entries.mechanism: Supplies folate, vitamin B6, omega-3 and polyphenols, lowers homocysteine and systemic inflammation, and improves insulin sensitivity; higher blood and follicular-fluid folate/B6 were seen with this pattern.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [profertility-diet], [folic-acid] and [omega3-fish]; also supports [weight-loss].
entries.caveats: All observational; association seen only in women under 35 in one study and no association with oocyte yield or embryo quality. A 2023 meta-analysis judged the evidence insufficient for clinical application.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, lowest vs highest tertile

entries.title: Mediterranean-style diet

entries.headline: Melatonin is a natural follicular antioxidant; in IVF RCTs it raised clinical pregnancy (OR 1.43) and egg/embryo counts in pooled low-quality data, but not live birth (OR 1.38, NS), and a placebo-controlled dose trial saw no change in follicle numbers.

dose.effective: 3 mg/day at night during IVF stimulation was the dose used in the early Japanese studies; not proven.
dose.studied_range: 3 mg/day to 8 mg twice daily.
dose.too_much: Higher doses (up to 8 mg twice daily) did not add benefit; doses below and above showed no live-birth difference in Cochrane comparisons.
dose.timeframe: Usually from early follicular phase to egg retrieval.
dose.notes: Melatonin is a hormone with circadian effects; doses up to 8 mg twice daily did not cause daytime sleepiness in an IVF trial, but there is no reason to use high doses.

entries.mechanism: Concentrated in follicular fluid, scavenges hydroxyl radicals and stimulates antioxidant enzymes; follicular melatonin was inversely related to 8-OHdG oxidative DNA damage.
entries.interactions: Frequently combined with [myo-inositol]; a large combination trial was retracted in 2026.
entries.caveats: Trials are heterogeneous (PCOS to poor responders), small and low quality; the key Tamura data were non-randomized.
entries.title: Melatonin

entries.headline: 20 mg/day MitoQ for 6 weeks improved flow-mediated dilation by 42% in 20 older adults with impaired endothelial function. This is a single small crossover trial without outcome data.

dose.effective: 20 mg/day
dose.studied_range: 20 mg/day for 6 weeks
dose.timeframe: 6 weeks
dose.notes: Proprietary compound; independent replication is limited.

entries.mechanism: A ubiquinone attached to a lipophilic cation that accumulates in the mitochondrial matrix, aiming to quench mitochondrial ROS where generic antioxidants cannot reach.
entries.interactions: Could in theory blunt mitohormetic signalling from exercise, like other antioxidants. This has not been tested.
entries.caveats: Small, short-term study measuring a surrogate endpoint only.
entries.title: Mitochondria-targeted antioxidant (MitoQ)

entries.headline: Lab studies show phone radiation can raise ROS in semen in a dish, but human studies are inconsistent and show no dose-response with hours of use.

dose.effective: Low-cost precaution: keep the phone out of the front trouser pocket when possible.
dose.studied_range: In vitro exposure of semen samples; self-reported daily use in observational studies.
dose.timeframe: Unknown.
dose.notes: Treat as a weak, uncertain factor; far below smoking, heat or varicocele.

entries.mechanism: Proposed: RF energy and local heating increase mitochondrial ROS in sperm (shown in vitro), without clear DNA damage in the key in vitro study.
entries.interactions: Far smaller and less certain than heat sources in [everyday-scrotal-heat].
entries.caveats: One meta-analysis found no effect in human studies; another found associations but no dose-response, which argues against a strong causal effect. Confounding (sedentary habits, socioeconomic factors) likely.
entries.title: Mobile phone radiofrequency exposure

entries.headline: Regular aerobic training raises the body's own antioxidant defences and, when it improves fitness, lowers resting lipid-peroxidation markers by roughly 5-15%; each session causes a brief, useful ROS pulse.

dose.effective: 150-300 min/week of moderate activity (brisk walking, easy cycling, swimming at about 60-75% of maximum heart rate, the range used in the trials; you can talk but not sing), e.g. 30-60 min on 5 days/week.
dose.studied_range: RCTs used 30-60 min, 3-5 days/week at 60-75% HRmax for 8 weeks to 12 months; the Campbell trial used >=45 min/day, 5 days/week at 60-75% HRmax for 12 months.
dose.too_much: No harmful ceiling at guideline volumes; oxidative damage rises mainly with very high volume plus high intensity (see [overtraining-ultraendurance]).
dose.timeframe: Enzyme up-regulation within weeks; resting F2-isoprostane reductions seen at 12 months and only in people who gained fitness (VO2max up >15%).
dose.notes: Fitness gain, not minutes logged, tracked the drop in F2-isoprostanes. Do not pair with high-dose vitamin C/E (see [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]).

entries.mechanism: Contracting muscle makes superoxide and H2O2 (mitochondria, NADPH oxidase NOX2/NOX4, xanthine oxidase). These transient ROS oxidize KEAP1 cysteines, releasing Nrf2 to induce SOD, catalase, GPx, glutathione synthesis enzymes and HO-1, and activate PGC-1alpha-driven mitochondrial biogenesis. Repeated pulses leave a higher resting antioxidant capacity (hormesis). Exercise also reduces visceral fat and improves insulin sensitivity, which removes two big chronic ROS sources.
entries.interactions: Adds to [weight-loss] (diet-induced weight loss lowered F2-isoprostanes more than exercise alone in the Duggan trial). Improves [glycemic-control]. High-dose vitamin C/E can blunt molecular adaptations ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). Post-exercise [cold-water-immersion] may blunt strength adaptations.
entries.caveats: Overall effects on resting oxidative markers in healthy, already-fit people are small and heterogeneous; most benefit appears in sedentary, overweight or unhealthy people. Measuring oxidative markers right after a session shows a rise; that is the signal, not damage.

key_numbers.label: F2-isoprostane change, exercisers with VO2max gain >15% (12 mo)
F2-isoprostane change, all exercisers (12 mo, NS)

entries.title: Regular moderate aerobic exercise

entries.headline: Active men have better sperm counts, and one large RCT found moderate continuous training improved sperm DNA integrity more than high-intensity training.

dose.effective: About 30-45 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise (brisk walking, jogging, swimming, gym cardio), 3-5 days a week, plus less TV/sitting time.
dose.studied_range: Moderate continuous, high-intensity continuous and interval training, 3 sessions/week for 24 weeks (280 men); >=15 h/week moderate-vigorous activity in observational data.
dose.too_much: Very high training loads and long-distance cycling may worsen semen ([cycling]); in the RCT moderate beat high-intensity.
dose.timeframe: Improvements by 12-24 weeks; benefits faded within about a month of stopping training.
dose.notes: Over 20 h/week of TV was linked to 44% lower concentration.

entries.mechanism: Regular moderate exercise up-regulates endogenous antioxidant enzymes (SOD, catalase) via hormetic Nrf2 signalling, lowers inflammation, improves insulin sensitivity and weight.
entries.interactions: Supports [weight-loss]. High-dose antioxidant pills can blunt exercise adaptations in other tissues, a reason not to stack them.
entries.caveats: The key RCTs come from one Iranian group (Hajizadeh Maleki/Tartibian); its moderate-exercise trial in infertile men (Cytokine 2017) and its combined-exercise trial (J Strength Cond Res 2019) were retracted, so the remaining healthy-men trial should be treated with caution. Observational data are confounded.
entries.title: Moderate regular exercise (and less sitting)

entries.headline: Moderate activity (e.g. brisk walking, cycling) is linked to slightly higher fecundability (FR 1.18 at >= 5 h/week) and, in women with reproductive problems, exercise interventions roughly doubled pregnancy rates in small trials.

dose.effective: Regular moderate activity; >= 5 h/week of moderate activity was associated with slightly higher fecundability, and any activity type helped women with BMI >= 25.
dose.studied_range: Moderate activity < 1 to >= 5 h/week; intervention trials mainly in PCOS and obesity.
dose.too_much: See [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]: >= 5 h/week vigorous activity in lean women.
dose.timeframe: Insulin sensitivity improves within weeks; ovulatory changes over months.
dose.notes: Pre-IVF activity (median 2.8 h/week moderate-to-vigorous) was not harmful.

entries.mechanism: Improves insulin sensitivity and reduces inflammation; regular moderate exercise up-regulates endogenous antioxidant defenses (hormesis).
entries.interactions: Combines with [weight-loss] in overweight women.
entries.caveats: Intervention trials are few and small; the benefit is clearest in women with PCOS or overweight.

key_numbers.label: Pregnancy, PA intervention vs no therapy

entries.title: Moderate physical activity

factors.name: Mustard powder on cooked crucifers (myrosinase add-back)

entries.headline: Sprinkling 1 g of powdered brown mustard on 200 g of cooked broccoli raised sulforaphane metabolite excretion about 4.5-fold, restoring much of what cooking destroys.

dose.effective: About 1 g (roughly 1/2 teaspoon) powdered brown mustard per 200 g cooked broccoli, added after cooking.
dose.studied_range: 1 g mustard powder with 200 g cooked broccoli, single meal, crossover in 12 adults.
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Add after cooking, once the food is below boiling; heat inactivates mustard myrosinase too. Raw daikon radish or a little broccoli seed powder works on the same principle (daikon myrosinase was used to make sulforaphane-rich beverages).

entries.mechanism: Exogenous myrosinase hydrolyses glucoraphanin remaining in cooked broccoli to sulforaphane in the meal and gut, then Nrf2 activation.
entries.interactions: Turns [broccoli-mature] cooked into a meaningful sulforaphane source; same redundancy considerations as other Nrf2 inducers.
entries.caveats: One small pharmacokinetic trial; no outcome data.

key_numbers.label: Urinary SF-NAC, cooked broccoli + 1 g mustard

entries.title: Mustard powder on cooked crucifers (myrosinase add-back)

entries.headline: Widely used in PCOS, but the Cochrane review rated the evidence very low quality and could not show a live-birth benefit (OR 2.42, 95% CI 0.75-7.83); the 2023 PCOS guideline review calls it limited and inconclusive.

dose.effective: Trials commonly used 4 g/day myo-inositol with 400 ug folic acid (e.g. the now-retracted Pacchiarotti trial); no dose is proven to raise live birth.
dose.studied_range: 11 of 13 Cochrane trials used myo-inositol as pre-treatment before IVF; 2 during ovulation induction.
dose.too_much: Mild GI effects; fewer GI effects than metformin.
dose.timeframe: Pre-treatment before IVF stimulation in most trials.
dose.notes: D-chiro-inositol may help ovulation per the guideline review, but evidence is very uncertain. One widely cited myo-inositol plus melatonin RCT (526 women) was retracted in 2026.

entries.mechanism: Inositol phosphoglycans act as second messengers for insulin and FSH signalling; may improve insulin sensitivity in PCOS.
entries.interactions: Alternative to or adjunct with metformin; often combined with [melatonin] and [folic-acid].
entries.caveats: Industry-linked trials, poor reporting and a retraction. Not relevant for women without PCOS.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, MI vs standard (2 RCTs)

entries.title: Myo-inositol (in PCOS)

entries.headline: NAC raises glutathione and improved performance and oxidative markers only in people with low baseline glutathione. In replete people it blunts muscle repair signalling. In mouse cancer models it accelerated tumour growth and metastasis.

dose.effective: 1,200 mg/day (600 mg twice daily) for 30 days in people with low baseline glutathione
dose.studied_range: 1,200 mg/day for 30 days (performance trial); short courses in exercise-recovery studies
dose.too_much: No defined toxicity threshold at these doses, but caution in people with active or past cancer (mouse data) and around training (blunted adaptation).
dose.timeframe: Glutathione restored within 30 days in deficient individuals
dose.notes: Benefit depends on baseline redox status; there is no routine clinical test, and this is a research approach.

entries.mechanism: Supplies cysteine, the limiting substrate for glutathione synthesis via glutamate-cysteine ligase. By raising GSH it can blunt redox-sensitive signalling (Akt/mTOR, NF-kB) needed for repair, and in tumour cells it can increase glutathione-dependent migration.
entries.interactions: Combined with glycine as [glynac]. Redundant with a high-protein diet rich in sulfur amino acids, and with Nrf2 activators that induce GCL. Antagonises exercise adaptation like [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Popular as a 'master antioxidant' supplement. Human outcome data in healthy people are lacking, and the tumour-promotion findings come from mice with existing tumours.
entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)

entries.headline: NAC 600 mg/day for 3 months lowered SDF and improved motility in an uncontrolled study; no placebo-controlled live-birth data.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day for 3 months (studied dose).
dose.studied_range: 600 mg/day in 50 men with asthenoteratozoospermia.
dose.too_much: Higher doses add GI upset; no proven extra benefit.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

entries.mechanism: Cysteine donor for glutathione synthesis; also reported to induce Nrf2 target genes in sperm.
entries.interactions: Part of many combination products.
entries.caveats: Before-after design without placebo. Some widely cited NAC/selenium RCTs come from an author several of whose other papers have been retracted; they are not used here.
entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)

entries.headline: In PCOS, NAC added to clomiphene improved ovulation and pregnancy vs placebo in small, biased trials, but it was inferior to metformin and live-birth data are thin.

dose.effective: 1.2 g/day (with clomiphene in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) in the original RCT.
dose.studied_range: 1.2 g/day in the main RCT; 8 RCTs (910 women) pooled in meta-analysis.
dose.timeframe: During ovulation-induction cycles.
dose.notes: A glutathione precursor; available as a supplement in some countries and a drug in others.

entries.mechanism: Supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis; may improve insulin sensitivity.
entries.interactions: Compared against metformin and [l-carnitine] in trials; the NAC-vs-carnitine trial in the Cochrane review was flagged for integrity concerns.
entries.caveats: Many trials come from a few centres; high risk of selection, attrition and reporting bias. The 1.2 g/day trial's 49% vs 1% ovulation contrast is implausibly large.

key_numbers.label: Ovulation, NAC + clomiphene vs placebo + clomiphene

entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in PCOS

entries.headline: Night work suppresses melatonin and was linked to much lower excretion of repaired oxidative DNA lesions (20% of night-sleep levels), suggesting impaired DNA repair.

dose.effective: Limit consecutive night shifts where possible; sleep in a dark room; keep a stable schedule on days off. Melatonin before day sleep is being studied.
dose.studied_range: Observational studies of rotating and permanent night workers; one 4-week melatonin RCT (n=40).
dose.too_much: Long-term rotating night work.
dose.timeframe: Melatonin trial: 4 weeks.
dose.notes: The melatonin result was borderline and needs confirmation.

entries.mechanism: Light at night suppresses melatonin; melatonin supports OGG1-mediated repair of 8-oxoguanine and acts as an antioxidant. Circadian misalignment also disturbs glucose and lipid metabolism and clock-controlled Nrf2 rhythms.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [short-sleep]; worsens [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Reduced urinary 8-OH-dG is read as reduced repair, not reduced damage; interpretation depends on that assumption. Evidence is mostly observational.
entries.title: Night-shift work and circadian disruption

entries.headline: NAD+ falls in ageing mouse eggs and NMN restored egg quality and fertility in aged mice, but there are no human data on egg quality, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: No human fertility dose exists; all egg data are from mice.
dose.studied_range: Animal studies only.
dose.too_much: Unknown in pregnancy; safety in early embryos not studied in humans.
dose.notes: Marketed heavily as 'egg rejuvenation'; this is extrapolation from mice.

entries.mechanism: Raises NAD+, a cofactor for sirtuins (e.g. SIRT2) and mitochondrial metabolism; in aged mice restored spindle assembly, mitochondrial function and lowered ROS.
entries.interactions: Shares the mitochondrial-ageing target with [coq10]; sirtuin overlap with [isolated-polyphenol-supplements].
entries.caveats: Mouse reproductive ageing differs from human (human egg aneuploidy is driven largely by cohesin loss over decades).
entries.title: NMN / NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR)

factors.name: Oily fish & omega-3
aliases: Fish and omega-3 fatty acids (food and fish oil/DHA)

entries.headline: Although EPA/DHA are highly peroxidizable, 3.4 g/day fish oil did not raise plasma F2-isoprostanes or MDA vs oleic or linoleic oils; long-chain omega-3s slightly reduce CHD events and lower triglycerides ~15%.

dose.effective: 1-2 servings of oily fish per week (salmon, sardines, mackerel), baked or poached rather than deep-fried.
dose.studied_range: 0.5 to >5 g/day long-chain omega-3 in RCTs (86 trials, 162,796 people).
dose.too_much: Cochrane found little or no effect of increased omega-3 on serious adverse events.
dose.timeframe: Weeks for triglycerides.
dose.notes: Oxidized (rancid) oils and deep-fried fish deliver dietary lipid oxidation products.

entries.mechanism: EPA/DHA alter membrane composition, eicosanoids and resolvins (anti-inflammatory); their double bonds are substrates for lipid peroxidation, so oxidized products in food or capsules matter more than the fats themselves.
entries.interactions: Eat with polyphenol-rich foods and avoid [oxidized-frying-oils]. TBARS rose with fish oil while F2-isoprostanes did not, illustrating how marker choice changes conclusions.
entries.caveats: Cochrane: little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97) or total CV events; modest CHD reduction is low-certainty.
entries.title: Oily fish and omega-3 fats

entries.headline: Fish eaters have higher sperm counts, and a small RCT of 1.5 g/day DHA lowered sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Oily fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel, herring) 2-3 times a week; if supplementing, about 1-1.5 g/day EPA+DHA.
dose.studied_range: 1.5 g/day DHA for 10 weeks (n=74); fish-oil use on >=60 days in 1679 young men; fish-intake quartiles.
dose.too_much: Above ~3 g/day EPA+DHA raises bleeding risk; choose low-mercury fish.
dose.timeframe: 10-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Swap processed meat for fish: the fish-sperm association was strongest when fish replaced processed red meat.

entries.mechanism: DHA is a key structural lipid of sperm membranes; supplementation raised seminal antioxidant capacity. Paradoxically more PUFA means more oxidisable substrate, so benefit depends on adequate antioxidant status.
entries.interactions: Pairs with [walnuts-nuts] (plant omega-3) and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Supplement trials are small; the Danish fish-oil study is cross-sectional; reviews note heterogeneity.

key_numbers.label: Total count, lowest vs highest fish quartile

entries.title: Fish and omega-3 fatty acids (food and fish oil/DHA)

entries.headline: Each 1% higher serum long-chain omega-3 was associated with 8% higher probability of IVF live birth; in mice omega-3-rich diets preserved egg quality into older age.

dose.effective: Eat lower-mercury fatty fish regularly as part of the diet; studies measured serum levels and dietary share rather than a fixed supplement dose (replacing 1% of energy from saturated fat with long-chain omega-3 was associated with RR 2.37 for live birth).
dose.studied_range: Serum omega-3 4.7% median (IQR 3.8-5.8%) of total fatty acids.
dose.too_much: High-mercury fish (see [heavy-metals]).
dose.timeframe: Adopt within the 3-month preconception window.
dose.notes: Human evidence is from observational IVF cohorts; no adequate RCT on live birth.

entries.mechanism: Incorporation into membranes, anti-inflammatory lipid mediators, possible effects on follicular steroidogenesis.
entries.interactions: Trade-off with [heavy-metals]; part of [mediterranean-diet] and [profertility-diet].
entries.caveats: Small cohort (100 women); mouse data on reproductive ageing have not been replicated in humans.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth probability per +1% serum LC omega-3

entries.title: Omega-3 fats (EPA/DHA from fish)

factors.name: Other berries & cherries (strawberry, raspberry, chokeberry, blackcurrant, cranberry, cherries)

entries.headline: Berry RCTs pooled together show small improvements in LDL, systolic blood pressure, glucose and TNF-alpha, and anthocyanin foods improve flow-mediated dilation; specific oxidative-stress effects are inconsistent.

dose.effective: About 1 cup (150 g) of mixed berries daily, or ~3 servings per week in cohort data.
dose.studied_range: Juices, powders and whole fruit in 22 RCTs (1251 people); cranberry juice dose-response trials.
dose.timeframe: Acute (hours) for FMD; weeks for lipids and blood pressure.
dose.notes: Chokeberry and blackcurrant are far denser in anthocyanins than strawberries, but higher content has not been shown to give proportionally more benefit.

entries.mechanism: Anthocyanin and ellagitannin metabolites; vitamin C in strawberries.
entries.interactions: Substitutes for [blueberries]; not additive beyond plateau.
entries.caveats: Meta-analytic effects are small (LDL -0.21 mmol/L, SBP -2.7 mmHg) and heterogeneous. Cohort link: >3 servings/week of blueberries plus strawberries tended toward lower MI risk in young women (not significant on its own).
entries.title: Other berries & cherries (strawberry, raspberry, chokeberry, blackcurrant, cranberry, cherries)

factors.name: Other crucifers (kale, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower)

entries.headline: Supply other isothiocyanates and indoles plus vitamin C and carotenoids; cohort data link crucifer intake to lower CVD and mortality, but oxidative-stress trials are few.

dose.effective: 1-2 servings (80-160 g) most days, some raw or lightly cooked.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes; feeding studies 250 g/day cooked crucifers for 12 days.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Same cooking rules as broccoli: chopping and gentle cooking preserve myrosinase activity.

entries.mechanism: Isothiocyanates (Nrf2), vitamin C, carotenoids, fiber.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [broccoli-mature] and [leafy-greens].
entries.caveats: Inverse associations of cruciferous vegetables with CVD and mortality are observational.
entries.title: Other crucifers (kale, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower)

entries.headline: Fine particles raise oxidative and inflammatory markers within days; each 10 µg/m³ of short-term PM2.5 was linked to ~1.6% higher malondialdehyde. Individually modest, but it affects everyone in polluted areas.

dose.effective: Aim to live and exercise where annual PM2.5 is near the WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³; on high-pollution days (AQI 'unhealthy') move hard exercise indoors or away from traffic, and use HEPA filtration indoors (see [hepa-air-purifier]).
dose.studied_range: Epidemiology across typical urban levels (roughly 10-100 µg/m³ PM2.5).
dose.too_much: WHO 2021: annual PM2.5 above 5 µg/m³ and peak-season 8-h ozone above 60 µg/m³ are associated with harm; no clear safe threshold.
dose.timeframe: Marker changes within hours to days of exposure.
dose.notes: Distance from heavy traffic and indoor filtration are the practical levers for individuals.

entries.mechanism: Particles carry transition metals and quinones that redox-cycle (Fenton chemistry), activate NADPH oxidase in airway and immune cells, and trigger systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Ozone directly oxidizes lung-lining lipids and proteins.
entries.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking] and [secondhand-smoke]. Reduced by [hepa-air-purifier].
entries.caveats: Effect sizes on systemic markers are small per unit exposure; most evidence is observational. Air pollution is also linked to poorer semen quality (cross-link to sperm area).
entries.title: Outdoor air pollution (PM2.5, ozone, traffic)

entries.headline: Periods of high air pollution are linked to higher SDF (about +9.7 points across studies) even when other semen measures look normal.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure on high-pollution days (air-quality alerts): avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors, keep car windows closed in traffic.
dose.studied_range: Episodes at or above US air-quality standard limits (Teplice, Czech Republic); PM and NO2 in later studies.
dose.timeframe: Effects appear in sperm produced during and after exposure (~2-3 months later).
dose.notes: Individual control is limited; the effect size is a population average.

entries.mechanism: Fine particles and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons cause systemic oxidative stress and inflammation, and some PAH metabolites form DNA adducts in germ cells.
entries.interactions: Additive with [tobacco-smoking], which delivers similar compounds at much higher doses.
entries.caveats: Ecological and repeated-measures studies; exposure misclassification likely.
entries.title: Air pollution

entries.headline: Higher traffic-related NO2 exposure is associated with lower AMH and lower IVF live birth (e.g. OR 0.76 per 0.01 ppm after embryo transfer); effect sizes per person are modest and hard to separate from other urban factors.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure where practical: avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors on high-pollution days.
dose.studied_range: Residential and IVF-lab NO2, ozone, PM2.5 and PM10 from monitoring models.
dose.too_much: No safe threshold established; associations were per 0.01 ppm (Legro) or 20 ppb (Gaskins) increase in NO2.
dose.timeframe: Exposure in the ~3 months before IVF was studied.
dose.notes: In one IVF cohort the NO2-live birth association was absent in women taking >= 800 ug/day supplemental folate (hypothesis-generating).

entries.mechanism: Inhaled particles and NO2 cause systemic inflammation and oxidative stress; PAHs adsorbed on particles are ovotoxic.
entries.interactions: Possible modification by [folic-acid]. Overlaps with [tobacco-smoking] (shared PAH exposure).
entries.caveats: All observational, with exposure estimated from home address. Individual control is limited; do not let this become a source of anxiety.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per +0.01 ppm NO2 (post-transfer)
Lower odds of live birth per +20 ppb NO2 (folate < 800 ug/day)

entries.title: Air pollution (NO2, fine particles)

entries.headline: Overeating by ~1000 kcal/day for 28 days raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and muscle protein carbonyls; 6000 kcal/day caused systemic oxidative stress within 2-3 days; BMI is one of the strongest correlates of urinary isoprostanes in the population.

dose.effective: Eat to energy balance; avoid sustained surplus.
dose.studied_range: +1040 kcal/day for 28 days; ~6000 kcal/day for 1 week.
dose.too_much: Any chronic surplus that drives weight gain, especially visceral fat.
dose.timeframe: Oxidative stress rises within days of overfeeding.
dose.notes: Avoiding a surplus probably outweighs any single 'antioxidant food'.

entries.mechanism: Nutrient excess overloads mitochondrial electron transport, increasing superoxide; adipose tissue oxidative stress carbonylated GLUT4, impairing insulin action; adipose inflammation.
entries.interactions: Reversed by [calorie-restriction]; compounded by [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] and [alcohol].
entries.caveats: Overfeeding studies are short and small; the Framingham link is cross-sectional.

key_numbers.label: Weight gain in 1 week at ~6000 kcal/day
Weight gain after 28 days at +1040 kcal/day

entries.title: Excess calories / overfeeding and weight gain

entries.headline: Very long or excessive exercise raises oxidative damage markers sharply (F2-isoprostanes up ~75% after a 50 km race; up to 7-fold in overreaching), usually returning to baseline within 24-96 h if recovery is adequate.

dose.effective: Stay within a load you recover from: performance, sleep and mood should not decline across weeks. Build volume gradually.
dose.studied_range: Studies: 50 km ultramarathon (~6.5 h); 12-week resistance block peaking at 14 t/week; 4-week progressive endurance overload.
dose.too_much: Signs of excess: falling performance, persistent fatigue, poor sleep, frequent illness. One study found impaired glucose tolerance in world-class endurance athletes.
dose.timeframe: Acute rise lasts about 24 h after an ultramarathon; overreaching markers stayed high 96 h after sessions.
dose.notes: Occasional long events are not a health problem for trained people; chronic under-recovery is.

entries.mechanism: Prolonged high oxygen flux plus muscle damage and immune-cell activation (neutrophil NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase) overwhelm glutathione and vitamin E; ROS shift from signal to damage, impairing mitochondrial function.
entries.interactions: Adequate sleep ([short-sleep]) and energy intake matter for recovery. High-dose antioxidants do not solve this and may hinder adaptation.
entries.caveats: Most data come from small samples of athletes. Spikes after an event do not prove long-term harm.
entries.title: Overtraining and ultra-endurance events

entries.headline: Ozone is a strong oxidant and a regulated air pollutant; 'ozone therapy' is marketed as hormetic, but a Cochrane review could draw no firm conclusions even for its best-studied use (diabetic foot ulcers).

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress.
dose.studied_range: Clinical trials of ozone for wounds and other conditions; small and high risk of bias.
dose.too_much: Inhaled ozone is toxic to the lungs; WHO's peak-season 8-h outdoor guideline is 60 µg/m³.
dose.notes: Intravenous and blood-handling procedures carry their own procedural risks.

entries.mechanism: Ozone reacts with lipids to form ozonides, aldehydes and H2O2; proponents claim this triggers Nrf2-mediated hormesis.
entries.interactions: Opposite of [outdoor-air-pollution] advice: ozone exposure is a recognized harm.
entries.caveats: Hormesis claims are mechanistic; human outcome evidence is poor.
entries.title: Ozone therapy (autohemotherapy, ozone saunas)

entries.headline: SDF rises steadily with age, with a clear jump after 50 (about +12.6 points on average), alongside more new mutations in offspring.

dose.effective: Not modifiable, but relevant to timing: SDF climbs from the 20s with no threshold; effects are largest from about age 45-50.
dose.studied_range: Men aged 20-80.
dose.too_much: Age >=50 associated with the largest SDF increase.
dose.timeframe: Lifelong, gradual.
dose.notes: Older men gain the most from removing other risk factors, because damage is additive. Partner's age matters too: older eggs repair paternal DNA damage less well.

entries.mechanism: Age-related decline in testicular antioxidant defence and mitochondrial function, more oxidative stress, less efficient apoptotic culling of damaged germ cells, and accumulating replication errors in spermatogonial stem cells.
entries.interactions: Combined with older maternal age, high SDF has a bigger effect on embryo quality and miscarriage (see [testicular-sperm-icsi]).
entries.caveats: Age is confounded with weight, illness and varicocele duration; the absolute risk to any one child remains low.
entries.title: Paternal age

entries.headline: Farm workers exposed to organophosphate/carbamate pesticides have higher SDF; high-residue produce seems to cancel the benefit of fruit and vegetables.

dose.effective: Use protective equipment for occupational spraying; wash produce; choose lower-residue or organic options for high-residue items if affordable.
dose.studied_range: Occupational cholinesterase-inhibiting exposure; dietary residues by produce type.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Do not cut fruit and vegetables to avoid pesticides; the net effect of produce is positive or neutral.

entries.mechanism: Organophosphates generate ROS and lipid peroxidation in testis and disrupt the HPG axis.
entries.interactions: See [high-fruit-vegetable-intake].
entries.caveats: Small cross-sectional occupational studies; dietary findings come from one cohort.
entries.title: Pesticides (occupational and dietary)

factors.name: Plastics chemicals (phthalates, BPA)
aliases: Endocrine disruptors: phthalates and bisphenol A

entries.headline: Phthalate metabolites are associated with higher urinary oxidative-stress markers in pregnancy, but associations for persistent pollutants (PFAS, PCBs, pesticides) are mostly inconsistent.

dose.effective: Reasonable low-cost steps: don't microwave food in plastic, prefer glass/steel for hot foods, eat fewer ultra-processed and packaged foods, and reduce fragranced personal-care products.
dose.studied_range: Observational studies of urinary metabolites.
dose.timeframe: Phthalates and BPA clear within hours to days, so exposure reduction changes levels quickly.
dose.notes: Evidence that these steps change health outcomes is lacking.

entries.mechanism: Proposed: mitochondrial disruption and NADPH-oxidase activation; endocrine disruption.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with diet quality (ultra-processed foods).
entries.caveats: Associations from spot urine samples are noisy; causality unproven. Keep expectations modest.
entries.title: Plastic-associated chemicals (phthalates, bisphenols) and persistent pollutants

entries.headline: Higher urinary phthalate and BPA levels are linked to more sperm DNA damage (about 10-18% more Comet damage per interquartile rise).

dose.effective: Practical reduction: avoid heating food in plastic, prefer glass/steel containers, eat less ultra-processed and canned food, choose fragrance-free personal care products.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary levels (median BPA 1.3 ng/mL).
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels fall within days; any sperm effect would take ~3 months.
dose.notes: No intervention trial shows that lowering exposure improves SDF.

entries.mechanism: Anti-androgenic and estrogenic receptor effects plus induction of oxidative stress in germ cells.
entries.interactions: Exposure falls naturally with a less processed diet ([mediterranean-diet]).
entries.caveats: Single-centre cross-sectional studies with spot urine samples; inconsistent replication.

key_numbers.label: Comet tail DNA rise per IQR BPA

entries.title: Endocrine disruptors: phthalates and bisphenol A

entries.headline: In the EARTH IVF cohort, women in the top quartile of urinary DEHP metabolites had fewer eggs and about 19 percentage points lower live birth per cycle than the bottom quartile.

dose.effective: Lower exposure: eat more fresh, less ultra-processed and packaged food; avoid heating food in plastic; choose fragrance-free personal-care products.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of urinary phthalate metabolites (spot urine samples).
dose.too_much: No established threshold; risk scaled with quartile.
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels vary day to day, reflecting recent exposure; follicles develop over ~3 months, so reduce exposure across that window.
dose.notes: Single EARTH cohort with 256 women; replication is limited.

entries.mechanism: Anti-androgenic and endocrine-disrupting effects on granulosa-cell steroidogenesis; animal studies show follicular oxidative stress and atresia.
entries.interactions: Often co-occurs with [plastics-chemicals] exposure from packaged food.
entries.caveats: Urine levels fluctuate day to day, so single samples misclassify exposure; confounding by diet quality is possible.

key_numbers.label: Live birth difference, top vs bottom DEHP quartile

entries.title: Phthalates (DEHP and related plasticizers)

entries.headline: Each log-unit increase in urinary BPA was associated with 12% fewer eggs retrieved in IVF; BPA causes egg aneuploidy in animals, but human outcome data are small and inconsistent.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure: fewer canned foods, avoid polycarbonate containers and heating food in plastic, minimise thermal-paper receipts.
dose.studied_range: Urinary BPA < 0.4 to 25.5 ug/L.
dose.timeframe: Reduce exposure across the ~3-month follicle-growth window.
dose.notes: Human data come from small IVF cohorts at one clinic.

entries.mechanism: Estrogen-receptor activity; in animals disrupts meiotic spindle formation and steroidogenesis and increases oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: [plastics-chemicals] come from similar sources.
entries.caveats: Small cohorts (84 women); human evidence is not strong enough to quantify live-birth effects.

key_numbers.label: Oocytes retrieved per log-unit urinary BPA

entries.title: Bisphenol A (BPA)

entries.headline: PCOS carries measurable systemic oxidative stress (malondialdehyde about 47% higher, glutathione about 50% lower than controls, independent of weight); fertility problems are mainly ovulatory, and IVF outcomes are worse when PCOS coexists with obesity.

dose.effective: Management per the 2023 international guideline: healthy lifestyle first, then evidence-based medical and fertility treatment. In overweight women, losing 5% or more of body weight improved insulin, SHBG and cycles in an early study.
dose.studied_range: Weight loss studies 5-22% of body weight; lifestyle RCTs mostly 3-12 months.
dose.timeframe: Metabolic and ovulatory improvement over 3-6 months of weight loss.
dose.notes: Insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism, not oocytes per se, drive most of the problem; egg quality in lean, ovulating PCOS is often normal.

entries.mechanism: Hyperinsulinaemia and hyperandrogenism alter the follicular environment; chronic low-grade inflammation and lower antioxidant reserve (glutathione, paraoxonase-1) increase lipid peroxidation. Obesity adds lipotoxicity and further insulin resistance.
entries.interactions: Strongly interacts with [excess-adiposity] and [glycemic-control]; supplements studied mainly in PCOS: [myo-inositol], [n-acetylcysteine]. Weight loss is covered by [weight-loss].
entries.caveats: Raised oxidative markers in blood do not prove oxidative damage to eggs is the cause of infertility in PCOS; most infertility is anovulation, which is treatable. Lifestyle RCTs in PCOS have not reported live birth (Cochrane 2019 found none).
entries.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

entries.headline: Polyphenols reach only about 0-4 µmol/L in plasma, mostly as metabolites. Effects in human trials are small and mostly on biomarkers, and no outcome benefit is established for capsules.

dose.effective: Not established for outcomes.
dose.studied_range: Tens to hundreds of mg/day in short biomarker studies
dose.timeframe: Transient plasma exposure after each dose
dose.notes: Bioavailability varies over 100-fold by compound (urinary recovery 0.3-43%); isoflavones and gallic acid are best absorbed, proanthocyanidins and anthocyanins worst.

entries.mechanism: Direct scavenging in plasma is implausible at these concentrations. Likely actions are mild electrophilic Nrf2 activation, modulation of NF-kB and endothelial signalling, and local effects in the gut, where much of the dose and its microbial metabolites act.
entries.interactions: May act additively with other Nrf2 activators in vitro; human interaction data are lacking. The rise in plasma antioxidant capacity after polyphenol foods is mostly uric acid.
entries.caveats: Cell-culture 'antioxidant' effects are often artefacts of polyphenols oxidising in culture media. Whole foods with the same polyphenols carry fibre and other components.

key_numbers.label: Peak plasma metabolites per 50 mg dose

entries.title: Isolated polyphenol capsules (quercetin, resveratrol, grape-seed, etc.)

entries.headline: Resveratrol may improve some follicular markers (an 800 mg/day RCT in PCOS raised oocyte maturity without changing pregnancy rates), but it suppresses endometrial decidualization, and 200 mg/day during embryo-transfer cycles was associated with lower pregnancy (OR 0.54) and more miscarriage (OR 2.60).

dose.effective: Not recommended while trying to conceive or around embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: 200 mg/day (retrospective IVF cohort); 800 mg/day for 60 days (PCOS RCT, 56 women).
dose.too_much: Any use in the luteal phase or early pregnancy (possible anti-implantation effect; teratogenicity not excluded).
dose.notes: A clear example where an 'anti-ageing' antioxidant may harm the uterus even if it helps the ovary.

entries.mechanism: SIRT1 activation and antioxidant effects in the ovary; in endometrium it down-regulates the CRABP2-RAR pathway, inhibiting decidualization needed for implantation.
entries.interactions: Sirtuin-pathway overlap with [nmn-nad].
entries.caveats: Harm signal is retrospective; benefit signal is a single small RCT on surrogate outcomes.

key_numbers.label: Clinical pregnancy, resveratrol during transfer cycles

entries.title: Resveratrol

entries.headline: A famous 10-patient study reported dramatic falls in LDL oxidation and carotid thickness, but an 18-month RCT in 289 people found no effect on carotid progression and a meta-analysis found no lipid effect.

dose.effective: Not established; 240 mL/day was ineffective for carotid progression overall.
dose.studied_range: 50-240 mL/day for up to 3 years.
dose.too_much: Juice adds free sugar.
dose.notes: Punicalagins are converted by gut bacteria to urolithins; some people produce few.

entries.mechanism: Ellagitannins (punicalagin) -> ellagic acid -> urolithins; raised paraoxonase-1 in the small study.
entries.interactions: None notable.
entries.caveats: Industry-funded small studies drove early enthusiasm; possible benefit only in exploratory subgroups with high oxidative stress.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, Folin assay, pure juice

entries.title: Pomegranate juice

entries.headline: IARC classifies processed meat as carcinogenic (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (2A); heme iron catalyses lipid peroxidation and N-nitroso compound formation in the gut, with fecal N-nitroso compounds rising linearly with red-meat intake.

dose.effective: Keep processed meat rare and red meat to a few modest portions per week.
dose.studied_range: 0-420 g/day red meat in controlled feeding (dose-response for fecal N-nitroso compounds); white meat at 420-600 g/day had no effect.
dose.too_much: Each 50 g/day of processed meat raised colorectal cancer risk ~18% (IARC). Highest vs lowest heme intake: colon cancer RR 1.18.
dose.timeframe: Fecal markers change within days; cancer risk over years.
dose.notes: Meat eaten with red-wine polyphenols or polyphenol-rich spices produced less postprandial MDA in animal and human meal studies.

entries.mechanism: Heme iron catalyses peroxidation of dietary PUFA in the stomach and colon, producing malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal, and promotes endogenous N-nitrosation; processed meats add nitrite and pre-formed nitrosamines; high-heat cooking adds HCAs and PAHs.
entries.interactions: Worse with [high-temperature-cooking]; partly offset by [herbs-spices] and polyphenol-rich foods eaten in the same meal.
entries.caveats: Oxidative mechanism evidence is strongest for the gut lumen; effects on systemic markers are less studied. For sperm, only processed meat (not unprocessed red meat) has been linked to worse semen; see [unprocessed-red-meat].

key_numbers.label: Colon cancer RR, highest vs lowest heme iron
Fecal N-nitroso compounds per g red meat/day

entries.title: Processed and red meat

entries.headline: Processed meat is the meat signal for sperm: men eating the most had fewer normal-shaped sperm (1.7 points) and, in young men, about 78 million fewer sperm per ejaculate. Unprocessed red meat was not linked to worse semen.

dose.effective: Keep processed meat (bacon, ham, sausages, deli meats) to less than one serving a week; replace with fish or legumes.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of intake in 155 clinic patients.
dose.too_much: Highest quartile associated with worse morphology.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.

entries.mechanism: Heme iron, nitrites and advanced glycation/lipoxidation products may increase oxidative stress; may also mark a Western diet.
entries.interactions: Replace with [omega3-fish] or unprocessed meat/poultry; see [unprocessed-red-meat].
entries.caveats: Observational only, small effects, and confounding by overall diet and abstinence time is possible (the young-men study noted heavy meat eaters also had shorter abstinence). The finding is specific to processed meat; see [unprocessed-red-meat].

key_numbers.label: Fewer normal forms, highest vs lowest quartile

entries.title: Processed meat (bacon, ham, hot dogs, deli meats)

entries.headline: Inactivity harms metabolic health quickly (bed rest cut insulin sensitivity 42%), but direct human evidence that sitting itself raises oxidative markers is weak; the harm runs mostly through fitness loss, fat gain and glucose control.

dose.effective: Break up sitting every 30-60 min with a few minutes of light movement; replace sitting with any activity (WHO: 'some is better than none').
dose.studied_range: Bed rest studies of several days; WHO observational evidence on daily sitting time.
dose.too_much: Long uninterrupted sitting; very low daily steps.
dose.timeframe: Insulin resistance appears within days of bed rest.
dose.notes: Moderate-to-vigorous activity offsets much of the risk linked to high sitting time.

entries.mechanism: Loss of muscle contraction reduces glucose uptake and mitochondrial capacity; over time this leads to fat gain, hyperglycemia and inflammation, which raise ROS from NADPH oxidase and mitochondria.
entries.interactions: Reversed by [aerobic-exercise-moderate]; worsens [weight-loss] and [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: A careful bed-rest study found no rise in muscle mitochondrial H2O2 or oxidative markers despite large insulin resistance, so 'sitting causes oxidative stress' is not established directly.
entries.title: Prolonged sitting and physical inactivity

entries.headline: Chronic stress and depression are associated with higher oxidative damage markers (depression: F2-isoprostanes effect size ~0.5), but causality and the size of any modifiable effect are uncertain.

dose.effective: Treat depression and anxiety with proven methods (therapy, medication when indicated, exercise, sleep); reduce chronic stressors where possible.
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional comparisons of high vs low perceived stress and depressed vs non-depressed groups.
dose.timeframe: Unknown for oxidative markers.
dose.notes: Exercise and sleep improvements are the best-evidenced stress interventions that also affect oxidative stress.
