entries.mechanism: Chronic stress raises cortisol and catecholamines, increases metabolic rate and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), and is associated with lower telomerase activity; catecholamine auto-oxidation produces ROS.
entries.interactions: Stress worsens [short-sleep], drinking ([alcohol]), smoking and eating, which are likely bigger oxidative contributors than stress itself.
entries.caveats: The famous Epel 2004 study was cross-sectional in 58 women; it shows association, not cause. Confounding by health behaviours is likely in most studies.
entries.title: Chronic psychological stress and depression

entries.headline: A high salivary alpha-amylase stress marker was linked to 29% lower fecundability in one cohort, but a meta-analysis of 3583 IVF patients found pre-treatment anxiety or depression did not affect pregnancy rates.

dose.effective: Stress management for wellbeing (counselling, CBT, mindfulness, exercise); not proven to raise pregnancy rates.
dose.notes: Reassure people that stress caused by infertility does not ruin their IVF chances.

entries.mechanism: Sympathetic and HPA-axis activation can suppress GnRH/LH and raise systemic oxidative stress, but direct evidence of oocyte damage in humans is lacking.
entries.interactions: Linked with [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Reverse causation (infertility causes stress) is likely in many studies; avoid blaming patients.
entries.title: Psychological stress

entries.headline: A glass of red wine contains well under 1 mg trans-resveratrol, oral resveratrol is almost entirely conjugated before it reaches blood, and urinary resveratrol levels did not predict mortality; the ethanol itself raises lipid peroxidation in a dose-dependent way.

dose.effective: No antioxidant reason to drink. If you drink, wine polyphenols taken with a fatty meal may limit postprandial lipid oxidation in the stomach (animal data).
dose.studied_range: Resveratrol supplements in trials range from tens to thousands of mg; a 25 mg oral dose left <5 ng/mL free resveratrol in plasma.
dose.too_much: Alcohol raises urinary isoprostanes dose-dependently; see [alcohol].
dose.notes: Trans-resveratrol ~0.18 mg/100 mL (about 0.3 mg per 150 mL glass), so reaching supplement doses would take hundreds of glasses.

entries.mechanism: Resveratrol is absorbed (~70%) but rapidly sulfated and glucuronidated; wine's other polyphenols (anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols) are similar to those in grapes and berries without the ethanol.
entries.interactions: Ethanol counteracts the polyphenols; grapes, berries or dealcoholised wine provide the polyphenols without it.
entries.caveats: Associations of urinary resveratrol metabolites with better lipids in PREDIMED are cross-sectional and confounded by wine drinking patterns.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, chromatography, red wine (sum of compounds)
Free resveratrol in plasma after 25 mg oral dose

entries.title: Red wine and resveratrol

factors.name: Refined sugar, sugary drinks & high-GI meals

entries.headline: A 75 g glucose drink more than doubled leukocyte ROS generation at 2 h in healthy people and lowered plasma vitamin E; large post-meal glucose and triglyceride spikes drive transient oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction.

dose.effective: Limit sugary drinks and large refined-starch meals; pair carbohydrates with fiber, protein, fat and vinegar or acidic foods.
dose.studied_range: 75 g oral glucose; single high-fat or high-carbohydrate meals.
dose.too_much: Repeated large spikes; sugar-sweetened beverages.
dose.timeframe: Peaks at 1-3 h after the meal.
dose.notes: Cream (fat) and casein (protein) also raised leukocyte ROS, so the size of the meal matters, not only sugar.

entries.mechanism: Nutrient surges increase leukocyte NADPH oxidase (p47phox) and mitochondrial superoxide; hyperglycemia fuels AGE and polyol pathways and NF-kB activation.
entries.interactions: Additive with [overfeeding]. Blunted by [whole-grains], [legumes], [dietary-fiber-microbiome] and polyphenol-rich foods with the meal (e.g. [tomatoes-lycopene], [herbs-spices]).
entries.caveats: Acute leukocyte ROS assays are not the same as chronic tissue damage; whether postprandial spikes in non-diabetic people cause disease independent of overall diet is debated.

key_numbers.label: Peak leukocyte (PMNL) ROS after 75 g glucose

entries.title: Refined sugar and high-glycemic meals

entries.headline: Young men drinking 1.3+ sugary drinks a day had about 10 points lower progressive motility.

dose.effective: Under one sugary drink a week; water, unsweetened tea or coffee instead.
dose.studied_range: <0.2 to >=1.3 servings/day.
dose.too_much: >=1.3 servings/day associated with lower motility.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Caffeinated soft drinks also looked worse than coffee in reviews.

entries.mechanism: Glycaemic load drives insulin resistance, advanced glycation end-products and inflammation.
entries.interactions: Linked with [excess-adiposity].
entries.caveats: Cross-sectional, single semen sample; association only in lean men.
entries.title: Sugar-sweetened beverages

entries.headline: Reheating PUFA-rich oils generates lipid hydroperoxides and aldehydes that are partly absorbed; humans excrete more MDA after eating oxidized fat, and animal studies show raised blood pressure and vascular inflammation.

dose.effective: Avoid reused deep-frying oil and burnt or smoking oil; prefer EVOO or high-oleic oils for heat.
dose.studied_range: Mostly animal feeding studies; human postprandial studies.
dose.too_much: Repeatedly heated oil (common in fast food) is the main exposure.
dose.timeframe: Postprandial and chronic.
dose.notes: Polyphenols eaten in the same meal reduced stomach lipid peroxidation in animal models.

entries.mechanism: Thermal oxidation of linoleic and linolenic acids forms hydroperoxides, 4-hydroxynonenal, acrolein and other advanced lipid oxidation end-products that are absorbed and inflame the gut, liver and vessels.
entries.interactions: Worsens [processed-red-meat]; offset partly by [herbs-spices], [extra-virgin-olive-oil].
entries.caveats: Human outcome data are sparse; the evidence is largely mechanistic and from rodents.
entries.title: Repeatedly heated / oxidized frying oils

entries.headline: Strength training raises glutathione peroxidase in older adults but has inconsistent effects on other antioxidant markers; its main value is muscle and metabolic health.

dose.effective: At least 2 sessions/week (WHO) on non-consecutive days covering the major muscle groups; a common program is 2-3 sets of 8-12 repetitions per exercise, stopping a couple of reps short of failure.
dose.studied_range: RCTs in older adults typically used 2-3 sessions/week for 8-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Rapid jumps in weekly volume caused large oxidative-stress rises in an overreaching study (isoprostanes up 7-fold at peak load).
dose.timeframe: 8-12 weeks for enzyme changes.
dose.notes: WHO recommends muscle strengthening on >=2 days/week in addition to aerobic activity.

entries.mechanism: Mechanical and metabolic stress cause local ROS production and inflammation-linked repair; repeated stimulus up-regulates glutathione peroxidase. Added muscle mass improves glucose disposal, indirectly lowering glycemic oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: High-dose vitamin C/E blunted lean-mass gains in older men ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). Post-workout [cold-water-immersion] blunted strength and muscle gains.
entries.caveats: Meta-analysis found a small decrease in SOD and no change in catalase, so 'strength training is an antioxidant' is an overstatement.
entries.title: Resistance (strength) training

factors.name: Sauna, hot tubs & hot baths
aliases: Saunas, hot tubs and hot baths

entries.headline: Frequent sauna use is linked to lower cardiovascular death and inflammation in Finnish cohorts, and heat therapy improves vascular function in trials, but direct oxidative-stress benefits are unproven; sauna clearly impairs sperm (reversibly).

dose.effective: Cohort 'high' group: 4-7 sessions/week, sessions longer than 19 min, in a traditional Finnish sauna (hot and dry, ~80-90 C as in the sperm study); trial: 40.5 C hot-water immersion for 60 min, 4-5x/week for 8 weeks.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 1 to 4-7 sessions/week, <11 to >19 min; sperm study: 2 x 15 min/week at 80-90 C for 3 months.
dose.too_much: Men trying to conceive should avoid sauna: 2 sessions/week at 80-90 C for 3 months reduced sperm count and motility and damaged chromatin; avoid alcohol in the sauna; caution with unstable heart disease, pregnancy and low blood pressure.
dose.timeframe: Vascular changes in 8 weeks; sperm recovered ~6 months after stopping.
dose.notes: Cohort men who used saunas more often were also fitter and healthier; benefits may partly reflect that.

entries.mechanism: Heat stress induces heat-shock proteins, increases shear stress and nitric oxide production (like exercise), and may trigger mild hormetic ROS signalling. For testes, heat disrupts spermatogenesis and increases sperm oxidative/chromatin damage.
entries.interactions: Partially mimics [aerobic-exercise-moderate] vascular effects but is not a substitute for exercise. Cross-link to sperm area: heat is a strong, reversible harm to sperm.
entries.caveats: The KIHD cohort found no association between sauna frequency and GGT (the oxidative-stress proxy studied) despite lower CRP. Oxidative claims for sauna are mostly extrapolation.
entries.title: Sauna bathing (Finnish sauna) and passive heat

entries.headline: Regular sauna or hot-tub use reversibly damages sperm count, motility and chromatin packaging; effects take 3-6 months to clear.

dose.effective: Avoid while trying to conceive. Harm shown with sauna at 80-90 C for 15 min twice a week for 3 months, and with scrotal water at 43 C for 30 min on 10 occasions.
dose.studied_range: Sauna 80-90 C x 15 min, 2x/week, 12 weeks; scrotal bath 43 C x 30 min, daily or every 3 days, 10 sessions; habitual hot tubs/baths.
dose.too_much: Testes work best about 2-4 C below core temperature; any wet heat above ~40 C held for 30 min is a risk. Daily (consecutive) exposure was worse than intermittent.
dose.timeframe: Recovery by about 16 weeks after short exposure and fully by 6 months after 3 months of sauna use.
dose.notes: If you will not give it up, keep sessions short, sit with the scrotum away from hot surfaces, and stop for at least 3 months before trying.

entries.mechanism: Scrotal hyperthermia disrupts histone-to-protamine exchange and mitochondrial function in developing sperm, raises heat-shock and hypoxia gene expression and triggers apoptosis, making DNA more susceptible to oxidative breaks.
entries.interactions: Adds to [varicocele] and [everyday-scrotal-heat]. Same pathway as [febrile-illness].
entries.caveats: Trials are small (10-20 normozoospermic men), but they are interventional with clear reversal, so causality is convincing. Benefits of sauna for cardiovascular health are real; this is a temporary trade-off.

key_numbers.label: Total motile count rise after stopping hot tubs (responders)

entries.title: Saunas, hot tubs and hot baths

entries.headline: Secondhand smoke raises coronary heart disease risk about 30%, and even brief exposures produce vascular and oxidative effects averaging 80-90% of active smoking.

dose.effective: Keep home and car completely smoke-free; avoid indoor smoky venues.
dose.studied_range: Experimental exposures of 30 min to a few hours; cohort exposure from household smoking.
dose.too_much: No safe level identified for cardiovascular effects; 30 min of exposure impaired coronary flow reserve in healthy nonsmokers.
dose.timeframe: Acute vascular effects within minutes to hours.
dose.notes: Ventilation and smoking in another room do not remove the exposure.

entries.mechanism: Sidestream smoke contains the same radical-generating tar and oxidant gases as mainstream smoke; tar from secondhand smoke generates H2O2 and breaks DNA in cells.
entries.interactions: Adds to [outdoor-air-pollution] and [indoor-combustion-smoke].
entries.caveats: One cross-sectional study of women with modest exposure (>=15 min, 2 days/week) found no difference in 8-isoprostane, so low-level exposure may not show up on systemic markers even though vascular effects are documented.
entries.title: Secondhand (passive) smoke

entries.headline: No cancer prevention (Cochrane RR 1.01). In people who already have adequate selenium, 200 µg/day may raise type 2 diabetes risk (HR 1.55) and high-grade prostate cancer (+91%). Benefit is plausible only if status is low.

dose.effective: Only correct a documented deficiency or very low intake. Most people in North America get enough from food.
dose.studied_range: 100 µg/day (SU.VI.MAX) to 200 µg/day selenomethionine or selenised yeast (SELECT, NPC)
dose.too_much: 200 µg/day in replete people: diabetes HR 1.55 (2.70 in top baseline tertile); high-grade prostate cancer +91% if baseline selenium is high.
dose.timeframe: Diabetes signal over ~7.7 years; prostate cancer over 5-7 years
dose.notes: U-shaped relationship with health.

entries.mechanism: Selenium is the active-site element of glutathione peroxidases and thioredoxin reductases, so deficiency impairs peroxide removal. Above repletion there is no further gain, and the reason for the diabetes signal in replete people is not established.
entries.interactions: Interacts with vitamin E status in prostate cancer risk [vitamin-e-supplement]. Selenium co-treatment enhanced sulforaphane's cytoprotection in vitro, but this has not been studied in humans.
entries.caveats: Cancer results from trials have been mixed, and SELECT and the Cochrane review found no benefit. Many 'antioxidant' blends include 50-200 µg selenium, which adds to dietary intake.
entries.title: Selenium supplements

entries.headline: Selenium helps motility mainly in men with low selenium status; little reason to supplement if diet is adequate.

dose.effective: About 100-200 ug/day only if intake is low (e.g. parts of Europe); 1-2 Brazil nuts provide a similar amount.
dose.studied_range: 3 months of selenium with or without vitamins A, C, E (69 men); MOXI used 200 ug.
dose.too_much: Do not exceed the US tolerable upper intake of 400 ug/day; chronic excess causes selenosis.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

entries.mechanism: Cofactor of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPx4), which becomes a structural protein of the sperm midpiece and protects against lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: Part of [male-antioxidant-combination].
entries.caveats: Small, older trials; benefit limited to deficient men.
entries.title: Selenium

entries.headline: Cutting sleep raises oxidative stress in human studies (endothelial oxidative stress after 6 weeks of 1.5 h less sleep; lower glutathione after one sleepless night), but the dramatic 'sleep loss kills via gut ROS' finding is from flies and mice.

dose.effective: 7-9 h per night on a regular schedule (adults; AASM/SRS: 7 h or more).
dose.studied_range: Human studies: one night of total deprivation; 6 weeks of 1.5 h/night restriction; observational comparison of <=6 h vs >8 h.
dose.too_much: Regularly <=6 h was associated with ~12% higher urinary 8-isoprostane; chronic restriction increased endothelial oxidative stress.
dose.timeframe: Glutathione drop after a single night; endothelial changes within 6 weeks.
dose.notes: Consistency matters as well as duration. Treat sleep apnea if present (see [sleep-apnea]).

entries.mechanism: Wakefulness raises metabolic rate and sympathetic tone, consumes glutathione and cysteine, and reduces melatonin (itself a radical scavenger and regulator of DNA repair). In animals, ROS accumulate in the gut with severe deprivation. Short sleep also worsens insulin resistance and appetite regulation.
entries.interactions: Interacts with [shift-work-circadian]. Poor sleep worsens [glycemic-control] and weight gain ([weight-loss]) and impairs recovery from [overtraining-ultraendurance].
entries.caveats: Vaccaro 2020 (Cell) was done in flies and mice with extreme deprivation; antioxidants rescued survival there, which does not mean antioxidant pills replace sleep in humans. Human data are small or observational.
entries.title: Short or insufficient sleep

entries.headline: Sleeping under 6 hours or over 9 hours, or poor sleep quality, is associated with roughly 15-20% lower sperm counts, but estimates are imprecise.

dose.effective: 7-9 hours per night with regular timing.
dose.studied_range: <6 h, 7-8.9 h and >=9 h per night; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index >5 vs <=5.
dose.too_much: Both short and long sleep were associated with lower counts.
dose.timeframe: Unknown; plausibly one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: No SDF-specific human data.

entries.mechanism: Sleep loss lowers testosterone and raises systemic inflammation and oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: Interlinked with [excess-adiposity].
entries.caveats: Observational; confidence intervals mostly cross zero.
entries.title: Short or poor-quality sleep

entries.headline: Frequent trouble sleeping was associated with about 13% lower monthly chance of conception; shift work is linked to menstrual disruption and night shifts to early miscarriage, but not clearly to infertility.

dose.effective: Aim for 7-9 h/night with a regular schedule; treat insomnia and sleep apnea.
dose.studied_range: Sleep < 6 to >= 9 h/day; shift vs day work.
dose.too_much: Trouble sleeping > 50% of nights: FR 0.87; night shifts: aOR 1.41 for early pregnancy loss.
dose.notes: Melatonin supplements are discussed separately ([melatonin]); they are not a substitute for sleep.

entries.mechanism: Ovarian and pituitary clocks regulate the LH surge; circadian disruption alters melatonin (a follicular antioxidant), cortisol and insulin sensitivity.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [psychological-stress]. The shift-work findings also apply to [shift-work-circadian].
entries.caveats: Observational and confounded by depression and stress; shift work-infertility association lost significance after adjustment.

key_numbers.label: Fecundability, trouble sleeping > 50% of the time

entries.title: Poor sleep and circadian disruption

entries.headline: Soy does not change male hormones in clinical trials and male soy intake was unrelated to IVF success; one small study linked very high intake to lower concentration.

dose.effective: Normal dietary amounts (1-2 servings/day of tofu, soy milk, edamame) are fine.
dose.studied_range: Up to the highest intake category in 99 clinic patients; 41 clinical studies of hormones.
dose.too_much: Very high intake (top of distribution) associated with 41 million/mL lower concentration in one study, mainly in overweight men.

entries.mechanism: Isoflavones are weak phytoestrogens; hormone-level trials show no feminising effect in men.
entries.interactions: Can replace [processed-meat] as protein.
entries.caveats: The negative association comes from one small cross-sectional study.
entries.title: Soy foods

entries.headline: A daily standard multivitamin cut total cancer by about 8% in older men (PHS II), with no cardiovascular effect. USPSTF rates the evidence insufficient. It works as nutrient insurance, not as an antioxidant.

dose.effective: One standard multivitamin/mineral daily with nutrients near RDA levels (not 'mega' or 'antioxidant formula').
dose.studied_range: RDA-level combinations; SU.VI.MAX: vitamin C 120 mg, E 30 mg, beta-carotene 6 mg, Se 100 µg, Zn 20 mg
dose.too_much: Avoid formulas with high-dose beta-carotene or vitamin A (especially smokers), vitamin E ≥400 IU, or selenium ≥200 µg.
dose.timeframe: Cancer effect seen after ~11 years in PHS II; 7.5 years in SU.VI.MAX
dose.notes: Benefit is most plausible in people with poor diets or low baseline status (SU.VI.MAX: effect in men, who had lower baseline beta-carotene).

entries.mechanism: Probably corrects marginal micronutrient shortfalls, including selenium, zinc and B vitamins that support endogenous antioxidant enzymes and DNA synthesis and repair, rather than any scavenging effect.
entries.interactions: Do not confuse with [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]. Adds to dietary selenium and vitamin A [selenium-supplement] [beta-carotene-supplement].
entries.caveats: Evidence comes mostly from male physicians and French adults; the results may not transfer to women or well-nourished groups. The effect size is small and USPSTF calls the evidence insufficient.
entries.title: Standard multivitamin/mineral (nutritional doses)

entries.headline: Product type decides everything: glucoraphanin-only pills (no active myrosinase) convert only ~5-20% and very unevenly, whereas sulforaphane-rich or myrosinase-active products deliver ~70% and far more consistently.

dose.effective: Products that deliver free sulforaphane or include active myrosinase, at doses in the tens of µmol sulforaphane per day.
dose.studied_range: 25-225 µmol/day sulforaphane in trials; glucoraphanin 25-600 µmol/day.
dose.too_much: Not established; doses above ~200 µmol/day are poorly tolerated (taste, GI).
dose.timeframe: Hours (pulsatile); daily dosing showed no decline in bioavailability over 12 weeks.
dose.notes: Check whether the label states active myrosinase or stabilised sulforaphane. A glucoraphanin-only supplement produced dramatically lower plasma isothiocyanates than 40 g fresh sprouts. Taking glucoraphanin plus sulforaphane blends gives a peak plus a slower, steadier tail.

entries.mechanism: Nrf2 activation. Glucoraphanin without myrosinase depends on gut microbial myrosinase-like activity, which antibiotics and bowel cleansing abolish and which differs greatly between people.
entries.interactions: Redundant with [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder]. Interindividual 'converter' status is fairly stable within a person, so poor converters gain more from myrosinase-active forms.
entries.caveats: Commercial labels are often unverified (independent assay did not match the claimed dose in one diabetes trial). The COPD trial at 150 µmol/day showed no target-gene induction in lung cells. Long-term strong Nrf2 activation still has open safety questions. One 2-month RCT of glucoraphanin capsules in men with fatty liver reported lower ALT and urinary 8-OHdG.
entries.title: Sulforaphane / broccoli extract supplements

factors.name: Sun/UV exposure (skin oxidative damage vs vitamin D)

entries.headline: UV is a major source of oxidative damage to skin (photoaging, DNA damage), and daily sunscreen slowed skin aging by 24% in an RCT; vitamin D is better obtained by brief exposure or supplements than by tanning.

dose.effective: Avoid sunburn; apply broad-spectrum sunscreen daily to exposed skin (as in the Nambour trial), reapply during long outdoor periods, and use shade and clothing around midday.
dose.studied_range: Nambour RCT: daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years in adults under 55.
dose.too_much: Sunburn and cumulative high exposure; tanning beds.
dose.timeframe: Skin-aging differences measurable over years.
dose.notes: If vitamin D is low, short sub-burning exposures or a modest supplement can correct it; vitamin D pills did not prevent cancer or heart disease in VITAL.

entries.mechanism: UVB directly damages DNA (pyrimidine dimers); UVA is absorbed by skin chromophores that generate singlet oxygen and superoxide, causing 8-oxoguanine, lipid peroxidation and collagen-degrading MMP induction.
entries.interactions: Smoking and air pollution add to skin oxidative aging ([tobacco-smoking], [outdoor-air-pollution]).
entries.caveats: Systemic (whole-body) oxidative-marker effects of normal sun exposure are not well documented; the evidence is about skin. Organic filters that soak in can increase skin ROS after about an hour, one more reason to reapply.
entries.title: Sun/UV exposure (skin oxidative damage vs vitamin D)

factors.name: Testicular sperm for ICSI when ejaculated SDF stays high

entries.headline: Sperm taken directly from the testis have about 25 percentage points less DNA fragmentation than ejaculated sperm, and pooled studies show higher pregnancy and live birth with ICSI.

dose.effective: Testicular sperm aspiration/extraction (TESA/TESE) for ICSI in non-azoospermic men with confirmed high SDF, usually after failed IVF/ICSI or recurrent miscarriage.
dose.studied_range: 5 studies with paired SDF (143 men); 4 studies, 507 cycles with clinical outcomes.
dose.too_much: Invasive; small risks of bleeding, infection and testicular damage; testicular sperm have higher aneuploidy in some studies.
dose.timeframe: Single procedure at the time of egg retrieval.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM 2024: may consider. EAU: experimental (weak). Try reversible causes and short-abstinence ejaculates first; a meta-analysis found testicular SDF ~9.5 points lower than short-abstinence ejaculates.

entries.mechanism: Much oxidative DNA damage occurs during epididymal transit and storage, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS; testicular sperm bypass this exposure.
entries.interactions: Compare with [short-abstinence], which reduces epididymal storage time non-invasively.
entries.caveats: Evidence is from small, mostly non-randomised studies. Not appropriate as first-line care.
entries.title: Testicular sperm for ICSI when ejaculated SDF stays high

entries.headline: Smoking roughly doubles plasma F2-isoprostanes, which fall measurably within 2 weeks of quitting. It raises urinary 8-OHdG and turns beta-carotene supplements harmful.

dose.effective: Complete cessation.
dose.too_much: Any smoking
dose.timeframe: F2-isoprostanes fell significantly after 2 weeks of abstinence
dose.notes: Smokers should avoid beta-carotene and high-dose vitamin A supplements.

entries.mechanism: Cigarette smoke delivers large amounts of radicals and oxidants directly and recruits activated inflammatory cells to the lung. Tumours with activating NRF2 mutations are enriched in smokers.
entries.interactions: Strongly interacts with [beta-carotene-supplement] (lung cancer RR 1.18-1.28). NRF2-mutant tumours occur especially in smokers.
entries.caveats: No antioxidant supplement offsets smoking.
entries.title: Tobacco smoking

entries.headline: Smoking roughly doubles circulating F2-isoprostanes in a dose-dependent way; quitting lowers them within 2 weeks and to a new steady state by about 4 weeks, making it the single largest lifestyle lever.

dose.effective: Quit completely. In an RCT, cutting down from ~27 to ~18 cigarettes/day did not lower F2-isoprostanes or any other harm marker except carbon monoxide.
dose.studied_range: Studies compared heavy, moderate and non-smokers; cessation studies followed people from 2 weeks to 1 year.
dose.too_much: No safe level: urinary 8-epi-PGF2a was ~1.7x the nonsmoker level in moderate and ~3.3x in heavy smokers.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostanes fall within days, are ~20-40% lower at 2-3 weeks, and plateau about 4 weeks after quitting; cardiovascular risk falls ~39% within 5 years but takes 10-15+ years to approach never-smoker levels.
dose.notes: Nicotine replacement did not prevent the fall in isoprostanes, suggesting combustion products, not nicotine, drive most of it.

entries.mechanism: Each puff delivers large amounts of free radicals in the gas and tar phases (semiquinone radicals, NO, peroxynitrite, H2O2), plus metals and aldehydes. Smoke also activates neutrophils and vascular NADPH oxidase, depletes vitamin C and E, and uncouples eNOS.
entries.interactions: Effects add to [alcohol], [secondhand-smoke] and [outdoor-air-pollution]. Weight gain after quitting does not cancel the drop in oxidative markers. Smoking is also the main source of cadmium ([heavy-metals]) and worsens [periodontal-disease].
entries.caveats: Five days of 2 g/day vitamin C lowered smokers' isoprostanes in Reilly 1996 (vitamin E alone did not), but that is not a substitute for quitting. Smoking harms sperm parameters (meta-analysis) and is relevant to egg health (cross-link to fertility areas).
entries.title: Smoking tobacco (and quitting)

entries.headline: Smokers average about 9 percentage points higher SDF and lower count, motility and morphology; quitting improves semen within 3-6 months.

dose.effective: Quit completely; harm rises with cigarettes per day (moderate/heavy smokers, roughly >10/day, show larger effects).
dose.studied_range: Light (<10/day) to heavy (>20/day) smokers in clinic and population samples.
dose.too_much: No safe level identified; avoid second-hand smoke too.
dose.timeframe: Semen improved at 3 months and further at 6 months after quitting.
dose.notes: Nicotine replacement is far less harmful than smoking. Vaping data for sperm are sparse.

entries.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers oxidants, cadmium, lead and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; seminal leukocytes and ROS rise, antioxidant levels fall, and sperm show more 8-OHdG and strand breaks.
entries.interactions: Stacks with [varicocele] and [outdoor-air-pollution]. Non-responders to stopping heat exposure in one series were mostly smokers. Antioxidant pills do not offset smoking.
entries.caveats: Effects on standard semen parameters are moderate; the clearest harm is on DNA integrity and on offspring and partner health.
entries.title: Tobacco smoking

entries.headline: Smoking is the largest avoidable toxic exposure for eggs: about 60% higher odds of infertility, roughly halved odds of IVF live birth (OR 0.54), lower AMH and twice the risk of early menopause.

dose.effective: Zero. Risk is dose-dependent (cigarettes/day, years smoked, pack-years).
dose.studied_range: Current vs never smokers; dose-response up to >20 cigarettes/day and 15-20+ years.
dose.too_much: Any active smoking. 11-15 pack-years: ~4-fold risk of premature menopause; 15-20 years' duration: much higher.
dose.timeframe: Quitting at least 3 months before trying covers one follicle-growth cycle; menopause-timing risk normalises about 10 years after quitting.
dose.notes: ASRM's 2024 opinion also reviews nicotine and marijuana as potential reproductive harms.

entries.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cadmium and other oxidants that accelerate follicle loss (lower AMH), raise follicular oxidative stress and impair oocyte maturation.
entries.interactions: Adds to [maternal-age]. Cadmium overlaps with [heavy-metals]. Cessation is covered by [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Evidence is observational, but consistent across designs and dose-dependent, which supports causation.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per cycle, smokers

entries.title: Cigarette smoking

entries.headline: Quitting removes the biggest avoidable egg toxin; former smokers' excess menopause risk is much smaller than current smokers' and disappears about 10 years after quitting.

dose.effective: Complete cessation, ideally at least 3 months before trying or before IVF stimulation.
dose.studied_range: Former vs current smokers, years since quitting.
dose.timeframe: One follicle-growth cycle (~3 months) for the follicular environment; longer for ovarian-reserve effects.
dose.notes: Lost follicles are not regained, so earlier is better. Use evidence-based cessation support.

entries.mechanism: Removes the exogenous oxidant and toxicant load (PAHs, cadmium) on growing follicles.
entries.interactions: See [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: No RCT has randomised women to quit and measured egg quality; the benefit is inferred from the dose-response and former-smoker data.
entries.title: Stopping smoking

factors.name: Tomatoes and tomato products (cooked with oil)

entries.headline: Lycopene is 2.5-3.8x more bioavailable from tomato paste than fresh tomatoes and needs fat to be absorbed; tomato interventions lower LDL and IL-6, improve FMD, and blunted LDL oxidation after a high-fat meal.

dose.effective: A serving of cooked tomato product (sauce, paste, puree) with a little olive oil most days.
dose.studied_range: 21 intervention trials of tomato products or lycopene; single meals with processed tomato.
dose.timeframe: Postprandial (same meal) for oxLDL; weeks for lipids and FMD.
dose.notes: Tomato puree has ~8x the lycopene of raw tomato per 100 g (USDA). Fat-free dressing gave essentially no carotenoid absorption from salad.

entries.mechanism: Lycopene is a lipid-phase singlet-oxygen quencher carried in LDL; processing breaks cell walls and isomerises lycopene, improving absorption; tomato also supplies vitamin C and naringenin chalcone.
entries.interactions: Pair with [extra-virgin-olive-oil] or avocado; eat with high-fat meals to blunt postprandial oxidation.
entries.caveats: Lycopene supplements lowered systolic BP in pooled trials but tomato products, not pills, gave the lipid and FMD effects. Most trials are short.

key_numbers.label: Lycopene AUC, paste vs fresh tomato

entries.title: Tomatoes and tomato products (cooked with oil)

entries.headline: A placebo-controlled trial of 14 mg/day lycopene improved fast motility and morphology, but missed its primary endpoint; no SDF data.

dose.effective: About 14 mg lycopene/day, roughly half a cup of tomato sauce or passata (content varies by product); cooked tomato with some oil is better absorbed than raw.
dose.studied_range: 14 mg/day lactolycopene for 12 weeks in 60 healthy men.
dose.timeframe: 12 weeks.
dose.notes: Getting lycopene from food also brings other carotenoids and fibre.

entries.mechanism: Lycopene is a potent singlet-oxygen quencher concentrated in the testes and seminal fluid.
entries.interactions: Part of [mediterranean-diet]; included in the MOXI supplement (10 mg), which was null.
entries.caveats: Single small trial in healthy men; primary outcome (motile sperm concentration) not significant (p=0.058).
entries.title: Tomatoes and lycopene

entries.headline: Curcumin is barely absorbed: 2 g alone gave undetectable or very low serum levels; 20 mg piperine raised bioavailability ~20-fold, but culinary turmeric doses are far below trial doses.

dose.effective: No reliable systemic antioxidant dose from culinary use; trials use 0.5-2 g/day curcumin, often enhanced formulations.
dose.studied_range: Up to 12 g/day curcumin was tolerated in phase I trials.
dose.too_much: Phase I trials tolerated up to 12 g/day; piperine works by inhibiting glucuronidation, the same pathway that clears many drugs.
dose.notes: A teaspoon (~3 g) of dried turmeric contains roughly 65 mg curcumin (Phenol-Explorer ~2.2 g/100 g).

entries.mechanism: Curcumin is a Michael acceptor that activates Nrf2 and scavenges radicals in vitro; rapid glucuronidation and poor absorption limit systemic exposure.
entries.interactions: Black pepper (piperine) increases absorption; fat helps.
entries.caveats: Classic case of strong in vitro data with weak human pharmacokinetics.
entries.title: Turmeric / curcumin

entries.headline: A routine 19 mg/day ferrous sulfate supplement for 2 weeks raised weakly bound fecal iron 5-fold and the fecal free-radical generating capacity by ~40% in healthy volunteers.

dose.effective: Take iron only to correct documented deficiency.
dose.studied_range: 19 mg elemental iron/day for 2 weeks.
dose.too_much: Iron supplements in iron-replete people; untreated hereditary hemochromatosis.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Most supplemental iron is not absorbed and stays in the colon.

entries.mechanism: Free ferrous iron drives Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 -> hydroxyl radical) and catalyses lipid peroxidation; heme iron from meat acts similarly in the gut.
entries.interactions: Avoid combining with high-dose vitamin C in iron overload. Tea and coffee reduce non-heme iron absorption.
entries.caveats: Fecal free-radical capacity is an ex vivo assay; systemic consequences not measured.

key_numbers.label: Rise in fecal free-radical production on 19 mg Fe/day

entries.title: Unneeded iron supplements / iron excess

entries.headline: Not linked to worse semen quality. In young US men unprocessed red meat showed no association with any semen measure, and a Chinese case-control study linked higher unprocessed meat intake to lower odds of poor motility (OR 0.61). The negative meat signal for sperm comes from processed meat.

dose.effective: No evidence-based target. Normal portions of unprocessed red meat are compatible with sperm health; cooking method may matter more than the meat itself.
dose.studied_range: Food-frequency quartiles/tertiles of habitual intake.
dose.timeframe: ~2-3 months (one spermatogenic cycle) for any dietary change to show in semen.
dose.notes: Red meat is a dense source of zinc, vitamin B12, iron and carnitine, which sperm production needs. That matters most if intake is low (e.g. restrictive diets). In men who were not deficient, adding 30 mg/day zinc (with folic acid) did not improve semen or live birth in the large FAZST trial.

entries.mechanism: No direct human evidence that red meat improves spermatogenesis or spermiogenesis. The plausible route is nutrient supply (zinc, B12, iron, carnitine) in people with low intake. The oxidative concerns that apply to processed meat (nitrites, preformed N-nitroso compounds) do not apply to fresh meat, while high-heat or stir-fry cooking can add oxidized products.
entries.interactions: Contrast with [processed-meat]. High-heat cooking was associated with worse motility in the case-control study. Extra zinc on top of an adequate diet did not help ([folate-zinc]).
entries.caveats: Two observational studies with different populations; no trials. The case-control result could reflect overall diet or recall bias. Absence of harm is not proof of benefit.
entries.title: Unprocessed red meat (beef, pork, lamb)

entries.headline: Repeated night-time oxygen drops and re-oxygenation act like ischemia-reperfusion; CPAP treatment raised total antioxidant capacity in a meta-analysis.

dose.effective: Get tested if you snore loudly, stop breathing during sleep, or have daytime sleepiness; use CPAP or other prescribed therapy nightly.
dose.studied_range: CPAP studies of weeks to months.
dose.timeframe: Changes within weeks to months of consistent CPAP use.
dose.notes: Weight loss often reduces apnea severity.

entries.mechanism: Cycles of hypoxia and re-oxygenation activate NADPH oxidase and xanthine oxidase and cause mitochondrial ROS bursts, much like ischemia-reperfusion injury.
entries.interactions: Strongly linked to [weight-loss]; worsened by [alcohol] at night.
entries.caveats: Total antioxidant capacity is a crude marker; studies are heterogeneous.
entries.title: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea

entries.headline: Repairing a clinical varicocele lowers SDF by about 7 percentage points on average, and more when SDF starts high.

dose.effective: One procedure (microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy is the reference technique) in men with a palpable varicocele plus abnormal semen or high SDF.
dose.studied_range: 19 studies, 1070 men; SCSA, TUNEL and SCD all showed reductions.
dose.timeframe: Re-test semen/SDF about 3-6 months after surgery; one spermatogenic cycle is ~64-74 days.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: consider varicocelectomy in men trying to conceive with palpable varicocele, infertility and abnormal semen (not azoospermia). EAU adds that the female partner should have good ovarian reserve, because the benefit takes months.

entries.mechanism: Removes venous reflux, restoring testicular cooling and oxygenation and cutting seminal ROS, which lowers oxidative DNA damage in newly made sperm.
entries.interactions: Lifestyle changes ([tobacco-smoking], [sauna]) should be made in parallel. If the female partner is older, time may favour going straight to ART, optionally with [testicular-sperm-icsi] or short abstinence [short-abstinence].
entries.caveats: The SDF drop is solid; the pregnancy benefit is less certain (Cochrane: pregnancy RR 1.55, low certainty; live birth uncertain). Not useful for subclinical varicocele with normal semen.
entries.title: Varicocele repair (microsurgical varicocelectomy or embolisation)

factors.name: Vigorous exercise and high-intensity interval training (HIIT)

entries.headline: Vigorous training (including low-volume HIIT) produced larger improvements in antioxidant status than non-vigorous training in a 2025 meta-analysis of RCTs; keep total volume moderate.

dose.effective: 75-150 min/week of vigorous activity (hard breathing, only a few words at a time), or 2-3 interval sessions/week, e.g. 4-6 x 4-6 min at >90% of maximum heart rate with easy recovery between (the Paulsen 2014 protocol).
dose.studied_range: Trials used 2-4 sessions/week for 6-16 weeks; Paulsen 2014 combined 4-6 x 4-6 min intervals at >90% HRmax with 30-60 min steady sessions at 70-90% HRmax, 3-4 times/week.
dose.too_much: High intensity combined with high volume (daily hard sessions, many hours/week) carries the highest oxidative load; in one study ramping training load over 4 weeks impaired mitochondrial function and glucose tolerance.
dose.timeframe: Antioxidant-enzyme changes in 6-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Low-volume HIIT gives much of the redox benefit for less time. Allow 48 h between very hard sessions.

entries.mechanism: Higher intensity gives a larger ROS and calcium signal per session, which drives stronger Nrf2 and PGC-1alpha responses (hormesis). Excess volume leads to sustained ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction and glutathione depletion.
entries.interactions: Same caution about [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]. Combines with [resistance-training]. Volume beyond recovery capacity leads to [overtraining-ultraendurance].
entries.caveats: The meta-analysis included only 7 RCTs (267 people). 'More intense is better' holds only while total volume and recovery stay reasonable.
entries.title: Vigorous exercise and high-intensity interval training (HIIT)

factors.name: Vitamin C + E supplements (fertility trials)
aliases: Vitamin E and vitamin C supplements

entries.headline: An uncontrolled study found 1 g vitamin C + 1 g vitamin E for 2 months lowered SDF and boosted the next ICSI's pregnancy rate, but controlled trials of similar mixes are null.

dose.effective: If used before ICSI for high SDF: about 500-1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E daily for 2-3 months, under medical advice.
dose.studied_range: 1 g C + 1 g E daily for 2 months (38 men).
dose.too_much: Vitamin C contributed to opening protamine disulphide bridges (sperm decondensation) in one study; vitamin E above 1000 mg/day raises bleeding risk.
dose.timeframe: 2-3 months.
dose.notes: Both are in MOXI at lower doses, which was null.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin C is the main water-soluble antioxidant of seminal plasma; vitamin E protects PUFA-rich membranes from lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: See [male-antioxidant-combination] and [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Greco 2005 was a before-after comparison after a failed cycle, so regression to the mean and cycle-to-cycle variation can explain much of the effect.
entries.title: Vitamins C and E

entries.headline: Vitamin E (600 mg/day) lowered follicular oxidative markers in a tiny study, and supplement use was associated with slightly shorter time to pregnancy in some subgroups, but there is no convincing RCT evidence of more live births.

dose.effective: Meet needs from food (nuts, seeds, vegetable oils, fruit, vegetables); routine high-dose supplements are not supported.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin E 600 mg/day (Tamura); vitamin C and E in mixed antioxidant trials in the Cochrane review.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown, so there is no reason to take high-dose supplements.
dose.notes: Typical prenatal vitamins already contain modest amounts.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin E is the main lipid-phase chain-breaking antioxidant; vitamin C regenerates it. Neither targets mitochondrial ROS production.
entries.interactions: Part of [female-antioxidant-supplements].
entries.caveats: Classic antioxidant paradox: big mechanistic story, no clinical proof.
entries.title: Vitamin E and vitamin C supplements

factors.name: Vitamin C foods (citrus, kiwi, peppers, strawberries)

entries.headline: Plasma vitamin C saturates near 200 mg/day (white cells saturate at 100 mg), easily reached from foods; extra beyond that is excreted and high-dose pills show no mortality benefit.

dose.effective: About 200 mg/day from food: e.g. 1 red pepper, or 2 kiwifruit, or 1 orange + 1 cup strawberries.
dose.studied_range: 30-2500 mg/day in depletion-repletion pharmacokinetics.
dose.too_much: Doses above ~400 mg/day have no evident value; at 1000 mg/day oxalate and urate excretion rise (kidney stone risk).
dose.timeframe: Steady state in 2-3 weeks.
dose.notes: Benefit is concentrated in people with low intake (smokers, low produce eaters).

entries.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant and regenerates vitamin E; kiwifruit also raised lymphocyte DNA resistance to H2O2 ex vivo beyond what its vitamin C explained.
entries.interactions: Vitamin C enhances non-heme iron absorption (good if iron-deficient; avoid iron + vitamin C supplements in iron overload, see [iron-excess]). High-dose vitamin C + E blunted exercise adaptation (covered in exercise sections).
entries.caveats: In the Cochrane review vitamin C supplements had no effect on mortality; beta-carotene and vitamin E increased it.

key_numbers.label: Dose at which plasma vitamin C plateaus

entries.title: Vitamin C foods (citrus, kiwi, peppers, strawberries)

entries.headline: No effect on cardiovascular disease, cancer or mortality in large RCTs. Shortens colds by about 8% and halves cold risk only under extreme physical stress. About 1 g/day doubles kidney-stone risk in men.

dose.effective: Body stores saturate with diet alone: cells saturate at ~100 mg/day and plasma at ~1,000 mg/day. 1-2 servings of fruit or vegetables rich in vitamin C cover the steep part of the curve (30-100 mg).
dose.studied_range: 120 mg/day (SU.VI.MAX) to 500 mg/day (PHS II) for outcomes; 200 mg to 2 g/day for colds
dose.too_much: ≥1,000 mg/day: about twice the kidney-stone risk in men (RR 1.95); 1 g/day blunted endurance-training adaptations.
dose.timeframe: Outcome trials ran for ~8 years with no effect
dose.notes: Oral absorption is tightly controlled (1.25 g oral peak ~135 µmol/L vs ~885 µmol/L IV), so megadoses mostly end up in urine. Pharmacological levels need IV dosing.

entries.mechanism: Water-soluble electron donor that regenerates vitamin E and is a cofactor for many enzymes. A true antioxidant at physiological levels, but once someone is replete, extra intake does not raise tissue levels and cannot compete with peroxiredoxins and GPx for H2O2. Large doses can blunt ROS-dependent training signals (PGC-1α, mitochondrial biogenesis).
entries.interactions: Taken around training it can cancel adaptive signalling, the same issue as [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]. Combined with vitamin E it showed no benefit in PHS II. Correcting deficiency is useful; adding more on top of a vegetable-rich diet adds nothing measurable.
entries.caveats: The 'megadose vitamin C' claims come from oral pharmacokinetics that cannot reach the plasma levels seen with IV dosing. Cold prevention works only for marathon runners, skiers and soldiers in subarctic conditions. Kidney-stone risk is relevant for men and people prone to stones.
entries.title: Vitamin C supplements (ascorbic acid)

entries.headline: In a 330-man RCT, high-dose vitamin D did not improve semen quality in men with low vitamin D, though live birth rose in a small oligozoospermic subgroup.

dose.effective: Correct deficiency (25OHD <50 nmol/L) for general health; not a sperm treatment.
dose.studied_range: 300,000 IU loading dose then 1400 IU/day plus 500 mg calcium for 150 days.
dose.too_much: Avoid chronic intake above 4000 IU/day without monitoring.
dose.timeframe: 150 days studied.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in testis and sperm; proposed effects on calcium signalling and inhibin B.
entries.caveats: The subgroup benefit is hypothesis-generating only.
entries.title: Vitamin D

entries.headline: Vitamin D-replete women had about 33% higher odds of IVF live birth than deficient women, but RCTs of supplementation in deficient women improved only chemical pregnancy, not clinical pregnancy.

dose.effective: Test 25(OH)D and correct deficiency with a clinician; there is no evidence that extra vitamin D helps women who are already replete.
dose.studied_range: Observational: replete vs deficient/insufficient 25(OH)D; 5 RCTs of supplementation in deficient women.
dose.too_much: Avoid unsupervised megadoses.
dose.timeframe: Correct deficiency before IVF or trying, within the 3-month preparation window.
dose.notes: Benefit, if any, is limited to correcting deficiency.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in granulosa cells and endometrium; vitamin D influences AMH signalling and immune tolerance.
entries.interactions: Part of [profertility-diet].
entries.caveats: Observational links are confounded by overall health, BMI and outdoor activity; RCT evidence is small.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, replete vs deficient

entries.title: Vitamin D (correcting deficiency)

entries.headline: No cardiovascular or cancer benefit in more than 100,000 trial participants. 400 IU/day raised prostate cancer by 17%, hemorrhagic stroke by 22-74% and heart failure by 13%, and high doses slightly raise mortality.

dose.effective: No supplemental dose has shown an outcome benefit; get vitamin E from food (nuts, seeds, plant oils).
dose.studied_range: 50 mg/day (ATBC) to 400 IU/day (HOPE, SELECT) or 600 IU every other day (WHS); 200-3,200 IU in biomarker studies
dose.too_much: ≥400 IU/day: +39 deaths per 10,000 (meta-analysis); risk rises above ~150 IU/day. Prostate cancer HR 1.17 at 400 IU/day (SELECT).
dose.timeframe: Lowering F2-isoprostanes needed ≥1,600 IU/day for 16 weeks; outcome trials ran 4.5-10 years
dose.notes: Doses used in outcome trials (400 IU) were too low to change oxidative-stress markers but high enough for bleeding effects. USPSTF grade D (recommends against).

entries.mechanism: Lipid-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes and LDL. In replete people extra intake does not lower lipid peroxidation at practical doses. The pattern of more hemorrhagic and fewer ischemic strokes is consistent with an antithrombotic effect, though the exact mechanism was not established in these trials.
entries.interactions: Effect on prostate cancer depended on selenium status (risk raised in low-selenium men) [selenium-supplement]. Combined with vitamin C it blunted exercise-induced insulin-sensitivity gains [vitamin-c-supplement]. Combined with NAC it accelerated tumour growth in mice [n-acetylcysteine].
entries.caveats: Observational data (supplement users had less heart disease) were confounded by healthy-user bias, and RCTs reversed the conclusion. WHS showed a 24% reduction in CV death as a secondary outcome, which was not replicated. Hemorrhagic stroke risk matters for people on anticoagulants.
entries.title: Vitamin E supplements (alpha-tocopherol)

entries.headline: A handful a day (30 g) lowers LDL and apoB and, in PREDIMED, cut major CVD events by ~28%; walnuts improved endothelial function, but direct oxidation markers were unchanged in several trials.

dose.effective: 30 g (a small handful) of mixed nuts or walnuts daily.
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day mixed nuts (PREDIMED); walnuts replacing ~32% of monounsaturated-fat energy for 4 weeks; 26 walnut trials (1059 people).
dose.too_much: Calories; walnut-enriched diets did not cause weight gain in trials.
dose.timeframe: 4 weeks for lipids and endothelial function.
dose.notes: Walnuts are rich in alpha-linolenic acid and gamma-tocopherol.

entries.mechanism: Lipid lowering (fewer oxidizable LDL particles), gamma-tocopherol, ellagitannins (converted to urolithins), ALA.
entries.interactions: Walnut PUFAs are oxidizable; store nuts cool and dark. Overlaps with [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: In the walnut endothelial trial, oxidation biomarkers did not differ from the Mediterranean control diet; in PREDIMED the nut arm did not improve LDL oxidation traits (the EVOO arm did).

key_numbers.label: PREDIMED major CVD events HR, MedDiet + nuts

entries.title: Walnuts and other nuts

entries.headline: Two RCTs found that adding 60-75 g of nuts a day improved sperm vitality, motility and morphology, and one also lowered sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: 60 g/day mixed nuts (walnuts, almonds, hazelnuts) or 75 g/day walnuts (about a large handful to two handfuls), added to the usual diet.
dose.studied_range: 60 g/day for 14 weeks (FERTINUTS, n=119); 75 g/day walnuts for 12 weeks (n=117).
dose.too_much: 75 g walnuts is about 490 kcal; swap for other snacks to avoid weight gain. Avoid if allergic.
dose.timeframe: 12-14 weeks.
dose.notes: Unsalted, unroasted or dry-roasted nuts were used. Walnuts are rich in alpha-linolenic acid (plant omega-3).

entries.mechanism: Provides ALA omega-3, vitamin E, polyphenols, magnesium, selenium and zinc; raised blood omega-3 and correlated with lower sperm aneuploidy; FERTINUTS showed lower SDF and miR-34b-3p expression.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [mediterranean-diet] and [omega3-fish].
entries.caveats: Healthy young men on Western diets; not infertile men; no pregnancy outcomes; FERTINUTS was partly funded by the nut industry.
entries.title: Walnuts and mixed nuts

entries.headline: Each 90 g/day (3 servings) of whole grain is associated with ~19% lower CHD and 17% lower all-cause mortality; the oxidative-stress link is indirect, through lower glycemic spikes and fermentable fiber.

dose.effective: 3 servings (90 g) per day or more; associations continued up to ~210-225 g/day.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes; RCTs show lower body weight, blood pressure and cholesterol with higher fiber and whole grain.
dose.timeframe: Long-term.
dose.notes: Oats contain avenanthramides and beta-glucan; most grain phenolics (ferulic acid) are bound to fiber and released by gut bacteria.

entries.mechanism: Fiber-bound ferulic acid released in the colon, short-chain fatty acids, lower glycemic load.
entries.interactions: Replaces [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] carbohydrate.
entries.caveats: Observational for hard outcomes; refined grains and white rice showed little association.

key_numbers.label: CHD RR per 90 g/day whole grain

entries.title: Whole grains

mechanisms.name: Aitken's two-step hypothesis of sperm DNA damage
mechanisms.description: Step 1: defective spermiogenesis leaves sperm with poor histone-to-protamine replacement, retained cytoplasm and loose chromatin. Step 2: oxidative stress (from the sperm's own mitochondria, from leukocytes, or from heat and toxicants) attacks this vulnerable DNA, forming 8-OHdG; OGG1 excises the lesion, leaving abasic sites that break into the strand breaks measured as SDF.

mechanisms.name: Cohesin loss and egg aneuploidy
mechanisms.description: Eggs pause in meiosis I from before birth until ovulation. The cohesin complexes that hold chromosome pairs together are not replaced, so they erode over decades; in older women this centromeric cohesion loss drives chromosome mis-segregation, giving a U-shaped aneuploidy curve with a steep rise after the mid-30s. This is the main reason age dominates egg quality, and it is not an oxidative process that antioxidants are known to fix.

mechanisms.name: Declining NAD+ in ageing oocytes
mechanisms.description: In mice, oocyte NAD+ falls with age; restoring it with NMN improved mitochondrial function, spindle assembly and fertility. Human evidence is lacking.

mechanisms.name: Direct radical scavenging by dietary antioxidants
mechanisms.description: The classic idea is that vitamin C, vitamin E, carotenoids and polyphenols protect us by reacting with free radicals before those radicals reach lipids, proteins or DNA. This chemistry is real in the test tube, but in the body it is limited by kinetics, concentration and location. Peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases remove H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides so quickly, and are present in such amounts, that small-molecule antioxidants cannot capture a meaningful share of peroxide inside cells. Forman, Davies and Ursini conclude that in vivo radical scavenging is kinetically ineffective as a defence, and that enzymatic two-electron reduction of hydroperoxides is the real mechanism. Sies states that the main role in antioxidant defence is played by enzymes, not small molecules. Vitamin E as the chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes, and vitamin C, are genuine exceptions, but their effect plateaus once deficiency is corrected. Oral vitamin C is tightly controlled: plasma is saturated at about 1 g/day, and cells at about 100 mg/day. Vitamin E reduced F2-isoprostanes only at 1,600-3,200 IU/day, far above trial doses. Polyphenols reach only about 0-4 µmol/L in plasma, mostly as conjugated metabolites. That is negligible next to urate and ascorbate, and the rise in plasma 'antioxidant capacity' after eating flavonoid-rich food is explained by uric acid. Food ORAC values therefore do not predict in vivo effects, and USDA withdrew its ORAC database in 2012. Direct scavenging may still matter locally in the gut lumen, where polyphenol concentrations are much higher. Elsewhere, the benefits of plant foods are better explained by signalling (Nrf2, NF-kB) and by the microbiome.

mechanisms.name: Endothelial nitric oxide
mechanisms.description: Flavanols, anthocyanin metabolites and dietary nitrate raise nitric-oxide bioavailability; flow-mediated dilation (FMD) is the most reproducible human outcome for polyphenol foods and partly reflects reduced vascular superoxide.

mechanisms.name: Follicular fluid oxidative stress
mechanisms.description: Follicular fluid surrounds the maturing egg. Higher ROS, lipid peroxidation and 8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage) in follicular fluid are associated with degenerate oocytes, fertilization failure and poor embryos. Obesity raises follicular insulin, triglycerides and CRP. These markers are research tools, not validated clinical tests.

mechanisms.name: Folliculogenesis timeline (why 3 months)
mechanisms.description: A resting follicle takes several months to reach the preantral stage, then about 70-85 more days to grow to the selectable 2-5 mm stage and ovulate. The egg ovulated in a given month has therefore been developing in the follicular environment of the preceding ~3 months, which is the window lifestyle changes can influence.

mechanisms.name: Glutathione system and endogenous antioxidant enzymes
mechanisms.description: The enzymatic network does almost all of the body's antioxidant work. Superoxide dismutases (SOD1 in the cytosol, SOD2 in mitochondria, SOD3 outside cells) convert superoxide to H2O2. Catalase, the selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidases and the six peroxiredoxins reduce H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides to water and alcohols. Glutathione reductase and the thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase system regenerate these enzymes using NADPH. Glutathione (GSH), a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine and glycine, is the most abundant non-protein thiol, at millimolar concentrations inside cells. Its synthesis is limited by cysteine supply and by glutamate-cysteine ligase, which is itself an Nrf2 target. This is why Nrf2 activators raise glutathione and why cysteine donors such as NAC can raise it in people who are short of it. In older adults, red-cell glutathione and its synthesis rate were about half those of young adults, and F2-isoprostanes were higher. Glycine plus NAC restored these values, and a small 16-week RCT reported metabolic and functional improvements. NAC at 1,200 mg/day improved exercise performance and oxidative markers only in people with low baseline glutathione. In replete people it blunted training signals, and in mouse tumour models it accelerated cancer progression and metastasis by raising tumour glutathione. Measuring the GSH/GSSG ratio needs immediate thiol trapping with N-ethylmaleimide, because GSSG is otherwise greatly overestimated. Selenium status matters for GPx activity, but in replete people extra selenium brings no benefit and may raise diabetes risk.

mechanisms.name: Gut microbial metabolism of polyphenols
mechanisms.description: Most anthocyanins, flavan-3-ol oligomers, chlorogenic acids and ellagitannins reach the colon, where bacteria convert them into phenolic acids, valerolactones and urolithins that circulate for up to 48 h. Inter-individual differences in this metabolism are large and partly explain variable responses.

mechanisms.name: Hormesis, mitohormesis and xenohormesis
mechanisms.description: Hormesis describes a two-phase dose response: a low dose of a stressor triggers protective adaptations, while a high dose causes harm. Mild stressors such as heat, exercise, caloric restriction and some phytochemicals extend lifespan or increase stress resistance in many animal models. 'Mitohormesis' applies this idea to mitochondrial ROS. The transient rise in ROS during exercise or energy restriction triggers lasting increases in antioxidant enzymes, mitochondrial biogenesis and insulin sensitivity, and antioxidant supplements can block these responses. In humans, vitamin C plus vitamin E abolished the gain in insulin sensitivity from four weeks of training, and vitamin C alone blunted mitochondrial biogenesis. Calabrese argues that Nrf2 activation is a common mechanism of hormesis and stresses that the maximal response is modest and capped. Sulforaphane shows a biphasic pattern in vitro: low micromolar levels increased cell proliferation and migration, including in cancer cell lines, while higher levels inhibited them. 'Xenohormesis' proposes that animals evolved to sense plant stress molecules such as polyphenols and isothiocyanates as signals to prepare their own defences. This would explain why such compounds act through signalling pathways and not as stoichiometric scavengers. Forman and colleagues call the electrophilic version 'para-hormesis'. The implications for guidance are that occasional, moderate challenges are the goal, that more stimulus is not always better, and that antioxidant megadoses around training can cancel the benefit.

mechanisms.name: Hormonal regulation (melatonin, cortisol, catecholamines)
mechanisms.description: Melatonin, suppressed by light at night, supports repair of oxidative DNA lesions; cortisol and catecholamines from chronic stress or cold raise metabolic rate and inflammatory signalling.

mechanisms.name: How oxidative stress is measured in diet trials
mechanisms.description: Validation work found plasma/urinary F2-isoprostanes and MDA measured by mass spectrometry, and urinary 8-OHdG, to be the most reliable general markers; TBARS, 'total antioxidant capacity' (TAC, FRAP, ORAC of plasma) and many ELISA kits are non-specific. Even 8-iso-PGF2alpha can rise from enzymatic COX activity during inflammation. Many positive food trials rely on the weaker markers.

mechanisms.name: Hyperglycaemia, glycation and advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)
mechanisms.description: High glucose drives oxidative stress through several linked routes. Brownlee proposed a unifying mechanism: hyperglycaemia makes the mitochondrial electron transport chain overproduce superoxide, which partly inhibits GAPDH and diverts glycolytic intermediates into four damaging pathways. These are polyol flux, formation of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), protein kinase C activation, and hexosamine flux. AGEs form when reducing sugars and reactive dicarbonyls such as methylglyoxal modify proteins and lipids. They crosslink matrix proteins and, by binding the receptor RAGE, trigger NOX activation and NF-kB-driven inflammation, which creates more oxidants. Glucose swings may matter more than average glucose. In type 2 diabetes, urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha correlated strongly with glycaemic variability (MAGE, r = 0.86) and with the postprandial glucose area, but not with HbA1c. 'Postprandial oxidative stress' after high-glucose and high-fat meals is a recognised phenomenon, and a large part of the day is spent in the postprandial state. AGEs also come from the diet. Dry-heat cooking such as grilling, roasting and frying raises the AGE content of foods 10- to 100-fold compared with the uncooked state, while moist-heat methods such as boiling, stewing and steaming generate far less. Practical measures follow from the mechanism: reduce glucose spikes through meal composition, fibre and post-meal activity, and favour moist cooking. Another research area covers the food-specific details.

mechanisms.name: Inflammation and NF-kB
mechanisms.description: Inflammation and oxidative stress drive each other. At sites of inflammation, neutrophils and macrophages assemble NOX2 and release myeloperoxidase, producing superoxide, H2O2 and hypochlorous acid. These oxidants kill microbes, but they also open endothelial junctions, damage nearby tissue and recruit more inflammatory cells. The transcription factor NF-kB controls many inflammatory genes (cytokines, adhesion molecules, inducible enzymes). ROS can activate or inhibit NF-kB signalling depending on the cell and the context, and NF-kB targets in turn regulate how much ROS a cell produces. This two-way link means chronic low-grade inflammation, for example from visceral adiposity, smoking, periodontal disease or autoimmune disease, keeps oxidant production high. It also helps explain why plant compounds that modulate signalling, such as Nrf2 activators that dampen NF-kB-driven inflammation, may have effects that scavenging cannot explain. Adipose tissue is a clear example: in obesity, fatty acids activate adipocyte NADPH oxidase and the resulting oxidative stress disrupts adipokines, raising IL-6 and MCP-1 and lowering adiponectin, which feeds systemic inflammation. Treating the inflammatory source (weight loss, stopping smoking, treating infection or autoimmune disease) is the effective lever. Broad antioxidant supplements have not reduced inflammatory cardiovascular or cancer outcomes in large trials.

mechanisms.name: Iron, Fenton chemistry and ferroptosis
mechanisms.description: Ferrous iron (and copper) react with hydrogen peroxide in the Fenton reaction. This produces the hydroxyl radical or highly reactive iron-oxo species that oxidise almost any nearby molecule. Since H2O2 is always present at low levels, the body controls oxidative damage largely by keeping iron tightly bound to transferrin, ferritin and heme proteins and limiting the 'labile' iron pool. Free or poorly chelated iron at sites of injury and inflammation greatly increases damage. Iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation drives ferroptosis, a regulated, non-apoptotic form of cell death. In ferroptosis, lipid hydroperoxides build up when glutathione-dependent defences fail, and the process is blocked by iron chelators and lipophilic radical-trapping agents such as ferrostatin-1. Ferroptosis links three mechanisms on this page: the glutathione system, lipid peroxidation, and iron status. It is relevant to neurodegeneration, ischemic injury and cancer therapy. Vitamin C can reduce ferric to ferrous iron in vitro. This is one reason pro-oxidant effects of high-dose antioxidants are discussed, though their importance in vivo at oral doses is unclear because oral vitamin C plasma levels are tightly capped. For the website, the practical messages are to avoid iron supplements unless iron deficiency is documented, and to recognise that iron overload conditions are a genuine source of oxidative stress. Dietary measures that control labile iron in healthy people have not been shown to change outcomes.

mechanisms.name: Leukocyte NADPH oxidase
mechanisms.description: Activated neutrophils and macrophages in semen generate superoxide via NOX2 at far higher rates than sperm; infection and inflammation therefore produce oxidative bursts that overwhelm seminal antioxidants.

mechanisms.name: Lipid peroxidation
mechanisms.description: Lipid peroxidation is a free-radical chain reaction in polyunsaturated fatty acids, most often in membranes and lipoproteins. An initiating radical removes a hydrogen atom next to a double bond. The lipid radical picks up oxygen to become a peroxyl radical, which attacks the next fatty acid, and so on. The chain is broken mainly by vitamin E in membranes, and the resulting hydroperoxides are reduced by glutathione peroxidases. The products are both damage and signals. F2-isoprostanes form non-enzymatically from arachidonic acid. When measured by mass spectrometry they are the best-validated in vivo marker of oxidative stress in humans: they rose consistently in the NIH BOSS validation study, are about twice as high in smokers, fall within two weeks of quitting, and track BMI and glucose in the Framingham cohort. Reactive aldehydes such as malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal form adducts with proteins and DNA and act as signalling molecules at low levels. Measuring MDA with the TBARS assay is unreliable because it is non-specific and prone to artefacts. Oxidised phospholipids on LDL are associated with angiographic coronary disease. Uncontrolled, iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation executes ferroptosis. Supplements show the gap between mechanism and practice: vitamin E 200-2,000 IU/day did not lower isoprostanes in healthy people, and 1,600 IU/day or more was needed in people with high cholesterol. Lifestyle factors that raise lipid peroxidation (smoking, adiposity, hyperglycaemia) are therefore better targets than chain-breaking supplements.

mechanisms.name: Lipotoxicity in obesity
mechanisms.description: Excess lipid in the follicle leads to lipid accumulation in the oocyte, endoplasmic-reticulum stress, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and cumulus-cell apoptosis, lowering fertilization.

mechanisms.name: Mitochondrial ROS (electron transport chain leak)
mechanisms.description: Mitochondria are a major source of superoxide inside cells. Electrons leak from the electron transport chain, mainly at complex I and also at complex III, and reduce oxygen to superoxide in the matrix. SOD2 then converts it to H2O2. Murphy showed that the leak depends on conditions. Superoxide production is high when mitochondria are not making ATP, so the protonmotive force is high and the coenzyme Q pool is reduced, and when the matrix NADH/NAD+ ratio is high. Both situations arise with nutrient excess and physical inactivity. When mitochondria are actively making ATP, production is much lower. For that reason the old textbook figure of '1-2% of oxygen becoming superoxide', based on isolated mitochondria, cannot be applied to living tissue. Mitochondrial ROS have two roles. They signal from mitochondria to the nucleus and drive adaptations such as mitochondrial biogenesis after exercise, a concept called mitohormesis, and antioxidant supplements can block these adaptations. In chronic hyperglycaemia, Brownlee proposed that mitochondrial superoxide overproduction is the single upstream event behind the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways of diabetic vascular damage. Plasma antioxidants cannot easily reach the mitochondrial matrix. That led to mitochondria-targeted compounds such as MitoQ, which improved endothelial function by 42% in a small six-week trial in older adults. The most reliable ways to keep mitochondrial ROS in the signalling range are lifestyle measures that keep mitochondria working and lower nutrient overload: regular activity, avoiding chronic energy excess, and good glucose control.

mechanisms.name: Mitochondrial ROS and apoptosis in sperm
mechanisms.description: Stressed or defective sperm leak electrons at mitochondrial complex I, producing superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; this triggers a truncated apoptotic cascade. Hydrogen peroxide from the midpiece crosses into the nucleus and damages DNA, while lipid peroxidation products (e.g. 4-hydroxynonenal) further poison mitochondria in a self-propagating loop.

mechanisms.name: NADPH oxidases and other enzymatic ROS sources (xanthine oxidase, NOS/peroxynitrite)
mechanisms.description: NADPH oxidases (NOX1-5 and DUOX1/2) are the only enzyme family whose main job is to make ROS. NOX2 in neutrophils and macrophages produces the 'respiratory burst' that kills microbes. Other isoforms produce superoxide or H2O2 for signalling in blood vessels, fibroblasts and many other cells. DUOX enzymes supply H2O2 for thyroid hormone synthesis. Excess NOX activity is a recurring theme in chronic disease. In obesity, adipose tissue upregulates NADPH oxidase and downregulates antioxidant enzymes. This raises local and systemic oxidative stress and disrupts adipokines (lower adiponectin, higher IL-6, MCP-1 and PAI-1). A NOX inhibitor reversed these changes and improved diabetes and fatty liver in obese mice. Xanthine oxidase, which converts hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, also makes superoxide and H2O2. It contributes to ischemia-reperfusion injury and is the target of allopurinol and febuxostat. Nitric oxide synthase normally makes protective •NO. When •NO meets superoxide it forms peroxynitrite, a strong oxidant and nitrating agent, and superoxide therefore lowers •NO availability. This is a key mechanism of endothelial dysfunction. Because these enzymes are regulated sources, the most effective interventions target the triggers: excess fat mass, inflammation, hyperglycaemia and smoking. Giving scavengers after the oxidants have been made is less effective. Specific NOX inhibitors are still mostly experimental.

mechanisms.name: Nrf2 / KEAP1 pathway
mechanisms.description: Nrf2 (gene NFE2L2) is the master transcription factor for inducible cytoprotection. Its targets include NQO1, heme oxygenase-1, the glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits that limit glutathione synthesis, glutathione S-transferases, thioredoxin reductase, and enzymes that regenerate NADPH. Under resting conditions KEAP1 binds Nrf2 and acts as an adaptor for a Cul3 ubiquitin ligase, so Nrf2 is degraded with a half-life under 20 minutes. KEAP1 has reactive cysteines that act as sensors. Electrophiles such as sulforaphane and other isothiocyanates, Michael acceptors such as curcumin, oxidised lipids and H2O2 modify these cysteines and stop Nrf2 from being degraded. Nrf2 then accumulates in the nucleus and drives genes with antioxidant response elements. Because activation works by de-repression, it is fast and transient: when the activator is cleared, Nrf2 is degraded again within minutes. These 'indirect antioxidants' act through long-lived catalytic enzymes. Unlike direct scavengers, they are not consumed and are unlikely to act as pro-oxidants. In humans, sulforaphane from broccoli sprouts raises phase II enzyme expression in airway cells in a dose-dependent way. A full-strength sprout beverage increased benzene detoxification by 63%, while half and one-fifth doses did not. The effect persisted over 12 weeks without tolerance. Exercise and caloric restriction also activate Nrf2. Responses are modest and self-limiting by design. Chronic maximal activation is harmful: Keap1-null mice die soon after birth, cancers carry activating NRF2/KEAP1 mutations that confer chemoresistance, oncogenes raise Nrf2 to support tumours, and the potent drug activator bardoxolone methyl increased heart failure in kidney patients. The dietary goal is therefore intermittent, moderate activation, not maximal activation.

mechanisms.name: Oocyte mitochondria and maternally inherited mtDNA
mechanisms.description: The oocyte is the most mitochondria-rich cell in the body and its mitochondria supply the early embryo until embryonic mitochondrial biogenesis starts. mtDNA is inherited only from the mother (sperm mtDNA is eliminated) and passes through a genetic bottleneck, so oocyte mitochondrial quality matters for the next generation. With age, oocyte mitochondria produce less ATP, mtDNA becomes less stable and CoQ10-synthesis enzymes decline.

mechanisms.name: Oocyte repair of paternal DNA damage
mechanisms.description: After fertilisation the oocyte must complete base excision repair of the sperm's oxidised DNA before the first S-phase; unrepaired or misrepaired lesions become mutations present in every cell of the embryo. This repair capacity is limited and appears to fall with maternal age, which is why high SDF hurts ICSI outcomes mostly in women over 40.

mechanisms.name: Oxidative DNA damage and repair
mechanisms.description: Hydroxyl radicals and other strong oxidants damage DNA bases and sugars. The best-studied lesion is 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxoGua; as the nucleoside, 8-oxo-dG or 8-OHdG). If it is not repaired it can pair with adenine and cause G-to-T transversions, a mutation pattern seen in some cancers. Cells remove such lesions mainly by base-excision repair (OGG1 for 8-oxoGua, plus MUTYH and MTH1 to prevent misincorporation), and the excised products are excreted in urine. Measurement is the main problem. The European Standards Committee on Oxidative DNA Damage (ESCODD) found large disagreements between laboratories, because guanine oxidises artefactually during DNA extraction and processing. The true background in human cells is probably about 0.3-4.2 lesions per million guanines, much lower than early chromatographic estimates. Urinary 8-OHdG measured by chemical methods such as LC-MS/MS is more robust. A meta-analysis of 84 studies put the healthy-adult background at about 3.9 ng/mg creatinine and found higher levels in smokers. In the NIH BOSS study, urinary 8-OHdG rose with a known oxidant insult in most conditions, while DNA strand breaks did not. Cooke and colleagues note that many contradictory disease associations reflect biomarker shortcomings. In practice, urinary 8-oxo-dG by mass spectrometry is a reasonable research marker of whole-body oxidative DNA damage, but ELISA-based values and single-time-point results should be read cautiously. No antioxidant supplement has been shown to lower cancer risk by lowering this marker.

mechanisms.name: Redox signalling: oxidative eustress vs distress
mechanisms.description: Reactive oxygen species are not only damaging by-products. Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide are made on purpose by more than 40 enzymes, including NADPH oxidases and the mitochondrial electron transport chain, under the control of growth factors and cytokines. At low nanomolar concentrations, H2O2 acts as a second messenger. It reversibly oxidises specific cysteine thiols on phosphatases, kinases and transcription factors, changing what they do. Sies calls this physiological range (about 1-10 nM H2O2 inside cells) 'oxidative eustress'. Higher concentrations switch on adaptive programmes through master regulators such as Nrf2/KEAP1 and NF-kB. Above about 100 nM, oxidation of lipids, proteins and DNA becomes significant ('oxidative distress'). Peroxiredoxins sit at the centre of this system. They are very abundant peroxidases and also act as sensors: they can be switched off locally so that H2O2 builds up and carries a signal, and they can pass the oxidising equivalent to target proteins that react poorly with H2O2 on their own. The practical consequence is that oxidants are part of normal regulation, and indiscriminate antioxidant loading can block useful signals. Large doses of vitamins C and E, or NAC, blunted the gains in insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis and muscle repair signalling that normally follow exercise. This is the main conceptual reason why 'more antioxidants' is not automatically better. It also reframes the goal: keep oxidant production within its signalling range, by avoiding chronic overload such as smoking, nutrient excess and inflammation, rather than trying to remove oxidants altogether.

mechanisms.name: Reductive stress and chromatin compaction
