mechanisms.description: Some ROS are needed: protamine disulphide bridges form oxidatively during epididymal transit, and capacitation needs a controlled oxidative burst. Large antioxidant doses can reduce these bonds and impair compaction, a proposed reason why antioxidant trials are inconsistent.

mechanisms.name: ROS as a required ovulation signal
mechanisms.description: A transient burst of reactive oxygen species after the LH surge is needed for cumulus expansion, progesterone production, EGF-receptor/MAPK signalling and follicle rupture. In mice, flooding the ovary with antioxidants reduced ovulation. Oxidative stress is harmful only when ROS are excessive or prolonged, which is one reason high-dose antioxidant supplements are not automatically helpful.

mechanisms.name: Scrotal thermoregulation
mechanisms.description: Spermatogenesis needs a testicular temperature about 2-4 C below core. Heat disrupts protamination and mitochondrial function in developing germ cells and induces apoptosis, effects that appear 2-3 months later and reverse within about 3-6 months of removing the heat.

mechanisms.name: Sperm DNA fragmentation and oxidative stress tests
mechanisms.description: SCSA (flow cytometry after acid denaturation; DFI, classic cut-off 25-30%), TUNEL (labels strand-break ends; flow cut-off about 17-20%), SCD/Halo (halo size after protein removal; ~20-30%) and Comet (single-cell electrophoresis; alkaline detects single- and double-strand breaks, neutral mainly double-strand). Expert guidelines use thresholds near 20% (about 26% for alkaline Comet). ASRM (2013) and AUA/ASRM (2020/2024) do not recommend SDF in the initial work-up but do for recurrent pregnancy loss; EAU recommends it for recurrent pregnancy loss, ART failure and unexplained infertility. MiOXSYS ORP is quick but its normalisation to sperm concentration makes it highly sensitive and poorly specific (40.6%), and EAU advises against routine ROS testing.

mechanisms.name: Spermatogenesis timeline
mechanisms.description: The textbook duration of spermatogenesis is about 74 days, based on 1960s labelling studies. Direct isotope labelling found new sperm first reaching the ejaculate about 64 days (range 42-76) after they started forming, including epididymal transit. Changes made today therefore start to show in about 2 months and are fully reflected after about 3 months.

mechanisms.name: The egg repairs sperm DNA damage
mechanisms.description: Until the embryo's own genome switches on (4-8 cell stage), DNA repair relies on maternal transcripts and proteins stored in the egg. Good-quality eggs can partly compensate for sperm DNA fragmentation: in one cohort sperm DNA damage reduced pregnancy with patients' own eggs but not with donor eggs.

mechanisms.name: Thermal stress
mechanisms.description: Heat induces heat-shock proteins and exercise-like vascular shear stress; the testes are highly heat-sensitive, so heat that may benefit blood vessels harms sperm production.

mechanisms.name: What high sperm DNA fragmentation does clinically
mechanisms.description: High SDF is associated with longer time to natural pregnancy (fecundability falls as SCSA abnormal sperm rise, becoming small above 30-40%), about double the miscarriage risk (RR 2.16), higher SDF in partners of women with recurrent pregnancy loss (+11.9 points), and lower clinical pregnancy and live birth after IVF and, to a lesser extent, ICSI. Double-strand breaks may matter most for miscarriage. Associations are consistent but heterogeneous, and SDF predicts outcomes imperfectly.

mechanisms.name: Why sperm are uniquely vulnerable
mechanisms.description: Sperm membranes are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids such as DHA, which are easily peroxidised. During maturation sperm shed almost all cytoplasm, so they carry very little superoxide dismutase, catalase or glutathione peroxidase and rely on seminal plasma for protection. They are transcriptionally silent and have only the first enzyme of base excision repair (OGG1), so oxidised bases are excised but the gaps cannot be filled.

pmid:32231263.title: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) as pleiotropic physiological signalling agents
pmid:32231263.finding: H2O2 and superoxide, made by >40 enzymes incl. NOX and the mitochondrial ETC, act at nanomolar levels as physiological signals ('oxidative eustress'); higher levels cause damage ('distress').

pmid:28110218.title: Hydrogen peroxide as a central redox signaling molecule in physiological oxidative stress: Oxidative eustress
pmid:28110218.finding: Defines physiological H2O2 (~1-10 nM) as oxidative eustress; higher levels trigger adaptive responses via Nrf2/KEAP1 and NF-kB; >100 nM causes biomolecular damage (distress).

pmid:25588755.title: Oxidative stress: a concept in redox biology and medicine
pmid:25588755.finding: Frames oxidative stress as a redox-signalling concept and states that antioxidant enzymes, not small-molecule antioxidants, fulfil the major role in defence.

pmid:19061483.title: How mitochondria produce reactive oxygen species
pmid:19061483.finding: Mitochondrial superoxide comes mainly from complex I and is high only with high protonmotive force/reduced CoQ or high NADH/NAD+; rates from isolated mitochondria cannot be extrapolated to in vivo.

pmid:24854789.title: Cellular mechanisms and physiological consequences of redox-dependent signalling
pmid:24854789.finding: ROS signal through reversible oxidation of specific cysteine residues and regulate many physiological cell-fate decisions.

pmid:18421291.title: Reconciling the chemistry and biology of reactive oxygen species
pmid:18421291.finding: Kinetic analysis of which oxidants react with which targets in cells; highlights that reactivity and compartmentalisation determine antioxidant effectiveness.

pmid:22147704.authors: Rhee SG, Woo HA, Kil IS, et al.
pmid:22147704.title: Peroxiredoxin functions as a peroxidase and a regulator and sensor of local peroxides
pmid:22147704.finding: Peroxiredoxins act as locally constrained peroxidases and can be inactivated to let H2O2 accumulate for signalling, and transfer oxidation to target proteins as H2O2 sensors.

pmid:17237347.title: The NOX family of ROS-generating NADPH oxidases: physiology and pathophysiology
pmid:17237347.finding: Describes the NOX family (NOX1-5, DUOX1/2), the only enzymes whose primary function is ROS generation, and their physiology and pathology.

pmid:16507884.authors: Pacher P, Nivorozhkin A, Szabó C
pmid:16507884.title: Therapeutic effects of xanthine oxidase inhibitors: renaissance half a century after the discovery of allopurinol
pmid:16507884.finding: Xanthine oxidase generates superoxide and H2O2 and its inhibition (allopurinol, febuxostat) has therapeutic effects in conditions involving oxidative stress.

pmid:17237348.authors: Pacher P, Beckman JS, Liaudet L
pmid:17237348.title: Nitric oxide and peroxynitrite in health and disease
pmid:17237348.finding: Nitric oxide reacts with superoxide to form peroxynitrite, a potent oxidant/nitrating agent implicated in cardiovascular, inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease.

pmid:8597169.title: Toxicity of iron and hydrogen peroxide: the Fenton reaction
pmid:8597169.finding: The iron/H2O2 Fenton reaction generates hydroxyl radicals and higher iron oxidation states capable of oxidising a wide range of biomolecules.

pmid:24346035.title: The role of iron and reactive oxygen species in cell death
pmid:24346035.finding: Iron-catalysed ROS initiate and mediate several forms of cell death, including ferroptosis.

pmid:22632970.authors: Dixon SJ, Lemberg KM, Lamprecht MR, et al.
pmid:22632970.title: Ferroptosis: an iron-dependent form of nonapoptotic cell death
pmid:22632970.finding: Identified ferroptosis, an iron-dependent, lipid-peroxidation-driven form of nonapoptotic cell death, inhibited by ferrostatin-1.

pmid:24999379.authors: Ayala A, Muñoz MF, Argüelles S
pmid:24999379.title: Lipid peroxidation: production, metabolism, and signaling mechanisms of malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal
pmid:24999379.finding: Reviews lipid peroxidation chemistry and the formation, metabolism and signalling roles of MDA and 4-HNE.

pmid:12832285.authors: Cooke MS, Evans MD, Dizdaroglu M, et al.
pmid:12832285.title: Oxidative DNA damage: mechanisms, mutation, and disease
pmid:12832285.finding: Oxidative DNA lesions such as 8-oxoguanine are mutagenic and repaired by multiple pathways; biomarker shortcomings explain inconsistent disease associations.

pmid:22995213.title: Glutathione synthesis
pmid:22995213.finding: Glutathione is the most abundant non-protein thiol; synthesis is limited by cysteine availability and glutamate-cysteine ligase activity.

pmid:37714962.title: Understanding mechanisms of antioxidant action in health and disease
pmid:37714962.finding: Reviews endogenous, dietary and synthetic antioxidants, why most antioxidant trials failed, and the special antioxidant role of the gastrointestinal tract.

pmid:34194012.title: Targeting oxidative stress in disease: promise and limitations of antioxidant therapy
pmid:34194012.finding: Antioxidants work in preclinical models but clinical trials are disappointing; rational targeting requires understanding where and when oxidants cause pathology.

pmid:13332224.title: Aging: a theory based on free radical and radiation chemistry
pmid:13332224.finding: Original proposal of the free-radical theory of aging.

pmid:19524016.authors: Pérez VI, Bokov A, Van Remmen H, et al.
pmid:19524016.title: Is the oxidative stress theory of aging dead?
pmid:19524016.finding: Of 18 genetic manipulations of antioxidant enzymes in mice, only Sod1 deletion altered lifespan, challenging the oxidative stress theory of aging.

pmid:16968214.authors: Kensler TW, Wakabayashi N, Biswal S
pmid:16968214.title: Cell survival responses to environmental stresses via the Keap1-Nrf2-ARE pathway
pmid:16968214.finding: Nrf2-knockout mice are markedly more sensitive to toxicants, inflammation, cigarette smoke and carcinogens; KEAP1 retains and represses Nrf2 under quiescent conditions.

pmid:29717933.authors: Yamamoto M, Kensler TW, Motohashi H
pmid:29717933.title: The KEAP1-NRF2 System: a Thiol-Based Sensor-Effector Apparatus for Maintaining Redox Homeostasis
pmid:29717933.finding: Comprehensive review of KEAP1 as a cysteine-based redox sensor and NRF2 as the effector transcription factor; inducibility relies on rapid de-repression.

pmid:30610225.authors: Cuadrado A, Rojo AI, Wells G, et al.
pmid:30610225.title: Therapeutic targeting of the NRF2 and KEAP1 partnership in chronic diseases
pmid:30610225.finding: NRF2 activation protects against many chronic diseases; one NRF2 activator is clinically approved and others are in development; context matters in cancer.

pmid:15282312.authors: Kobayashi A, Kang MI, Okawa H, et al.
pmid:15282312.title: Oxidative stress sensor Keap1 functions as an adaptor for Cul3-based E3 ligase to regulate proteasomal degradation of Nrf2
pmid:15282312.finding: KEAP1 is an adaptor for a Cul3 E3 ligase that keeps Nrf2 half-life under 20 minutes by proteasomal degradation.

pmid:18327872.title: Direct and indirect antioxidant properties of inducers of cytoprotective proteins
pmid:18327872.finding: Distinguishes direct antioxidants (consumed, can be pro-oxidant) from indirect antioxidants that induce long-lived catalytic cytoprotective proteins via Keap1/Nrf2/ARE.

pmid:23747930.authors: Forman HJ, Davies KJ, Ursini F
pmid:23747930.title: How do nutritional antioxidants really work: nucleophilic tone and para-hormesis versus free radical scavenging in vivo
pmid:23747930.finding: Kinetic constraints make in vivo radical scavenging by nutritional antioxidants ineffective; their benefit is better explained by Nrf2 activation ('para-hormesis') maintaining nucleophilic tone.

pmid:14517554.authors: Wakabayashi N, Itoh K, Wakabayashi J, et al.
pmid:14517554.title: Keap1-null mutation leads to postnatal lethality due to constitutive Nrf2 activation
pmid:14517554.finding: Keap1-null mice with constitutive Nrf2 activation die postnatally from oesophageal/forestomach hyperkeratosis; rescued by Nrf2 deletion.

pmid:18757741.authors: Shibata T, Ohta T, Tong KI, et al.
pmid:18757741.title: Cancer related mutations in NRF2 impair its recognition by Keap1-Cul3 E3 ligase and promote malignancy
pmid:18757741.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:18757741.finding: Somatic NRF2 mutations disrupting KEAP1 recognition occur in human cancers, especially in smokers and squamous cell carcinoma, and confer poor prognosis and drug resistance.

pmid:21734707.authors: DeNicola GM, Karreth FA, Humpton TJ, et al.
pmid:21734707.title: Oncogene-induced Nrf2 transcription promotes ROS detoxification and tumorigenesis
pmid:21734707.finding: Oncogenic KRAS, BRAF and MYC raise Nrf2 transcription to lower ROS and promote tumorigenesis in mice.

pmid:18413364.authors: Wang XJ, Sun Z, Villeneuve NF, et al.
pmid:18413364.title: Nrf2 enhances resistance of cancer cells to chemotherapeutic drugs, the dark side of Nrf2
pmid:18413364.finding: Nrf2 overexpression made cancer cells resistant to cisplatin, doxorubicin and etoposide; Nrf2 knockdown sensitised them.

pmid:24206459.authors: de Zeeuw D, Akizawa T, Audhya P, et al.
pmid:24206459.title: Bardoxolone methyl in type 2 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease
pmid:24206459.n: 2,185 patients with type 2 diabetes and stage 4 CKD
pmid:24206459.finding: The potent Nrf2 activator bardoxolone methyl did not reduce ESRD or CV death and increased heart-failure hospitalisation or death (HR 1.83); trial terminated early.

pmid:22992073.authors: Gold R, Kappos L, Arnold DL, et al.
pmid:22992073.title: Placebo-controlled phase 3 study of oral BG-12 for relapsing multiple sclerosis
pmid:22992073.finding: Dimethyl fumarate (BG-12) reduced the annualised relapse rate by ~50% versus placebo over 2 years.

pmid:17384144.authors: Marzec JM, Christie JD, Reddy SP, et al.
pmid:17384144.title: Functional polymorphisms in the transcription factor NRF2 in humans increase the risk of acute lung injury
pmid:17384144.finding: A functional NRF2 promoter SNP (-617 C/A) lowered promoter activity and was associated with higher risk of acute lung injury after trauma (OR 6.44).

pmid:33667690.title: The hormetic dose-response mechanism: Nrf2 activation
pmid:33667690.finding: Proposes Nrf2 activation as a general mechanism of hormetic dose responses, with a quantitatively constrained, modest maximal stimulation; exercise and caloric restriction are activators.

pmid:25532034.authors: Bao Y, Wang W, Zhou Z, et al.
pmid:25532034.title: Benefits and risks of the hormetic effects of dietary isothiocyanates on cancer prevention
pmid:25532034.finding: Sulforaphane at 1-5 uM increased proliferation and migration of several human cell lines (to 120-143%), while 10-40 uM inhibited them: a biphasic, hormetic effect.

pmid:21656528.authors: Saw CL, Cintrón M, Wu TY, et al.
pmid:21656528.title: Pharmacodynamics of dietary phytochemical indoles I3C and DIM: Induction of Nrf2-mediated phase II drug metabolizing and antioxidant genes and synergism with isothiocyanates
pmid:21656528.finding: In HepG2 cells, low concentrations of indoles (I3C, DIM) combined with isothiocyanates (SFN, PEITC) induced ARE-mediated genes synergistically or additively.

pmid:1549603.authors: Zhang Y, Talalay P, Cho CG, et al.
pmid:1549603.title: A major inducer of anticarcinogenic protective enzymes from broccoli: isolation and elucidation of structure
pmid:1549603.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:1549603.finding: Isolated sulforaphane as the major inducer of anticarcinogenic phase 2 enzymes in broccoli.

pmid:9294217.authors: Fahey JW, Zhang Y, Talalay P
pmid:9294217.title: Broccoli sprouts: an exceptionally rich source of inducers of enzymes that protect against chemical carcinogens
pmid:9294217.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:9294217.finding: 3-day broccoli sprouts contain 10-100 times more glucoraphanin than mature plants, and sprout extracts reduced mammary tumours in rats.

pmid:21372038.authors: Egner PA, Chen JG, Wang JB, et al.
pmid:21372038.title: Bioavailability of Sulforaphane from two broccoli sprout beverages: results of a short-term, cross-over clinical trial in Qidong, China
pmid:21372038.finding: Sulforaphane bioavailability was ~70% from a sulforaphane-rich beverage versus ~5% from a glucoraphanin-rich one; glucoraphanin gave slower elimination and more interindividual variability.

pmid:24913818.authors: Egner PA, Chen JG, Zarth AT, et al.
pmid:24913818.title: Rapid and sustainable detoxication of airborne pollutants by broccoli sprout beverage: results of a randomized clinical trial in China
pmid:24913818.finding: Daily broccoli sprout beverage (600 umol glucoraphanin + 40 umol sulforaphane) for 12 weeks increased benzene (+61%) and acrolein (+23%) detoxification; bioavailability did not decline over time.

pmid:31268126.authors: Chen JG, Johnson J, Egner P, et al.
pmid:31268126.title: Dose-dependent detoxication of the airborne pollutant benzene in a randomized trial of broccoli sprout beverage in Qidong, China
pmid:31268126.finding: Full-dose broccoli sprout beverage (~25 umol/d urinary sulforaphane metabolites) raised benzene detoxification by 63%; half and one-fifth doses had no significant effect.

pmid:16284385.authors: Kensler TW, Chen JG, Egner PA, et al.
pmid:16284385.title: Effects of glucosinolate-rich broccoli sprouts on urinary levels of aflatoxin-DNA adducts and phenanthrene tetraols in a randomized clinical trial in He Zuo township, Qidong, People's Republic of China
pmid:16284385.finding: Broccoli sprout infusion (400 umol glucoraphanin) for 2 weeks had no overall effect on aflatoxin-DNA adducts, but adducts were inversely related to individual sulforaphane metabolite excretion.

pmid:19028145.authors: Riedl MA, Saxon A, Diaz-Sanchez D
pmid:19028145.title: Oral sulforaphane increases Phase II antioxidant enzymes in the human upper airway
pmid:19028145.finding: Oral sulforaphane from broccoli sprout homogenate dose-dependently increased GSTM1, GSTP1, NQO1 and HO-1 expression in nasal cells, maximal at 200 g sprouts.

pmid:25522265.authors: Atwell LL, Hsu A, Wong CP, et al.
pmid:25522265.title: Absorption and chemopreventive targets of sulforaphane in humans following consumption of broccoli sprouts or a myrosinase-treated broccoli sprout extract
pmid:25522265.finding: Fresh sprouts gave ~3x higher sulforaphane exposure than a myrosinase-treated extract at 200 umol/d; no dose responses were seen for HO-1, HDAC activity or p21 in blood cells.

pmid:22318753.authors: Fahey JW, Wehage SL, Holtzclaw WD, et al.
pmid:22318753.title: Protection of humans by plant glucosinolates: efficiency of conversion of glucosinolates to isothiocyanates by the gastrointestinal microflora
pmid:22318753.finding: Gut microbial conversion of glucoraphanin to isothiocyanates varied from ~1% to >40% of dose between people but was consistent within individuals; sulforaphane itself was 70-90% recovered.

pmid:26524341.authors: Fahey JW, Holtzclaw WD, Wehage SL, et al.
pmid:26524341.title: Sulforaphane Bioavailability from Glucoraphanin-Rich Broccoli: Control by Active Endogenous Myrosinase
pmid:26524341.finding: Sprouts or seeds with active myrosinase gave 3-4 fold more sulforaphane bioavailability than glucoraphanin without active myrosinase.

pmid:21910945.authors: Cramer JM, Teran-Garcia M, Jeffery EH
pmid:21910945.title: Enhancing sulforaphane absorption and excretion in healthy men through the combined consumption of fresh broccoli sprouts and a glucoraphanin-rich powder
pmid:21910945.finding: Combining fresh broccoli sprouts with a glucoraphanin powder recovered 65% of the dose versus 60% (sprouts) and 24% (powder) and gave earlier sulforaphane appearance.

pmid:16332662.authors: Gasper AV, Al-Janobi A, Smith JA, et al.
pmid:16332662.title: Glutathione S-transferase M1 polymorphism and metabolism of sulforaphane from standard and high-glucosinolate broccoli
pmid:16332662.finding: GSTM1-null subjects had slightly higher plasma sulforaphane AUC and faster urinary excretion than GSTM1-positive subjects after eating broccoli.

pmid:11085692.authors: London SJ, Yuan JM, Chung FL, et al.
pmid:11085692.title: Isothiocyanates, glutathione S-transferase M1 and T1 polymorphisms, and lung-cancer risk: a prospective study of men in Shanghai, China
pmid:11085692.n: 232 lung cancer cases and 710 controls nested in 18,244 men
pmid:11085692.finding: Detectable urinary isothiocyanates were linked to lower lung cancer risk (RR 0.65), most strongly in GSTM1-null (0.36) and GSTM1/GSTT1 double-null men (0.28).

pmid:17374652.authors: Steck SE, Gammon MD, Hebert JR, et al.
pmid:17374652.title: GSTM1, GSTT1, GSTP1, and GSTA1 polymorphisms and urinary isothiocyanate metabolites following broccoli consumption in humans
pmid:17374652.finding: GST genotypes did not substantially change urinary isothiocyanate excretion after broccoli; GSTM1-null subjects were more often high excreters (62% vs 39%).

pmid:31590459.authors: Yagishita Y, Fahey JW, Dinkova-Kostova AT, et al.
pmid:31590459.title: Broccoli or Sulforaphane: Is It the Source or Dose That Matters?
pmid:31590459.finding: Reviews the relationships between broccoli/sprout/supplement formulation, sulforaphane bioavailability, dose and efficacy across >50 clinical trials.

pmid:18316025.title: Stress-response hormesis and aging: "that which does not kill us makes us stronger"
pmid:18316025.finding: Stress-response hormesis: sublethal stressors induce protective responses that can extend lifespan in animal models.

pmid:18455976.title: Xenohormesis: sensing the chemical cues of other species
pmid:18455976.finding: Proposes xenohormesis: animals sense plant stress molecules as cues to activate their own defences.

pmid:24999941.title: Unraveling the truth about antioxidants: mitohormesis explains ROS-induced health benefits
pmid:24999941.finding: Argues that ROS-induced mitochondrial hormesis (mitohormesis) explains health benefits of exercise and caloric restriction and why antioxidants can block them.

pmid:19433800.authors: Ristow M, Zarse K, Oberbach A, et al.
pmid:19433800.title: Antioxidants prevent health-promoting effects of physical exercise in humans
pmid:19433800.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:19433800.finding: Vitamin C 1,000 mg/d plus vitamin E 400 IU/d during 4 weeks of exercise training abolished the training-induced gains in insulin sensitivity and endogenous antioxidant gene expression.

pmid:18175748.authors: Gomez-Cabrera MC, Domenech E, Romagnoli M, et al.
pmid:18175748.title: Oral administration of vitamin C decreases muscle mitochondrial biogenesis and hampers training-induced adaptations in endurance performance
pmid:18175748.finding: Vitamin C 1 g/d hampered training-induced endurance gains and blocked expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors and antioxidant enzymes.

pmid:26638792.title: Do antioxidant supplements interfere with skeletal muscle adaptation to exercise training?
pmid:26638792.finding: No convincing evidence that antioxidant supplements enhance training adaptations; they more consistently impair responses to resistance and high-intensity training.

pmid:23719546.authors: Michailidis Y, Karagounis LG, Terzis G, et al.
pmid:23719546.title: Thiol-based antioxidant supplementation alters human skeletal muscle signaling and attenuates its inflammatory response and recovery after intense eccentric exercise
pmid:23719546.finding: NAC raised muscle glutathione but blunted redox-sensitive signalling (Akt/mTOR/p70S6K), inflammation and recovery after eccentric exercise.

pmid:15721980.authors: Kadiiska MB, Gladen BC, Baird DD, et al.
pmid:15721980.title: Biomarkers of oxidative stress study II: are oxidation products of lipids, proteins, and DNA markers of CCl4 poisoning?
pmid:15721980.finding: BOSS study: in CCl4-poisoned rats, plasma/urinary F2-isoprostanes and MDA (GC-MS) and urinary 8-OHdG rose consistently; TBARS, protein carbonyls and others did not.

pmid:25614459.authors: Kadiiska MB, Peddada S, Herbert RA, et al.
pmid:25614459.title: Biomarkers of oxidative stress study VI. Endogenous plasma antioxidants fail as useful biomarkers of endotoxin-induced oxidative stress
pmid:25614459.finding: BOSS VI: plasma antioxidants (ascorbate, tocopherols, GSH/GSSG, total antioxidant capacity) failed as biomarkers of endotoxin-induced oxidative stress.

pmid:16298907.authors: Milne GL, Musiek ES, Morrow JD
pmid:16298907.title: F2-isoprostanes as markers of oxidative stress in vivo: an overview
pmid:16298907.finding: F2-isoprostanes, formed by free-radical peroxidation of arachidonic acid, are extremely accurate in vivo markers of lipid peroxidation when properly measured.

pmid:27789233.title: Assessment of lipid peroxidation by measuring malondialdehyde (MDA) and relatives in biological samples: Analytical and biological challenges
pmid:27789233.finding: Measuring MDA, HNE and 8-iso-PGF2a is analytically challenging; many methods, especially non-specific ones, are prone to artefacts.

pmid:12589963.authors: Dalle-Donne I, Rossi R, Giustarini D, et al.
pmid:12589963.title: Protein carbonyl groups as biomarkers of oxidative stress
pmid:12589963.finding: Protein carbonyls are relatively stable markers of protein oxidation, usually measured after DNPH derivatisation; their link to disease remains uncertain.

pmid:14989265.authors: Collins AR, Cadet J, Möller L, et al.
pmid:14989265.title: Are we sure we know how to measure 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine in DNA from human cells?
pmid:14989265.finding: ESCODD found major inter-laboratory disagreement in DNA 8-oxoguanine due to artefactual oxidation; true background is ~0.3-4.2 per 10^6 guanines.

pmid:32466448.authors: Graille M, Wild P, Sauvain JJ, et al.
pmid:32466448.title: Urinary 8-OHdG as a Biomarker for Oxidative Stress: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:32466448.finding: Background urinary 8-OHdG in healthy adults (chemical methods) is ~3.9 ng/mg creatinine; smoking is associated with higher levels.

pmid:23928499.authors: Giustarini D, Dalle-Donne I, Milzani A, et al.
pmid:23928499.title: Analysis of GSH and GSSG after derivatization with N-ethylmaleimide
pmid:23928499.finding: Artefactual GSH oxidation during acid deproteinisation markedly overestimates GSSG unless GSH is first derivatised with N-ethylmaleimide.

pmid:16000355.authors: Tsimikas S, Brilakis ES, Miller ER, et al.
pmid:16000355.title: Oxidized phospholipids, Lp(a) lipoprotein, and coronary artery disease
pmid:16000355.finding: Oxidised phospholipids on apoB-100 (an oxidised LDL measure) were strongly associated with angiographic coronary artery disease, especially at age 60 or younger.

pmid:17513413.title: Total antioxidant capacity: appraisal of a concept
pmid:17513413.finding: Critique of 'total antioxidant capacity': summed assay values lack a coherent chemical or biological meaning.

pmid:17157175.title: Consumption of flavonoid-rich foods and increased plasma antioxidant capacity in humans: cause, consequence, or epiphenomenon?
pmid:17157175.finding: The rise in plasma total antioxidant capacity after flavonoid-rich foods is not caused by flavonoids but likely by increased uric acid.

pmid:23601894.title: What has happened to the ORAC database?
pmid:23601894.finding: Explains USDA's 2012 withdrawal of its ORAC database: in-vitro antioxidant capacity has no demonstrated relevance to in-vivo effects and values were misused in marketing.

pmid:7700313.authors: Morrow JD, Frei B, Longmire AW, et al.
pmid:7700313.title: Increase in circulating products of lipid peroxidation (F2-isoprostanes) in smokers. Smoking as a cause of oxidative damage
pmid:7700313.finding: Plasma F2-isoprostanes were about twice as high in smokers and fell significantly after 2 weeks of smoking abstinence.

pmid:12615693.authors: Keaney JF Jr, Larson MG, Vasan RS, et al.
pmid:12615693.title: Obesity and systemic oxidative stress: clinical correlates of oxidative stress in the Framingham Study
pmid:12615693.finding: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a was independently associated with smoking, BMI, blood glucose/diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

pmid:8127329.authors: Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group
pmid:8127329.title: The effect of vitamin E and beta carotene on the incidence of lung cancer and other cancers in male smokers
pmid:8127329.finding: Beta-carotene 20 mg/d increased lung cancer incidence by 18% and total mortality by 8%; alpha-tocopherol 50 mg/d did not reduce lung cancer and was linked to more hemorrhagic-stroke deaths.

pmid:8602180.authors: Omenn GS, Goodman GE, Thornquist MD, et al.
pmid:8602180.title: Effects of a combination of beta carotene and vitamin A on lung cancer and cardiovascular disease
pmid:8602180.finding: Beta-carotene 30 mg + retinol 25,000 IU increased lung cancer (RR 1.28) and all-cause mortality (RR 1.17); stopped early.

pmid:19066370.authors: Lippman SM, Klein EA, Goodman PJ, et al.
pmid:19066370.title: Effect of selenium and vitamin E on risk of prostate cancer and other cancers: the Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT)
pmid:19066370.finding: Selenium 200 ug/d and/or vitamin E 400 IU/d did not prevent prostate or other cancers; non-significant increases in prostate cancer (vitamin E) and diabetes (selenium).

pmid:21990298.authors: Klein EA, Thompson IM Jr, Tangen CM, et al.
pmid:21990298.title: Vitamin E and the risk of prostate cancer: the Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT)
pmid:21990298.finding: With extended follow-up, vitamin E 400 IU/d significantly increased prostate cancer risk (HR 1.17).

pmid:24563519.authors: Kristal AR, Darke AK, Morris JS, et al.
pmid:24563519.title: Baseline selenium status and effects of selenium and vitamin e supplementation on prostate cancer risk
pmid:24563519.finding: Selenium raised high-grade prostate cancer by 91% in men with high baseline selenium; vitamin E raised prostate cancer risk in men with low selenium.

pmid:10639540.authors: HOPE Study Investigators (Yusuf S, et al.)
pmid:10639540.title: Vitamin E supplementation and cardiovascular events in high-risk patients
pmid:10639540.finding: Vitamin E 400 IU/d for 4.5 years had no effect on cardiovascular events (RR 1.05).

pmid:15769967.authors: Lonn E, Bosch J, Yusuf S, et al.
pmid:15769967.title: Effects of long-term vitamin E supplementation on cardiovascular events and cancer: a randomized controlled trial
pmid:15769967.finding: Long-term vitamin E 400 IU/d did not prevent cancer or major CV events and increased heart failure (RR 1.13).

pmid:18997197.authors: Sesso HD, Buring JE, Christen WG, et al.
pmid:18997197.title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
pmid:18997197.finding: Vitamin E 400 IU every other day and vitamin C 500 mg/d for 8 years had no effect on major CV events; vitamin E increased hemorrhagic stroke (HR 1.74).

pmid:19066368.authors: Gaziano JM, Glynn RJ, Christen WG, et al.
pmid:19066368.title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of prostate and total cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
pmid:19066368.finding: Neither vitamin E nor vitamin C reduced prostate or total cancer over 8 years.

pmid:12114037.title: MRC/BHF Heart Protection Study of antioxidant vitamin supplementation in 20,536 high-risk individuals: a randomised placebo-controlled trial
pmid:12114037.finding: Vitamin E 600 mg + vitamin C 250 mg + beta-carotene 20 mg daily raised blood levels but had no effect on vascular events, cancer or mortality over 5 years.

pmid:15998891.authors: Lee IM, Cook NR, Gaziano JM, et al.
pmid:15998891.title: Vitamin E in the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease and cancer: the Women's Health Study: a randomized controlled trial
pmid:15998891.finding: Vitamin E 600 IU every other day gave no overall benefit for CV events, cancer or total mortality; CV death was 24% lower (secondary outcome).

pmid:22419320.authors: Bjelakovic G, Nikolova D, Gluud LL, et al.
pmid:22419320.title: Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various diseases
pmid:22419320.finding: Antioxidant supplements increased mortality in low-bias trials (RR 1.04); beta-carotene (RR 1.05) and vitamin E (RR 1.03) significantly, vitamin C and selenium not.

pmid:15537682.authors: Miller ER 3rd, Pastor-Barriuso R, Dalal D, et al.
pmid:15537682.title: Meta-analysis: high-dosage vitamin E supplementation may increase all-cause mortality
pmid:15537682.finding: High-dose vitamin E (>=400 IU/d) increased all-cause mortality by 39 per 10,000; risk rose above ~150 IU/d.

pmid:21051774.authors: Schürks M, Glynn RJ, Rist PM, et al.
pmid:21051774.title: Effects of vitamin E on stroke subtypes: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
pmid:21051774.finding: Vitamin E increased hemorrhagic stroke by 22% and reduced ischemic stroke by 10%, with no effect on total stroke.

pmid:19876916.authors: Druesne-Pecollo N, Latino-Martel P, Norat T, et al.
pmid:19876916.title: Beta-carotene supplementation and cancer risk: a systematic review and metaanalysis of randomized controlled trials
pmid:19876916.finding: Beta-carotene had no effect on overall cancer but at 20-30 mg/d increased lung (RR 1.16) and stomach cancer, especially in smokers and asbestos workers.

pmid:11133814.authors: Liu C, Wang XD, Bronson RT, et al.
pmid:11133814.title: Effects of physiological versus pharmacological beta-carotene supplementation on cell proliferation and histopathological changes in the lungs of cigarette smoke-exposed ferrets
pmid:11133814.finding: In smoke-exposed ferrets, pharmacological beta-carotene (~30 mg/d human equivalent) lowered lung retinoic acid and caused squamous metaplasia; a physiological dose (~6 mg/d) did not.

pmid:24477002.authors: Sayin VI, Ibrahim MX, Larsson E, et al.
pmid:24477002.title: Antioxidants accelerate lung cancer progression in mice
pmid:24477002.finding: NAC and vitamin E accelerated lung tumour progression and shortened survival in mice by reducing ROS, DNA damage and p53 expression.

pmid:26446958.authors: Le Gal K, Ibrahim MX, Wiel C, et al.
pmid:26446958.title: Antioxidants can increase melanoma metastasis in mice
pmid:26446958.finding: NAC and Trolox increased lymph node metastasis of melanoma in mice by raising tumour-cell glutathione and RHOA activation.

pmid:17936185.authors: Roberts LJ 2nd, Oates JA, Linton MF, et al.
pmid:17936185.title: The relationship between dose of vitamin E and suppression of oxidative stress in humans
pmid:17936185.finding: Vitamin E lowered plasma F2-isoprostanes significantly only at 1,600 IU/d (-35%) and 3,200 IU/d (-49%), with maximum effect after 16 weeks.

pmid:11231747.authors: Meagher EA, Barry OP, Lawson JA, et al.
pmid:11231747.title: Effects of vitamin E on lipid peroxidation in healthy persons
pmid:11231747.finding: Vitamin E 200-2,000 IU/d for 8 weeks raised vitamin E levels but did not change urinary isoprostanes or 4-HNE.

pmid:35727271.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force, Mangione CM, Barry MJ, et al.
pmid:35727271.title: Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
pmid:35727271.finding: USPSTF recommends against beta-carotene or vitamin E for preventing CVD or cancer (grade D); evidence is insufficient for multivitamins and other single or paired nutrients.

pmid:35727272.authors: O'Connor EA, Evans CV, Ivlev I, et al.
pmid:35727272.title: Vitamin and Mineral Supplements for the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
pmid:35727272.finding: Multivitamins were associated with slightly lower cancer incidence (OR 0.93); beta-carotene increased lung cancer and CV mortality; vitamin E had no effect.

pmid:15557412.authors: Hercberg S, Galan P, Preziosi P, et al.
pmid:15557412.title: The SU.VI.MAX Study: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of the health effects of antioxidant vitamins and minerals
pmid:15557412.finding: Nutritional-dose antioxidant mix (vitamin C 120 mg, E 30 mg, beta-carotene 6 mg, Se 100 ug, Zn 20 mg) had no overall effect but lowered cancer (RR 0.69) and mortality in men, not women.

pmid:23117775.authors: Sesso HD, Christen WG, Bubes V, et al.
pmid:23117775.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
pmid:23117775.finding: A daily multivitamin for 11 years did not reduce major cardiovascular events, MI, stroke or CV mortality.

pmid:23162860.authors: Gaziano JM, Sesso HD, Christen WG, et al.
pmid:23162860.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
pmid:23162860.finding: A daily multivitamin for 11 years modestly reduced total cancer (HR 0.92).

pmid:8623000.authors: Levine M, Conry-Cantilena C, Wang Y, et al.
pmid:8623000.title: Vitamin C pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers: evidence for a recommended dietary allowance
pmid:8623000.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:8623000.finding: Vitamin C plasma concentration is sigmoid with dose: steep between 30-100 mg/d, cells saturated at 100 mg/d, plasma completely saturated at 1,000 mg/d.

pmid:15068981.authors: Padayatty SJ, Sun H, Wang Y, et al.
pmid:15068981.title: Vitamin C pharmacokinetics: implications for oral and intravenous use
pmid:15068981.finding: Oral vitamin C produces tightly controlled plasma levels (1.25 g oral peak ~135 umol/L vs ~885 umol/L IV); only IV achieves pharmacological levels.

pmid:23440782.title: Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold
pmid:23440782.finding: Regular vitamin C (>=200 mg/d) did not reduce cold incidence in the general population (RR 0.97) but halved it under extreme physical stress, and shortened colds by 8% in adults.

pmid:23381591.authors: Thomas LD, Elinder CG, Tiselius HG, et al.
pmid:23381591.title: Ascorbic acid supplements and kidney stone incidence among men: a prospective study
pmid:23381591.finding: Use of ascorbic acid supplements (~1,000 mg tablets) was associated with about double the risk of kidney stones (RR 1.95).

pmid:22381456.title: Selenium and human health
pmid:22381456.finding: Selenium has a U-shaped relation to health: supplementation may help those with low status but may harm (e.g. type 2 diabetes) those with adequate or high status.

pmid:17620655.authors: Stranges S, Marshall JR, Natarajan R, et al.
pmid:17620655.title: Effects of long-term selenium supplementation on the incidence of type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial
pmid:17620655.finding: Selenium 200 ug/d increased type 2 diabetes incidence (HR 1.55), especially in the top tertile of baseline selenium (HR 2.70).

pmid:29376219.authors: Vinceti M, Filippini T, Del Giovane C, et al.
pmid:29376219.title: Selenium for preventing cancer
pmid:29376219.finding: High-certainty evidence that selenium supplementation does not reduce cancer incidence (RR 1.01) or cancer mortality.

pmid:29233792.authors: Paschalis V, Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, et al.
pmid:29233792.title: N-acetylcysteine supplementation increases exercise performance and reduces oxidative stress only in individuals with low levels of glutathione
pmid:29233792.finding: NAC 1,200 mg/d for 30 days restored glutathione, reduced F2-isoprostanes and improved VO2max (~14%) only in people with low baseline glutathione.

pmid:21795440.authors: Sekhar RV, Patel SG, Guthikonda AP, et al.
pmid:21795440.title: Deficient synthesis of glutathione underlies oxidative stress in aging and can be corrected by dietary cysteine and glycine supplementation
pmid:21795440.finding: Older adults had lower red-cell glutathione and synthesis and higher F2-isoprostanes; glycine + cysteine supplementation restored these to young-adult values.

pmid:33783984.authors: Kumar P, Liu C, Hsu JW, et al.
pmid:33783984.title: Glycine and N-acetylcysteine (GlyNAC) supplementation in older adults improves glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, insulin resistance, endothelial dysfunction, genotoxicity, muscle strength, and cognition: Results of a pilot clinical trial
pmid:33783984.finding: 24 weeks of GlyNAC in older adults corrected glutathione deficiency and oxidative stress and improved several functional measures; benefits declined after stopping.

pmid:35975308.authors: Kumar P, Liu C, Suliburk J, et al.
pmid:35975308.title: Supplementing Glycine and N-Acetylcysteine (GlyNAC) in Older Adults Improves Glutathione Deficiency, Oxidative Stress, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, Inflammation, Physical Function, and Aging Hallmarks: A Randomized Clinical Trial
pmid:35975308.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
pmid:35975308.finding: In a placebo-controlled 16-week RCT, GlyNAC improved glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, insulin resistance and physical function in older adults.

pmid:29661838.authors: Rossman MJ, Santos-Parker JR, Steward CAC, et al.
pmid:29661838.title: Chronic Supplementation With a Mitochondrial Antioxidant (MitoQ) Improves Vascular Function in Healthy Older Adults
pmid:29661838.finding: MitoQ 20 mg/d for 6 weeks improved brachial flow-mediated dilation by 42% versus placebo, linked to reduced mitochondrial ROS suppression of endothelial function.

pmid:15113710.authors: Manach C, Scalbert A, Morand C, et al.
pmid:15113710.title: Polyphenols: food sources and bioavailability
pmid:15113710.finding: Reviews polyphenol food sources, intakes and bioavailability, which depends strongly on chemical structure.

pmid:15640486.authors: Manach C, Williamson G, Morand C, et al.
pmid:15640486.title: Bioavailability and bioefficacy of polyphenols in humans. I. Review of 97 bioavailability studies
pmid:15640486.finding: After 50 mg aglycone equivalents, plasma polyphenol metabolites reach only 0-4 umol/L and urinary excretion is 0.3-43% of dose, varying greatly by compound.

pmid:15640487.title: Bioavailability and bioefficacy of polyphenols in humans. II. Review of 93 intervention studies
pmid:15640487.finding: Polyphenol effects in humans are measurable but more limited than in vitro, due to lack of validated biomarkers, long-term studies and bioavailability-aware design.

pmid:17141749.title: Dietary polyphenols: good, bad, or indifferent for your health?
pmid:17141749.finding: Questions whether dietary polyphenols act as antioxidants in vivo and highlights possible gut-level effects and pro-oxidant artefacts.

pmid:18284912.title: Are polyphenols antioxidants or pro-oxidants? What do we learn from cell culture and in vivo studies?
pmid:18284912.finding: Neither antioxidant nor pro-oxidant effects of polyphenols are established in humans at achievable levels; many cell-culture results are artefacts of polyphenol oxidation in media.

pmid:22794138.authors: Del Rio D, Rodriguez-Mateos A, Spencer JP, et al.
pmid:22794138.title: Dietary (poly)phenolics in human health: structures, bioavailability, and evidence of protective effects against chronic diseases
pmid:22794138.finding: Most dietary (poly)phenolics are extensively metabolised, with large fractions reaching the colon where microbes produce absorbable phenolic catabolites.

pmid:22420826.title: The antioxidant paradox: less paradoxical now?
pmid:22420826.finding: The antioxidant paradox arises because endogenous defences are tightly regulated and body antioxidant status and oxidative damage are largely unresponsive to high-dose dietary antioxidants.

pmid:15599400.authors: Furukawa S, Fujita T, Shimabukuro M, et al.
pmid:15599400.title: Increased oxidative stress in obesity and its impact on metabolic syndrome
pmid:15599400.finding: Fat accumulation correlated with systemic oxidative stress in humans and mice; adipose NADPH oxidase drove ROS and adipokine dysregulation, and NOX inhibition improved metabolic disease in mice.

pmid:16609090.authors: Monnier L, Mas E, Ginet C, et al.
pmid:16609090.title: Activation of oxidative stress by acute glucose fluctuations compared with sustained chronic hyperglycemia in patients with type 2 diabetes
pmid:16609090.finding: Urinary 8-iso-PGF2a correlated strongly with glycaemic variability (MAGE, r=0.86) and postprandial glucose, not with HbA1c.

pmid:11742414.title: Biochemistry and molecular cell biology of diabetic complications
pmid:11742414.finding: Proposes that hyperglycaemia-induced mitochondrial superoxide overproduction underlies the four main pathways of diabetic vascular damage.

pmid:15867266.authors: Sies H, Stahl W, Sevanian A
pmid:15867266.title: Nutritional, dietary and postprandial oxidative stress
pmid:15867266.finding: Defines postprandial oxidative stress from hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia and notes that dietary antioxidants/polyphenols with meals can attenuate it.

pmid:20497781.authors: Uribarri J, Woodruff S, Goodman S, et al.
pmid:20497781.title: Advanced glycation end products in foods and a practical guide to their reduction in the diet
pmid:20497781.finding: Database of dietary AGE content; dry-heat cooking raises AGE content 10- to 100-fold over the uncooked state.

pmid:21187859.title: Crosstalk of reactive oxygen species and NF-κB signaling
pmid:21187859.finding: ROS and NF-kB regulate each other: NF-kB targets control ROS levels and ROS can activate or inhibit NF-kB signalling.

pmid:23991888.authors: Mittal M, Siddiqui MR, Tran K, et al.
pmid:23991888.title: Reactive oxygen species in inflammation and tissue injury
pmid:23991888.finding: Neutrophil-derived ROS at inflammatory sites cause endothelial dysfunction and tissue injury.

pmid:11352861.authors: Shapiro TA, Fahey JW, Wade KL, et al.
pmid:11352861.title: Chemoprotective glucosinolates and isothiocyanates of broccoli sprouts: metabolism and excretion in humans.
pmid:11352861.finding: Isothiocyanates were ~6x more bioavailable than glucosinolates; excretion was linear from 25-200 µmol; chewing sprouts thoroughly increased excretion.

pmid:16965241.authors: Shapiro TA, Fahey JW, Dinkova-Kostova AT, et al.
pmid:16965241.title: Safety, tolerance, and metabolism of broccoli sprout glucosinolates and isothiocyanates: a clinical phase I study.
pmid:16965241.finding: Glucosinolate extracts converted ~18-20% vs ~71% for isothiocyanate extracts; no toxicity including liver and thyroid tests over 7 days.

pmid:29573889.authors: López-Chillón MT, Carazo-Díaz C, Prieto-Merino D, et al.
pmid:29573889.title: Effects of long-term consumption of broccoli sprouts on inflammatory markers in overweight subjects.
pmid:29573889.finding: 30 g/day fresh broccoli sprouts for 10 weeks lowered IL-6 and CRP (uncontrolled before-after design).

pmid:21816223.authors: Clarke JD, Hsu A, Riedl K, et al.
pmid:21816223.title: Bioavailability and inter-conversion of sulforaphane and erucin in human subjects consuming broccoli sprouts or broccoli supplement in a cross-over study design.
pmid:21816223.finding: A myrosinase-free broccoli supplement produced dramatically lower plasma and urinary isothiocyanates than 40 g fresh sprouts.

pmid:21559038.authors: Bahadoran Z, Mirmiran P, Hosseinpanah F, et al.
pmid:21559038.title: Broccoli sprouts reduce oxidative stress in type 2 diabetes: a randomized double-blind clinical trial.
pmid:21559038.finding: 5-10 g/day broccoli sprout powder for 4 weeks lowered MDA, oxidized LDL and oxidative stress index and raised total antioxidant capacity.

pmid:22325157.authors: Bahadoran Z, Mirmiran P, Hosseinpanah F, et al.
pmid:22325157.title: Broccoli sprouts powder could improve serum triglyceride and oxidized LDL/LDL-cholesterol ratio in type 2 diabetic patients: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial.
pmid:22325157.finding: 10 g/day broccoli sprout powder for 4 weeks lowered triglycerides and the oxidized LDL/LDL ratio.

pmid:27832073.authors: Wise RA, Holbrook JT, Criner G, et al.
pmid:27832073.title: Lack of Effect of Oral Sulforaphane Administration on Nrf2 Expression in COPD: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo Controlled Trial.
pmid:27832073.finding: 25 or 150 µmol/day sulforaphane for 4 weeks was absorbed but did not induce Nrf2 target genes in lung cells or change oxidative stress or inflammation markers.

pmid:30735751.authors: Chartoumpekis DV, Ziros PG, Chen JG, et al.
pmid:30735751.title: Broccoli sprout beverage is safe for thyroid hormonal and autoimmune status: Results of a 12-week randomized trial.
pmid:30735751.finding: 84 days of a sulforaphane/glucoraphanin beverage did not change TSH, free T4, thyroglobulin or thyroid autoimmunity.

pmid:11525594.authors: Conaway CC, Getahun SM, Liebes LL, et al.
pmid:11525594.title: Disposition of glucosinolates and sulforaphane in humans after ingestion of steamed and fresh broccoli.
pmid:11525594.finding: After 200 g broccoli, 32% of isothiocyanates were excreted from fresh vs 10% from steamed broccoli (~3x difference).

pmid:18950181.authors: Vermeulen M, Klöpping-Ketelaars IW, van den Berg R, et al.
pmid:18950181.title: Bioavailability and kinetics of sulforaphane in humans after consumption of cooked versus raw broccoli.
pmid:18950181.finding: Sulforaphane bioavailability was 37% from raw vs 3.4% from cooked broccoli; peak at 1.6 vs 6 h; half-life ~2.5 h.

pmid:15184012.authors: Matusheski NV, Juvik JA, Jeffery EH
pmid:15184012.title: Heating decreases epithiospecifier protein activity and increases sulforaphane formation in broccoli.
pmid:15184012.finding: Heating broccoli to 60 °C increased sulforaphane and decreased inactive nitrile formation; 70 °C and above decreased both in florets.

pmid:29266773.authors: Sivapalan T, Melchini A, Saha S, et al.
pmid:29266773.title: Bioavailability of Glucoraphanin and Sulforaphane from High-Glucoraphanin Broccoli.
pmid:29266773.finding: Soups (myrosinase denatured) from high-glucoraphanin broccoli gave 3-5x higher circulating sulforaphane; excretion was 2-15% of glucoraphanin consumed.

pmid:29806738.authors: Okunade O, Niranjan K, Ghawi SK, et al.
pmid:29806738.title: Supplementation of the Diet by Exogenous Myrosinase via Mustard Seeds to Increase the Bioavailability of Sulforaphane in Healthy Human Subjects after the Consumption of Cooked Broccoli.
pmid:29806738.finding: Adding 1 g brown mustard powder to 200 g cooked broccoli raised urinary sulforaphane-NAC from 9.8 to 44.7 µmol/g creatinine.

pmid:26881038.authors: Houghton CA, Fassett RG, Coombes JS
pmid:26881038.title: Sulforaphane and Other Nutrigenomic Nrf2 Activators: Can the Clinician's Expectation Be Matched by the Reality?
pmid:26881038.finding: Sulforaphane activates Nrf2 more potently and is more bioavailable than curcumin, silymarin or resveratrol.

pmid:26604653.authors: Kikuchi M, Ushida Y, Shiozawa H, et al.
pmid:26604653.title: Sulforaphane-rich broccoli sprout extract improves hepatic abnormalities in male subjects.
pmid:26604653.finding: Glucoraphanin capsules for 2 months lowered ALT, gamma-GTP and urinary 8-OHdG vs placebo.

pmid:31136659.authors: Curtis PJ, van der Velpen V, Berends L, et al.
pmid:31136659.title: Blueberries improve biomarkers of cardiometabolic function in participants with metabolic syndrome-results from a 6-month, double-blind, randomized controlled trial.
pmid:31136659.finding: 1 cup (150 g)/day blueberries improved FMD (+1.45%) and arterial stiffness over 6 months; 1/2 cup had no effect; insulin resistance and plasma thiols unchanged.

pmid:24004888.authors: Rodriguez-Mateos A, Rendeiro C, Bergillos-Meca T, et al.
pmid:24004888.title: Intake and time dependence of blueberry flavonoid-induced improvements in vascular function: a randomized, controlled, double-blind, crossover intervention study with mechanistic insights into biological activity.
pmid:24004888.finding: FMD rose at 1-2 and 6 h after blueberry; dose-dependent up to 766 mg polyphenols then plateaued; linked to metabolites and lower neutrophil NADPH oxidase.

pmid:26024297.authors: Stull AJ, Cash KC, Champagne CM, et al.
pmid:26024297.title: Blueberries improve endothelial function, but not blood pressure, in adults with metabolic syndrome: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
pmid:26024297.finding: Blueberry smoothies twice daily for 6 weeks improved endothelial function (RHI) but not blood pressure or insulin sensitivity.

pmid:29019365.authors: Nair AR, Mariappan N, Stull AJ, et al.
pmid:29019365.title: Blueberry supplementation attenuates oxidative stress within monocytes and modulates immune cell levels in adults with metabolic syndrome: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
pmid:29019365.finding: 22.5 g freeze-dried blueberry twice daily for 6 weeks lowered superoxide and total ROS in whole blood and monocytes.

pmid:20660279.authors: Basu A, Du M, Leyva MJ, et al.
pmid:20660279.title: Blueberries decrease cardiovascular risk factors in obese men and women with metabolic syndrome.
pmid:20660279.finding: 50 g freeze-dried blueberries (~350 g fresh) daily for 8 weeks reduced blood pressure and oxidized LDL (-28%) and MDA/HNE more than control.

pmid:22733001.authors: Riso P, Klimis-Zacas D, Del Bo' C, et al.
pmid:22733001.title: Effect of a wild blueberry (Vaccinium angustifolium) drink intervention on markers of oxidative stress, inflammation and endothelial function in humans with cardiovascular risk factors.
pmid:22733001.finding: Wild blueberry drink (375 mg anthocyanins) for 6 weeks reduced oxidized DNA bases and H2O2-induced DNA damage; no effect on endothelial markers.

pmid:25578927.authors: Johnson SA, Figueroa A, Navaei N, et al.
pmid:25578927.title: Daily blueberry consumption improves blood pressure and arterial stiffness in postmenopausal women with pre- and stage 1-hypertension: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
pmid:25578927.finding: 22 g/day freeze-dried blueberry for 8 weeks lowered blood pressure and arterial stiffness and raised nitric oxide.

pmid:36847333.authors: Woolf EK, Terwoord JD, Litwin NS, et al.
pmid:36847333.title: Daily blueberry consumption for 12 weeks improves endothelial function in postmenopausal women with above-normal blood pressure through reductions in oxidative stress: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:36847333.finding: 22 g/day freeze-dried blueberry for 12 weeks improved FMD, and the smaller response to ascorbate infusion implied the gain came from reduced oxidative stress.

pmid:36150681.authors: Martini D, Marino M, Venturi S, et al.
pmid:36150681.title: Blueberries and their bioactives in the modulation of oxidative stress, inflammation and cardio/vascular function markers: a systematic review of human intervention studies.
pmid:36150681.finding: Blueberries most consistently improve vascular function; results on oxidative stress, inflammation and cardiometabolic markers conflict.

pmid:28825651.authors: Fairlie-Jones L, Davison K, Fromentin E, et al.
pmid:28825651.title: The Effect of Anthocyanin-Rich Foods or Extracts on Vascular Function in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
pmid:28825651.finding: Anthocyanin foods/extracts improved FMD acutely and chronically (chronic SMD 0.84) with high heterogeneity.

pmid:23604435.authors: Czank C, Cassidy A, Zhang Q, et al.
pmid:23604435.title: Human metabolism and elimination of the anthocyanin, cyanidin-3-glucoside: a (13)C-tracer study.
pmid:23604435.finding: Relative bioavailability of labelled cyanidin-3-glucoside including metabolites was ~12%; metabolites (phenolic, hippuric acids) circulated for up to 48 h.

pmid:27006201.authors: Huang H, Chen G, Liao D, et al.
pmid:27006201.title: Effects of Berries Consumption on Cardiovascular Risk Factors: A Meta-analysis with Trial Sequential Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
pmid:27006201.finding: Berries lowered LDL (-0.21 mmol/L), systolic BP (-2.7 mmHg), fasting glucose, HbA1c and TNF-alpha.

pmid:23319811.authors: Cassidy A, Mukamal KJ, Liu L, et al.
pmid:23319811.title: High anthocyanin intake is associated with a reduced risk of myocardial infarction in young and middle-aged women.
pmid:23319811.finding: Highest vs lowest anthocyanin quintile: MI HR 0.68; >3 servings/week of blueberries + strawberries HR 0.66 (CI crossed 1).

pmid:30096878.authors: Solverson PM, Rumpler WV, Leger JL, et al.
pmid:30096878.title: Blackberry Feeding Increases Fat Oxidation and Improves Insulin Sensitivity in Overweight and Obese Males.
pmid:30096878.finding: 600 g/day blackberries for 7 days on a high-fat diet lowered respiratory quotient and insulin AUC and improved HOMA-IR.

pmid:10962130.authors: Noda Y, Kneyuki T, Igarashi K, et al.
pmid:10962130.title: Antioxidant activity of nasunin, an anthocyanin in eggplant peels.
pmid:10962130.finding: Nasunin scavenged superoxide, inhibited hydroxyl radical generation by chelating iron, and protected rat brain homogenate from lipid peroxidation in vitro.

pmid:12744682.title: Distribution of hydroxycinnamic acid conjugates in fruit of commercial eggplant (Solanum melongena L.) cultivars.
pmid:12744682.finding: Chlorogenic acid is the predominant eggplant phenolic, with large differences among cultivars and fruit segments.

pmid:29195964.authors: Kaushik P, Gramazio P, Vilanova S, et al.
pmid:29195964.title: Phenolics content, fruit flesh colour and browning in cultivated eggplant, wild relatives and interspecific hybrids and implications for fruit quality breeding.
pmid:29195964.finding: Chlorogenic acid made up >65% of phenolic acids in cultivated eggplant; wild relatives had more phenolics.

pmid:31744060.authors: Nishimura M, Suzuki M, Takahashi R, et al.
pmid:31744060.title: Daily Ingestion of Eggplant Powder Improves Blood Pressure and Psychological State in Stressed Individuals: A Randomized Placebo-Controlled Study.
pmid:31744060.finding: 1.2 g/day eggplant powder for 12 weeks lowered blood pressure, attributed to acetylcholine (choline esters), not antioxidants.

pmid:27483219.authors: Martini D, Del Bo' C, Tassotti M, et al.
pmid:27483219.title: Coffee Consumption and Oxidative Stress: A Review of Human Intervention Studies.
pmid:27483219.finding: Coffee can raise glutathione and protect against DNA damage, especially with regular intake; effects on antioxidant capacity, enzymes and lipid/protein damage are unclear.

pmid:20589860.authors: Hoelzl C, Knasmüller S, Wagner KH, et al.
pmid:20589860.title: Instant coffee with high chlorogenic acid levels protects humans against oxidative damage of macromolecules.
pmid:20589860.finding: 800 mL/day high-chlorogenic-acid coffee for 5 days lowered urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha by 15% and 3-nitrotyrosine by 16%.

pmid:24740588.authors: Bakuradze T, Lang R, Hofmann T, et al.
pmid:24740588.title: Consumption of a dark roast coffee decreases the level of spontaneous DNA strand breaks: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:24740588.finding: 750 mL/day coffee for 4 weeks produced a 27% difference in spontaneous DNA strand breaks vs water.

pmid:26632023.authors: Bakuradze T, Lang R, Hofmann T, et al.
pmid:26632023.title: Coffee consumption rapidly reduces background DNA strand breaks in healthy humans: Results of a short-term repeated uptake intervention study.
pmid:26632023.finding: DNA strand breaks fell within 2 h of the first cup and by about one-third after 800 mL over 8 h.

pmid:29160894.authors: Clifford MN, Jaganath IB, Ludwig IA, et al.
pmid:29160894.title: Chlorogenic acids and the acyl-quinic acids: discovery, biosynthesis, bioavailability and bioactivity.
pmid:29160894.finding: Coffee is the major dietary source of chlorogenic (acyl-quinic) acids worldwide; much is metabolised by colonic microbiota.

pmid:29167102.authors: Poole R, Kennedy OJ, Roderick P, et al.
pmid:29167102.title: Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses of multiple health outcomes.
pmid:29167102.finding: Largest risk reductions at 3-4 cups/day (all-cause mortality RR 0.83); harms in pregnancy.

pmid:26572796.authors: Ding M, Satija A, Bhupathiraju SN, et al.
pmid:26572796.title: Association of Coffee Consumption With Total and Cause-Specific Mortality in 3 Large Prospective Cohorts.
pmid:26572796.finding: Caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were both inversely associated with mortality in never smokers.

pmid:9240930.title: The cholesterol-raising factor from coffee beans.
pmid:9240930.finding: Cafestol and kahweol raise LDL cholesterol; paper filters retain them, so filtered coffee does not raise cholesterol while boiled, cafetiere and Turkish coffee do.

pmid:9234024.authors: Urgert R, Weusten-van der Wouw MP, Hovenier R, et al.
pmid:9234024.title: Diterpenes from coffee beans decrease serum levels of lipoprotein(a) in humans: results from four randomised controlled trials.
pmid:9234024.finding: 10 mg/day cafestol corresponds to two to three cups of cafetiere coffee.

pmid:20167460.authors: Medina-Remón A, Zamora-Ros R, Rotchés-Ribalta M, et al.
pmid:20167460.title: Total polyphenol excretion and blood pressure in subjects at high cardiovascular risk.
pmid:20167460.finding: Fruit and vegetables, then coffee, then wine contributed most to urinary polyphenols; higher excretion associated with lower blood pressure.

pmid:14519830.authors: Hakim IA, Harris RB, Brown S, et al.
pmid:14519830.title: Effect of increased tea consumption on oxidative DNA damage among smokers: a randomized controlled study.
pmid:14519830.finding: 4 cups/day decaffeinated green tea for 4 months lowered urinary 8-OHdG by 31%; black tea had no effect.

pmid:20595643.authors: Basu A, Sanchez K, Leyva MJ, et al.
pmid:20595643.title: Green tea supplementation affects body weight, lipids, and lipid peroxidation in obese subjects with metabolic syndrome.
pmid:20595643.finding: 4 cups/day green tea for 8 weeks lowered plasma MDA and HNE vs control.

pmid:12376503.authors: Lee MJ, Maliakal P, Chen L, et al.
pmid:12376503.title: Pharmacokinetics of tea catechins after ingestion of green tea and (-)-epigallocatechin-3-gallate by humans: formation of different metabolites and individual variability.
pmid:12376503.finding: EGCG peaked in plasma at ~1.5 h with a 3.4 h half-life and large variability; valerolactone ring-fission metabolites peaked at 8-15 h.

pmid:32625874.authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS), Younes M, Aggett P, et al.
pmid:32625874.title: Scientific opinion on the safety of green tea catechins.
pmid:32625874.finding: Brewed green tea is generally safe (90-300 mg EGCG/day typical); supplement intakes >= 800 mg EGCG/day significantly raise serum transaminases in trials.

pmid:25975988.authors: Mazzanti G, Di Sotto A, Vitalone A
pmid:25975988.title: Hepatotoxicity of green tea: an update.
pmid:25975988.finding: Green-tea supplement liver injury cases were mostly hepatocellular in women; multi-ingredient products caused more severe injury with shorter latency.

pmid:42016115.authors: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA)
pmid:42016115.title: Scientific Opinion on the substantiation of a health claim related to cocoa flavanols and maintenance of normal endothelium-dependent vasodilation pursuant to Article 13(5) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.
pmid:42016115.finding: Cause-and-effect established; 200 mg cocoa flavanols/day (2.5 g high-flavanol cocoa powder or 10 g high-flavanol dark chocolate) needed.

pmid:22301923.authors: Hooper L, Kay C, Abdelhamid A, et al.
pmid:22301923.title: Effects of chocolate, cocoa, and flavan-3-ols on cardiovascular health: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.
pmid:22301923.finding: Cocoa improved FMD (chronic +1.34%, acute +3.19%) regardless of dose, insulin resistance and diastolic BP; >50 mg epicatechin/day gave larger BP effects.

pmid:26348767.authors: Sansone R, Rodriguez-Mateos A, Heuel J, et al.
pmid:26348767.title: Cocoa flavanol intake improves endothelial function and Framingham Risk Score in healthy men and women: a randomised, controlled, double-masked trial: the Flaviola Health Study.
pmid:26348767.finding: 450 mg cocoa flavanols twice daily for 1 month raised FMD by 1.2% and lowered BP, LDL and pulse wave velocity; FMD plateaued after ~2 weeks.

pmid:35294962.authors: Sesso HD, Manson JE, Aragaki AK, et al.
pmid:35294962.title: Effect of cocoa flavanol supplementation for the prevention of cardiovascular disease events: the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial.
pmid:35294962.finding: 500 mg/day cocoa flavanols for 3.6 years: total CVD events HR 0.90 (NS); CVD death HR 0.73 (secondary).

pmid:16954359.authors: Covas MI, Nyyssönen K, Poulsen HE, et al.
pmid:16954359.title: The effect of polyphenols in olive oil on heart disease risk factors: a randomized trial.
pmid:16954359.finding: 25 mL/day olive oil for 3 weeks: HDL rose and oxidized LDL and oxidative stress markers fell linearly with phenolic content (2.7, 164, 366 mg/kg).

pmid:42078706.authors: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA)
pmid:42078706.title: Scientific Opinion on the substantiation of health claims related to polyphenols in olive and protection of LDL particles from oxidative damage (ID 1333, 1638, 1639, 1696, 2865), maintenance of normal blood HDL cholesterol concentrations (ID 1639), maintenance of normal blood pressure (ID 3781), "anti-inflammatory properties" (ID 1882), "contributes to the upper respiratory tract health" (ID 3468), "can help to maintain a normal function of gastrointestinal tract" (3779), and "contributes to body defences against external agents" (ID 3467) pursuant to Article 13(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.
pmid:42078706.finding: EFSA opinion underpinning the authorised claim that olive oil polyphenols contribute to protecting blood lipids (LDL) from oxidative stress.

pmid:30884804.authors: Tsimidou MZ, Sotiroglou M, Mastralexi A, et al.
pmid:30884804.title: In House Validated UHPLC Protocol for the Determination of the Total Hydroxytyrosol and Tyrosol Content in Virgin Olive Oil Fit for the Purpose of the Health Claim Introduced by the EC Regulation 432/2012 for "Olive Oil Polyphenols".
pmid:30884804.finding: The EC 432/2012 claim requires at least 5 mg of olive oil polyphenols (hydroxytyrosol and derivatives) per 20 g of oil; measurement methods are still debated.

pmid:28371298.authors: Hernáez Á, Castañer O, Goday A, et al.
pmid:28371298.title: The Mediterranean Diet decreases LDL atherogenicity in high cardiovascular risk individuals: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:28371298.finding: MedDiet + virgin olive oil for 1 year raised LDL resistance to oxidation (+6.5%) and lowered LDL oxidative modifications (-36%) vs low-fat diet; the nut arm did not.

pmid:29897866.authors: Estruch R, Ros E, Salas-Salvadó J, et al.
pmid:29897866.title: Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease with a Mediterranean Diet Supplemented with Extra-Virgin Olive Oil or Nuts.
pmid:29897866.finding: Major CVD events HR 0.69 (EVOO) and 0.72 (nuts) vs reduced-fat diet over 4.8 years, robust to randomisation-protocol deviations.

pmid:22999065.authors: Mitjavila MT, Fandos M, Salas-Salvadó J, et al.
pmid:22999065.title: The Mediterranean diet improves the systemic lipid and DNA oxidative damage in metabolic syndrome individuals. A randomized, controlled, trial.
pmid:22999065.finding: After 1 year, urinary 8-oxo-dG fell more in both MedDiet arms (P<0.001) and F2-isoprostanes showed a borderline larger fall vs low-fat control.

pmid:15037535.authors: Ros E, Núñez I, Pérez-Heras A, et al.
pmid:15037535.title: A walnut diet improves endothelial function in hypercholesterolemic subjects: a randomized crossover trial.
pmid:15037535.finding: Walnuts replacing ~32% of MUFA energy for 4 weeks improved endothelium-dependent vasodilation and lowered LDL; oxidation biomarkers unchanged.

pmid:29931130.authors: Guasch-Ferré M, Li J, Hu FB, et al.
pmid:29931130.title: Effects of walnut consumption on blood lipids and other cardiovascular risk factors: an updated meta-analysis and systematic review of controlled trials.
pmid:29931130.finding: Walnut diets lowered total cholesterol (-7.0 mg/dL), LDL (-5.5 mg/dL), triglycerides and apoB without weight gain.

pmid:19703258.authors: López-Uriarte P, Bulló M, Casas-Agustench P, et al.
pmid:19703258.title: Nuts and oxidation: a systematic review.
pmid:19703258.finding: Reviews in vitro, animal and human studies of nut intake on oxidation; nuts are fat-rich but their skins carry antioxidants.

pmid:9209178.authors: Gärtner C, Stahl W, Sies H
pmid:9209178.title: Lycopene is more bioavailable from tomato paste than from fresh tomatoes.
pmid:9209178.finding: With 15 g oil, tomato paste gave 2.5x higher peak and 3.8x higher AUC lycopene than fresh tomatoes.

pmid:15735074.authors: Unlu NZ, Bohn T, Clinton SK, et al.
pmid:15735074.title: Carotenoid absorption from salad and salsa by humans is enhanced by the addition of avocado or avocado oil.
pmid:15735074.finding: Adding 150 g avocado or 24 g avocado oil raised carotenoid absorption 2.6-15-fold.

pmid:15277161.authors: Brown MJ, Ferruzzi MG, Nguyen ML, et al.
pmid:15277161.title: Carotenoid bioavailability is higher from salads ingested with full-fat than with fat-reduced salad dressings as measured with electrochemical detection.
pmid:15277161.finding: Essentially no carotenoid absorption with fat-free dressing; more with 6 g and most with 28 g oil.

pmid:22331646.authors: Burton-Freeman B, Talbot J, Park E, et al.
pmid:22331646.title: Protective activity of processed tomato products on postprandial oxidation and inflammation: a clinical trial in healthy weight men and women.
pmid:22331646.finding: Processed tomato with a high-fat meal attenuated postprandial LDL oxidation and IL-6 rise.

pmid:28129549.authors: Cheng HM, Koutsidis G, Lodge JK, et al.
pmid:28129549.title: Tomato and lycopene supplementation and cardiovascular risk factors: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:28129549.finding: Tomato interventions lowered LDL (-0.22 mmol/L) and IL-6 and improved FMD (+2.53%); lycopene supplements lowered systolic BP; oxidized LDL not significantly changed.

pmid:11588897.authors: Collins BH, Horská A, Hotten PM, et al.
pmid:11588897.title: Kiwifruit protects against oxidative DNA damage in human cells and in vitro.
pmid:11588897.finding: A kiwifruit juice drink increased lymphocyte resistance to H2O2-induced DNA damage ex vivo, not fully explained by vitamin C; no effect on endogenous damage.

pmid:17999464.authors: Anand P, Kunnumakkara AB, Newman RA, et al.
pmid:17999464.title: Bioavailability of curcumin: problems and promises.
pmid:17999464.finding: Curcumin is safe up to 12 g/day but poorly bioavailable due to poor absorption, rapid metabolism and elimination.

pmid:9619120.authors: Shoba G, Joy D, Joseph T, et al.
pmid:9619120.title: Influence of piperine on the pharmacokinetics of curcumin in animals and human volunteers.
pmid:9619120.finding: 2 g curcumin alone gave undetectable or very low serum levels; with 20 mg piperine bioavailability rose 2000%.

pmid:15158307.authors: Aviram M, Rosenblat M, Gaitini D, et al.
pmid:15158307.title: Pomegranate juice consumption for 3 years by patients with carotid artery stenosis reduces common carotid intima-media thickness, blood pressure and LDL oxidation.
pmid:15158307.finding: Pomegranate juice reduced LDL oxidation and carotid IMT in a tiny, non-randomised study.

pmid:19766760.authors: Davidson MH, Maki KC, Dicklin MR, et al.
pmid:19766760.title: Effects of consumption of pomegranate juice on carotid intima-media thickness in men and women at moderate risk for coronary heart disease.
pmid:19766760.finding: 240 mL/day pomegranate juice for up to 18 months had no effect on overall carotid IMT progression.

pmid:26857863.authors: Sahebkar A, Simental-Mendía LE, Giorgini P, et al.
pmid:26857863.title: Lipid profile changes after pomegranate consumption: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:26857863.finding: Pomegranate had no significant effect on plasma lipids.

pmid:33484037.authors: Askari M, Mozaffari H, Darooghegi Mofrad M, et al.
pmid:33484037.title: Effects of garlic supplementation on oxidative stress and antioxidative capacity biomarkers: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:33484037.finding: Garlic (80-4000 mg/day) raised TAC and SOD and lowered MDA, with very large heterogeneous effect sizes.

pmid:26764326.title: Garlic Lowers Blood Pressure in Hypertensive Individuals, Regulates Serum Cholesterol, and Stimulates Immunity: An Updated Meta-analysis and Review.
pmid:26764326.finding: Garlic lowered BP by 5.1/2.5 mmHg overall and 8.7/6.1 mmHg in hypertensives.

pmid:15333514.authors: Walle T, Hsieh F, DeLegge MH, et al.
pmid:15333514.title: High absorption but very low bioavailability of oral resveratrol in humans.
pmid:15333514.finding: A 25 mg oral dose was >=70% absorbed but only trace unchanged resveratrol (<5 ng/mL) appeared in plasma due to rapid sulfation.

pmid:24819981.authors: Semba RD, Ferrucci L, Bartali B, et al.
pmid:24819981.title: Resveratrol levels and all-cause mortality in older community-dwelling adults.
pmid:24819981.finding: Urinary resveratrol metabolites from diet did not predict mortality, inflammation, CVD or cancer over 9 years.

pmid:32114706.authors: Abdelhamid AS, Brown TJ, Brainard JS, et al.
pmid:32114706.title: Omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
pmid:32114706.finding: Long-chain omega-3 had little effect on mortality, slightly reduced CHD events (RR 0.91) and lowered triglycerides ~15%.

pmid:10966889.authors: Higdon JV, Liu J, Du SH, et al.
pmid:10966889.title: Supplementation of postmenopausal women with fish oil rich in eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid is not associated with greater in vivo lipid peroxidation compared with oils rich in oleate and linoleate as assessed by plasma malondialdehyde and F(2)-isoprostanes.
pmid:10966889.finding: Fish oil (2.0 g EPA + 1.4 g DHA/day) did not raise F2-isoprostanes or MDA vs sunflower or safflower oil, though TBARS was higher.

pmid:17854006.title: Dietary advanced lipid oxidation endproducts are risk factors to human health.
pmid:17854006.finding: Oxidized dietary fats yield absorbed cytotoxic lipid oxidation end-products; humans excrete more MDA after eating them; dietary antioxidants in the meal may limit this.

pmid:18540628.authors: Gorelik S, Ligumsky M, Kohen R, et al.
pmid:18540628.title: The stomach as a "bioreactor": when red meat meets red wine.
pmid:18540628.finding: In rats, red meat raised stomach lipid hydroperoxides and plasma MDA (+50%); adding red-wine polyphenols prevented the rise.

pmid:24632108.authors: Ng CY, Leong XF, Masbah N, et al.
pmid:24632108.title: Heated vegetable oils and cardiovascular disease risk factors.
pmid:24632108.finding: Repeatedly heated oils generate lipid oxidation products that raise blood pressure, cholesterol and vascular inflammation, mainly in animal models.

pmid:27468708.authors: Vlassara H, Cai W, Tripp E, et al.
pmid:27468708.title: Oral AGE restriction ameliorates insulin resistance in obese individuals with the metabolic syndrome: a randomised controlled trial.
pmid:27468708.finding: A 1-year low-AGE diet lowered HOMA-IR from 3.1 to 1.9 and reduced AGEs, oxidative stress and inflammation; the regular diet worsened them.

pmid:17490958.authors: Negrean M, Stirban A, Stratmann B, et al.
pmid:17490958.title: Effects of low- and high-advanced glycation endproduct meals on macro- and microvascular endothelial function and oxidative stress in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
pmid:17490958.finding: An identical meal cooked to be high-AGE cut FMD by 36% vs 21% for the low-AGE version and raised oxidative stress markers.

pmid:26938557.authors: Clarke RE, Dordevic AL, Tan SM, et al.
pmid:26938557.title: Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Risk Factors for Chronic Disease: A Systematic Review of Randomised Controlled Trials.
pmid:26938557.finding: High-AGE diets increased TNF-alpha and circulating AGEs, and 8-isoprostanes in healthy adults; evidence quality limited.

pmid:10946914.authors: Mohanty P, Hamouda W, Garg R, et al.
pmid:10946914.title: Glucose challenge stimulates reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation by leucocytes.
pmid:10946914.finding: 75 g glucose raised leukocyte ROS generation to ~240% of baseline at 2 h, increased p47phox and lowered alpha-tocopherol.

pmid:11916766.authors: Mohanty P, Ghanim H, Hamouda W, et al.
pmid:11916766.title: Both lipid and protein intakes stimulate increased generation of reactive oxygen species by polymorphonuclear leukocytes and mononuclear cells.
pmid:11916766.finding: Cream raised leukocyte ROS for 3 h and lipid peroxidation; casein raised ROS for 1 h.

pmid:18206731.authors: O'Keefe JH, Gheewala NM, O'Keefe JO
pmid:18206731.title: Dietary strategies for improving post-prandial glucose, lipids, inflammation, and cardiovascular health.
pmid:18206731.finding: Post-meal glucose and triglyceride spikes induce oxidant stress proportional to their size; minimally processed high-fiber plant foods blunt them.

pmid:26355033.authors: Boden G, Homko C, Barrero CA, et al.
pmid:26355033.title: Excessive caloric intake acutely causes oxidative stress, GLUT4 carbonylation, and insulin resistance in healthy men.
pmid:26355033.finding: ~6000 kcal/day for 1 week caused 3.5 kg gain and systemic and adipose oxidative stress and insulin resistance within 2-3 days.

pmid:22586466.authors: Samocha-Bonet D, Campbell LV, Mori TA, et al.
pmid:22586466.title: Overfeeding reduces insulin sensitivity and increases oxidative stress, without altering markers of mitochondrial content and function in humans.
pmid:22586466.finding: +1040 kcal/day for 28 days raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and muscle protein carbonyls and reduced insulin sensitivity.

pmid:21209396.authors: Bastide NM, Pierre FH, Corpet DE
pmid:21209396.title: Heme iron from meat and risk of colorectal cancer: a meta-analysis and a review of the mechanisms involved.
pmid:21209396.finding: Highest vs lowest heme intake: colon cancer RR 1.18; heme catalyses N-nitrosation and lipoperoxidation to cytotoxic aldehydes.

pmid:26514947.authors: Bouvard V, Loomis D, Guyton KZ, et al.
pmid:26514947.title: Carcinogenicity of consumption of red and processed meat.
pmid:26514947.finding: IARC classified processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A).

pmid:12421881.authors: Bingham SA, Hughes R, Cross AJ
pmid:12421881.title: Effect of white versus red meat on endogenous N-nitrosation in the human colon and further evidence of a dose response.
pmid:12421881.finding: Fecal N-nitroso compounds rose linearly with red meat from 0 to 420 g/day; white meat had no effect; fiber did not reduce them.

pmid:15199546.title: Meat-related mutagens/carcinogens in the etiology of colorectal cancer.
pmid:15199546.finding: High-temperature cooking forms HCAs and PAHs; endogenous N-nitroso exposure is dose-dependent on red meat.

pmid:20335545.authors: Li Z, Henning SM, Zhang Y, et al.
pmid:20335545.title: Antioxidant-rich spice added to hamburger meat during cooking results in reduced meat, plasma, and urine malondialdehyde concentrations.
pmid:20335545.finding: Spice blend cut burger MDA by 71%, prevented the plasma MDA rise and lowered urinary MDA by 49%.

pmid:19241593.authors: Smith JS, Ameri F, Gadgil P
pmid:19241593.title: Effect of marinades on the formation of heterocyclic amines in grilled beef steaks.
pmid:19241593.finding: Herb/spice marinades cut total HCAs in steaks grilled at 204 °C by 57-88%.
