pmid:21697300.authors: Skulas-Ray AC, Kris-Etherton PM, Teeter DL, et al.
pmid:21697300.title: A high antioxidant spice blend attenuates postprandial insulin and triglyceride responses and increases some plasma measures of antioxidant activity in healthy, overweight men.
pmid:21697300.finding: 14 g spice blend in a meal reduced postprandial insulin (21%) and triglycerides (31%) and raised plasma FRAP.

pmid:16611951.authors: Mozaffarian D, Katan MB, Ascherio A, et al.
pmid:16611951.title: Trans fatty acids and cardiovascular disease.
pmid:16611951.finding: Industrial trans fats adversely affect lipoproteins, inflammation and endothelial function and are strongly linked to coronary heart disease.

pmid:9989688.authors: Lund EK, Wharf SG, Fairweather-Tait SJ, et al.
pmid:9989688.title: Oral ferrous sulfate supplements increase the free radical-generating capacity of feces from healthy volunteers.
pmid:9989688.finding: 19 mg Fe/day for 2 weeks raised weakly bound fecal iron from 60 to 300 µmol/L and fecal free-radical production ~40%.

pmid:10491416.authors: Meagher EA, Barry OP, Burke A, et al.
pmid:10491416.title: Alcohol-induced generation of lipid peroxidation products in humans.
pmid:10491416.finding: Acute alcohol raised urinary isoprostanes in a time- and dose-dependent way tracking blood alcohol; levels were high in alcoholic liver disease.

pmid:29424490.authors: Il'yasova D, Fontana L, Bhapkar M, et al.
pmid:29424490.title: Effects of 2 years of caloric restriction on oxidative status assessed by urinary F2-isoprostanes: The CALERIE 2 randomized clinical trial.
pmid:29424490.finding: Prescribed 25% CR lowered 2,3-dinor-iPF2alpha-III by 17%/13% and iPF2alpha-III by 20%/27% at 12/24 months vs ad libitum.

pmid:16595757.authors: Heilbronn LK, de Jonge L, Frisard MI, et al.
pmid:16595757.title: Effect of 6-month calorie restriction on biomarkers of longevity, metabolic adaptation, and oxidative stress in overweight individuals: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:16595757.finding: 6 months of CR lowered fasting insulin and DNA damage; protein carbonyls unchanged.

pmid:10590217.authors: Thompson HJ, Heimendinger J, Haegele A, et al.
pmid:10590217.title: Effect of increased vegetable and fruit consumption on markers of oxidative cellular damage.
pmid:10590217.finding: Raising produce from 5.8 to 12 servings/day for 14 days lowered lymphocyte and urinary 8-OHdG and urinary 8-isoprostane (uncontrolled).

pmid:14578137.authors: Møller P, Vogel U, Pedersen A, et al.
pmid:14578137.title: No effect of 600 grams fruit and vegetables per day on oxidative DNA damage and repair in healthy nonsmokers.
pmid:14578137.finding: 600 g/day fruit and vegetables or matched vitamins for 24 days did not change oxidative DNA damage or repair.

pmid:12623938.authors: Lopes HF, Martin KL, Nashar K, et al.
pmid:12623938.title: DASH diet lowers blood pressure and lipid-induced oxidative stress in obesity.
pmid:12623938.finding: DASH lowered BP ~8/7 mmHg in obese hypertensives, raised FRAP and prevented the F2-isoprostane rise during lipid infusion.

pmid:29754952.authors: Sutton EF, Beyl R, Early KS, et al.
pmid:29754952.title: Early Time-Restricted Feeding Improves Insulin Sensitivity, Blood Pressure, and Oxidative Stress Even without Weight Loss in Men with Prediabetes.
pmid:29754952.finding: 5 weeks of 6-h early feeding lowered plasma 8-isoprostane by ~14% (p=0.05) vs 12-h feeding without weight loss.

pmid:17291990.authors: Johnson JB, Summer W, Cutler RG, et al.
pmid:17291990.title: Alternate day calorie restriction improves clinical findings and reduces markers of oxidative stress and inflammation in overweight adults with moderate asthma.
pmid:17291990.finding: 8 weeks of alternate-day CR (8% weight loss) reduced 8-isoprostane, nitrotyrosine, protein carbonyls and HNE adducts (uncontrolled).

pmid:31881139.title: Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Health, Aging, and Disease.
pmid:31881139.finding: Reviews metabolic switching and adaptive stress responses (including antioxidant defences) proposed to underlie fasting benefits.

pmid:28338764.authors: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, et al.
pmid:28338764.title: Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality-a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies.
pmid:28338764.finding: Per 200 g/day: all-cause mortality RR 0.90; reductions up to 800 g/day; strongest for citrus, apples/pears, green leafy and cruciferous vegetables.

pmid:27301975.authors: Aune D, Keum N, Giovannucci E, et al.
pmid:27301975.title: Whole grain consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all cause and cause specific mortality: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies.
pmid:27301975.finding: Per 90 g/day whole grain: CHD RR 0.81, all-cause mortality RR 0.83; reductions up to 210-225 g/day.

pmid:30638909.authors: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, et al.
pmid:30638909.title: Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
pmid:30638909.finding: Highest vs lowest fiber intake: 15-30% lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease; greatest benefit at 25-29 g/day.

pmid:21045839.authors: Pérez-Jiménez J, Neveu V, Vos F, et al.
pmid:21045839.title: Identification of the 100 richest dietary sources of polyphenols: an application of the Phenol-Explorer database.
pmid:21045839.finding: Total polyphenols by chromatography ranged from 15,000 mg/100 g (cloves) down; Folin values systematically exceed chromatography totals.

pmid:24103452.authors: Rothwell JA, Perez-Jimenez J, Neveu V, et al.
pmid:24103452.title: Phenol-Explorer 3.0: a major update of the Phenol-Explorer database to incorporate data on the effects of food processing on polyphenol content.
pmid:24103452.finding: Describes the Phenol-Explorer database and its retention factors for food processing.

diet:phenolexplorer.title: Phenol-Explorer database: polyphenol content of foods, food pages accessed 2026-09-30 (chromatography, Folin assay and pH-differential tables).
diet:phenolexplorer.finding: Source of per-food polyphenol values used here; 'chromatography (sum of compounds)' values were computed by summing the individual compounds listed in each food's chromatography table.

diet:usdafdc.title: FoodData Central, SR Legacy food records (e.g. FDC 168153 kiwifruit, 170108 red pepper, 170379 broccoli, 170457 tomato, 170460 tomato puree, 170393 carrot, 168462 spinach, 168421 kale, 169097 orange, 167762 strawberry), accessed 2026-09-30.
diet:usdafdc.finding: Source of vitamin C, carotenoid and lycopene contents per 100 g.

pmid:25772010.authors: van 't Erve TJ, Lih FB, Kadiiska MB, et al.
pmid:25772010.title: Reinterpreting the best biomarker of oxidative stress: The 8-iso-PGF(2α)/PGF(2α) ratio distinguishes chemical from enzymatic lipid peroxidation.
pmid:25772010.finding: 8-iso-PGF2alpha can also come from enzymatic (COX) synthesis during inflammation, so rises do not always mean more chemical oxidative stress.

pmid:23596162.authors: Siervo M, Lara J, Ogbonmwan I, et al.
pmid:23596162.title: Inorganic nitrate and beetroot juice supplementation reduces blood pressure in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:23596162.finding: Nitrate/beetroot lowered systolic BP by 4.4 mmHg, dose-dependently.

pmid:20096093.authors: Carlsen MH, Halvorsen BL, Holte K, et al.
pmid:20096093.title: The total antioxidant content of more than 3100 foods, beverages, spices, herbs and supplements used worldwide.
pmid:20096093.finding: FRAP antioxidant content varies several-thousand-fold between foods; spices and herbs are highest.

pmid:15186133.authors: Wu X, Beecher GR, Holden JM, et al.
pmid:15186133.title: Lipophilic and hydrophilic antioxidant capacities of common foods in the United States.
pmid:15186133.finding: ORAC values of >100 US foods; total phenolics (Folin) correlated only weakly with hydrophilic ORAC.

pmid:38428187.authors: Favari C, Rinaldi de Alvarenga JF, Sánchez-Martínez L, et al.
pmid:38428187.title: Factors driving the inter-individual variability in the metabolism and bioavailability of (poly)phenolic metabolites: A systematic review of human studies.
pmid:38428187.finding: Gut microbiota, genetics, age, sex and BMI drive high/low excretor gradients and producer/non-producer metabotypes (urolithins, equol) for polyphenol metabolites.

pmid:25530151.authors: Rodriguez-Mateos A, Hezel M, Aydin H, et al.
pmid:25530151.title: Interactions between cocoa flavanols and inorganic nitrate: additive effects on endothelial function at achievable dietary amounts.
pmid:25530151.finding: Cocoa flavanols and nitrate each raised FMD dose-dependently (peak at 1 h) and their effects were additive at low intake levels.

pmid:24492839.authors: Paulsen G, Cumming KT, Holden G, et al.
pmid:24492839.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation hampers cellular adaptation to endurance training in humans: a double-blind, randomised, controlled trial.
pmid:24492839.finding: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 235 mg vitamin E daily for 11 weeks of endurance training did not change VO2max gains (8% in both groups) but blunted training-induced increases in muscle mitochondrial markers.

pmid:21325105.authors: Yfanti C, Nielsen AR, Akerström T, et al.
pmid:21325105.title: Effect of antioxidant supplementation on insulin sensitivity in response to endurance exercise training.
pmid:21325105.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E during 12 weeks of intense endurance training (5x/week) did not change the ~17-19% training-induced gain in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake or VO2max.

pmid:26129928.authors: Bjørnsen T, Salvesen S, Berntsen S, et al.
pmid:26129928.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation blunts increases in total lean body mass in elderly men after strength training.
pmid:26129928.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 117.5 mg vitamin E around each of three weekly strength sessions for 12 weeks blunted lean-mass gain (1.4% vs 3.9% on placebo) but not strength gains.

pmid:31851538.authors: Clifford T, Jeffries O, Stevenson EJ, et al.
pmid:31851538.title: The effects of vitamin C and E on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: a systematic review and Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:31851538.finding: Across 9 aerobic and 9 resistance-training RCTs, vitamin C and/or E did not significantly attenuate gains in VO2max, endurance performance, lean mass or strength; trials were small.

pmid:32127289.authors: Mason SA, Trewin AJ, Parker L, et al.
pmid:32127289.title: Antioxidant supplements and endurance exercise: Current evidence and mechanistic insights.
pmid:32127289.finding: Review concluding that chronic intake of 1000 mg vitamin C plus vitamin E is not recommended during heavy training, and that most marketed antioxidant compounds lack supportive human evidence.

pmid:17869589.authors: Radak Z, Chung HY, Koltai E, et al.
pmid:17869589.title: Exercise, oxidative stress and hormesis.
pmid:17869589.finding: Review framing exercise as a hormetic stressor: repeated moderate ROS exposure up-regulates antioxidant and repair systems, with a bell-shaped dose-response curve.

pmid:26893258.authors: Powers SK, Radak Z, Ji LL
pmid:26893258.title: Exercise-induced oxidative stress: past, present and future.
pmid:26893258.finding: Review of sources of exercise-induced ROS (mitochondria, NADPH oxidases, xanthine oxidase) and evidence that these ROS act as signals required for training adaptation.

pmid:27770706.title: Nrf2 mediates redox adaptations to exercise.
pmid:27770706.finding: Review of evidence that acute exercise activates Nrf2 and that repeated bouts up-regulate Nrf2-controlled antioxidant defences, with emerging human data.

pmid:40834031.authors: Torres-Rojo FI, Enríquez-Del Castillo LA, González-Chávez SA, et al.
pmid:40834031.title: Effect of exercise intensity on redox biomarkers in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
pmid:40834031.finding: Chronic exercise training raised antioxidant capacity and lowered pro-oxidant markers in healthy adults; the effect was significant for vigorous protocols but not for non-vigorous ones.

pmid:36139825.authors: Zhou Z, Chen C, Teo EC, et al.
pmid:36139825.title: Intracellular Oxidative Stress Induced by Physical Exercise in Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:36139825.finding: Exercise-induced oxidative damage (8-OHdG, F2-isoprostanes, protein carbonyls) depends on intensity times volume; moderate continuous exercise and low-volume HIIT carried the lowest probability of large oxidative stress in unhealthy adults.

pmid:39914379.authors: Cordeiro LS, Linhares DG, Castro JBP, et al.
pmid:39914379.title: Impacts of Resistance Training on Endogenous Antioxidants in Older Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
pmid:39914379.finding: Resistance training in healthy older adults raised glutathione peroxidase (SMD 0.57) but did not significantly change catalase or total antioxidant activity.

pmid:20139793.authors: Campbell PT, Gross MD, Potter JD, et al.
pmid:20139793.title: Effect of exercise on oxidative stress: a 12-month randomized, controlled trial.
pmid:20139793.finding: 12 months of aerobic exercise (>=45 min/day, 5 days/week, 60-75% HRmax) lowered F2-isoprostanes 6% vs controls (not significant overall); women whose VO2max rose >15% had a 14% reduction.

pmid:33740420.authors: Flockhart M, Nilsson LC, Tais S, et al.
pmid:33740420.title: Excessive exercise training causes mitochondrial functional impairment and decreases glucose tolerance in healthy volunteers.
pmid:33740420.n: healthy volunteers (small progressive-load training study) plus elite athletes
pmid:33740420.finding: When training load was ramped up over 4 weeks, the highest-load week caused a sharp fall in intrinsic mitochondrial function and impaired glucose tolerance.

pmid:17697935.authors: Margonis K, Fatouros IG, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
pmid:17697935.title: Oxidative stress biomarkers responses to physical overtraining: implications for diagnosis.
pmid:17697935.finding: An overreaching resistance-training block raised urinary isoprostanes 7-fold, TBARS 56% and protein carbonyls 73% and lowered GSH 31%; markers tracked the performance decline.

pmid:11585710.authors: Mastaloudis A, Leonard SW, Traber MG
pmid:11585710.title: Oxidative stress in athletes during extreme endurance exercise.
pmid:11585710.finding: A 50 km ultramarathon (~6.5 h) raised plasma F2-isoprostanes from 75 to 131 pg/ml, with return to baseline by 24 h.

pmid:33239350.authors: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al.
pmid:33239350.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour.
pmid:33239350.finding: WHO 2020 guidelines: adults should do 150-300 min/week of moderate or 75-150 min/week of vigorous aerobic activity, muscle strengthening on >=2 days/week, and limit sedentary time.

pmid:31721213.authors: Dirks ML, Miotto PM, Goossens GH, et al.
pmid:31721213.title: Short-term bed rest-induced insulin resistance cannot be explained by increased mitochondrial H(2) O(2) emission.
pmid:31721213.finding: Short-term bed rest cut insulin sensitivity by 42% and lowered mitochondrial respiration, but did not raise resting mitochondrial H2O2 emission or oxidative stress markers.

pmid:32502393.authors: Vaccaro A, Kaplan Dor Y, Nambara K, et al.
pmid:32502393.title: Sleep Loss Can Cause Death through Accumulation of Reactive Oxygen Species in the Gut.
pmid:32502393.finding: In flies and mice, severe sleep deprivation caused ROS accumulation in the gut; oral antioxidants or gut-targeted antioxidant enzymes prevented early death.

pmid:37717072.authors: Shah R, Shah VK, Emin M, et al.
pmid:37717072.title: Mild sleep restriction increases endothelial oxidative stress in female persons.
pmid:37717072.finding: Six weeks of sleeping 1.5 h less than habitual (randomized crossover) increased endothelial-cell oxidative stress without a compensatory antioxidant response.

pmid:28738082.authors: Trivedi MS, Holger D, Bui AT, et al.
pmid:28738082.title: Short-term sleep deprivation leads to decreased systemic redox metabolites and altered epigenetic status.
pmid:28738082.finding: One night of total sleep deprivation significantly lowered plasma glutathione, cysteine, ATP and homocysteine.

pmid:28933565.authors: Nagata C, Tamura T, Wada K, et al.
pmid:28933565.title: Sleep duration, nightshift work, and the timing of meals and urinary levels of 8-isoprostane and 6-sulfatoxymelatonin in Japanese women.
pmid:28933565.finding: Women sleeping 6 h or less had about 12% higher urinary 8-isoprostane than women sleeping more than 8 h.

pmid:26039963.authors: Watson NF, Badr MS, Belenky G, et al.
pmid:26039963.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society.
pmid:26039963.finding: AASM/SRS consensus statement: adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis.

pmid:28652381.authors: Bhatti P, Mirick DK, Randolph TW, et al.
pmid:28652381.title: Oxidative DNA damage during night shift work.
pmid:28652381.finding: During night work (low melatonin) urinary 8-OH-dG excretion was only 20% of that during night sleep, interpreted as reduced repair of oxidative DNA lesions.

pmid:39993913.authors: Zanif U, Lai AS, Parks J, et al.
pmid:39993913.title: Melatonin supplementation and oxidative DNA damage repair capacity among night shift workers: a randomised placebo-controlled trial.
pmid:39993913.finding: Melatonin taken before day sleep for 4 weeks gave a borderline-significant 1.8-fold increase in urinary 8-OH-dG during day sleep, suggesting improved oxidative DNA repair.

pmid:36322225.authors: Hosseini H, Homayouni-Tabrizi M, Amiri H, et al.
pmid:36322225.title: The effect of continuous positive airway pressure on total antioxidant capacity in obstructive sleep apnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:36322225.finding: CPAP treatment of obstructive sleep apnea increased total antioxidant capacity (SMD 0.50).

pmid:8964113.authors: Reilly M, Delanty N, Lawson JA, et al.
pmid:8964113.title: Modulation of oxidant stress in vivo in chronic cigarette smokers.
pmid:8964113.finding: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a rose with smoking dose (heavy 177, moderate 93, nonsmokers 54 pmol/mmol) and fell within 2-3 weeks of quitting; high-dose vitamin C lowered it, vitamin E alone did not.

pmid:10944241.authors: Pilz H, Oguogho A, Chehne F, et al.
pmid:10944241.title: Quitting cigarette smoking results in a fast improvement of in vivo oxidation injury (determined via plasma, serum and urinary isoprostane).
pmid:10944241.finding: Isoprostanes in plasma, serum and urine dropped within days of quitting and reached a new steady state about 4 weeks after cessation.

pmid:27932354.authors: King CC, Piper ME, Gepner AD, et al.
pmid:27932354.title: Longitudinal Impact of Smoking and Smoking Cessation on Inflammatory Markers of Cardiovascular Disease Risk.
pmid:27932354.finding: Smoking heaviness was independently tied to urinary F2-isoprostanes; after one year, successful quitters had lower F2-isoprostanes and white-cell counts despite gaining weight.

pmid:18324566.authors: Joseph AM, Hecht SS, Murphy SE, et al.
pmid:18324566.title: Smoking reduction fails to improve clinical and biological markers of cardiac disease: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:18324566.finding: Cutting cigarettes from ~27 to ~18/day over 6 months did not change F2-isoprostanes, inflammatory markers or symptoms; only carbon monoxide fell.

pmid:11466122.authors: Otsuka R, Watanabe H, Hirata K, et al.
pmid:11466122.title: Acute effects of passive smoking on the coronary circulation in healthy young adults.
pmid:11466122.finding: A 30-minute exposure to environmental tobacco smoke reduced coronary flow velocity reserve in healthy nonsmokers (4.4 to 3.4), indicating acute coronary endothelial dysfunction.

pmid:31429895.authors: Duncan MS, Freiberg MS, Greevy RA Jr, et al.
pmid:31429895.title: Association of Smoking Cessation With Subsequent Risk of Cardiovascular Disease.
pmid:31429895.finding: Quitting was linked to 39% lower CVD risk within 5 years versus continued smoking, but heavy smokers' risk stayed above never-smokers for well over 5 years (10-15+ years).

pmid:9644196.authors: Bermúdez E, Stone K, Carter KM, et al.
pmid:9644196.title: Environmental tobacco smoke is just as damaging to DNA as mainstream smoke.
pmid:9644196.finding: Tar from environmental (secondhand) tobacco smoke generated hydrogen peroxide and nicked DNA in cells much like mainstream-smoke tar; catalase was protective.

pmid:15911719.title: Cardiovascular effects of secondhand smoke: nearly as large as smoking.
pmid:15911719.finding: Secondhand smoke raises coronary heart disease risk ~30%; even brief exposure produces effects on platelets, endothelium and oxidative stress averaging 80-90% of those of chronic active smoking.

pmid:30356972.authors: Siti Hajar MH, Zulkefli S, Juwita S, et al.
pmid:30356972.title: Metabolic, inflammatory, and oxidative stress markers in women exposed to secondhand smoke.
pmid:30356972.finding: Women with modest secondhand-smoke exposure (>=15 min on >=2 days/week) did not differ from unexposed women in 8-isoprostane, oxidized LDL or inflammatory markers.

pmid:27108682.authors: Carnevale R, Sciarretta S, Violi F, et al.
pmid:27108682.title: Acute Impact of Tobacco vs Electronic Cigarette Smoking on Oxidative Stress and Vascular Function.
pmid:27108682.finding: A single e-cigarette and a single tobacco cigarette both acutely raised 8-iso-PGF2a and NOX2 activation and lowered flow-mediated dilation; the e-cigarette's oxidative effects were smaller.

pmid:34289969.authors: Christensen CH, Chang JT, Rostron BL, et al.
pmid:34289969.title: Biomarkers of Inflammation and Oxidative Stress among Adult Former Smoker, Current E-Cigarette Users-Results from Wave 1 PATH Study.
pmid:34289969.finding: Former smokers who now only vape had F2-isoprostane levels similar to former smokers using nothing; dual users had 9% higher levels than cigarette-only smokers.

pmid:27113031.authors: Sharma R, Harlev A, Agarwal A, et al.
pmid:27113031.title: Cigarette Smoking and Semen Quality: A New Meta-analysis Examining the Effect of the 2010 World Health Organization Laboratory Methods for the Examination of Human Semen.
pmid:27113031.finding: Smoking was associated with lower sperm count, motility and morphology, with larger effects in moderate/heavy smokers.

pmid:18078827.title: CYP2E1 and oxidative liver injury by alcohol.
pmid:18078827.finding: Review: chronic ethanol induces CYP2E1, which leaks superoxide and hydrogen peroxide and drives lipid peroxidation in alcoholic liver injury.

pmid:22859618.authors: Schrieks IC, van den Berg R, Sierksma A, et al.
pmid:22859618.title: Effect of red wine consumption on biomarkers of oxidative stress.
pmid:22859618.finding: Four weeks of 450 ml/day red wine (4 drinks, 41 g alcohol) raised urinary 8-iso-PGF2a versus the same wine dealcoholized (157 vs 141 pg/mg creatinine).

pmid:29676281.authors: Wood AM, Kaptoge S, Butterworth AS, et al.
pmid:29676281.title: Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies.
pmid:29676281.finding: All-cause mortality was lowest at or below ~100 g alcohol per week and rose with higher intake; stroke, heart failure and fatal hypertensive disease rose roughly linearly.

pmid:17709633.authors: Pou KM, Massaro JM, Hoffmann U, et al.
pmid:17709633.title: Visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue volumes are cross-sectionally related to markers of inflammation and oxidative stress: the Framingham Heart Study.
pmid:17709633.finding: Visceral fat was more strongly associated with urinary isoprostanes than subcutaneous abdominal fat.

pmid:27803047.authors: Duggan C, Tapsoba JD, Wang CY, et al.
pmid:27803047.title: Dietary Weight Loss, Exercise, and Oxidative Stress in Postmenopausal Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
pmid:27803047.finding: 12 months of calorie-restricted weight-loss diet lowered F2-isoprostanes by ~23% (diet) and ~24% (diet plus exercise) vs 3% in controls; greater weight loss gave greater reductions.

pmid:28319890.authors: Monzo-Beltran L, Vazquez-Tarragón A, Cerdà C, et al.
pmid:28319890.title: One-year follow-up of clinical, metabolic and oxidative stress profile of morbid obese patients after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. 8-oxo-dG as a clinical marker.
pmid:28319890.n: morbidly obese patients vs normal-weight controls
pmid:28319890.finding: Morbidly obese patients had raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and 8-oxo-dG; after sleeve gastrectomy these declined progressively and antioxidant enzymes recovered over one year.

pmid:21959342.authors: Il'yasova D, Wang F, Spasojevic I, et al.
pmid:21959342.title: Urinary F2-isoprostanes, obesity, and weight gain in the IRAS cohort.
pmid:21959342.finding: Urinary F2-isoprostanes were higher with obesity cross-sectionally, yet some isoprostanes predicted less weight gain over 5 years, cautioning against naive reading of the marker.

pmid:23242914.authors: Sermondade N, Faure C, Fezeu L, et al.
pmid:23242914.title: BMI in relation to sperm count: an updated systematic review and collaborative meta-analysis.
pmid:23242914.finding: Obesity was associated with higher odds of oligozoospermia or azoospermia (OR 1.28; morbid obesity OR 2.04).

pmid:32835677.authors: Li Z, Liu Q, Xu Z, et al.
pmid:32835677.title: Association between short-term exposure to ambient particulate air pollution and biomarkers of oxidative stress: A meta-analysis.
pmid:32835677.finding: Each 10 ug/m3 rise in short-term PM2.5 was associated with 1.6% higher malondialdehyde and a borderline 2.1% higher 8-OHdG.

pmid:28669628.title: Role of oxidative stress in cardiovascular disease outcomes following exposure to ambient air pollution.
pmid:28669628.finding: Review of epidemiological, controlled-exposure and experimental data concluding that oxidative stress is central to the cardiovascular effects of ambient air pollution.

pmid:26022815.authors: Chen R, Zhao A, Chen H, et al.
pmid:26022815.title: Cardiopulmonary benefits of reducing indoor particles of outdoor origin: a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of air purifiers.
pmid:26022815.finding: 48 h of real vs sham air purification cut indoor PM2.5 by 57% (96 to 41 ug/m3) and lowered inflammatory and thrombotic markers (e.g., myeloperoxidase -33%) and blood pressure.

pmid:33682970.authors: Wang Y, Zhao Y, Xue L, et al.
pmid:33682970.title: Effects of air purification of indoor PM(2.5) on the cardiorespiratory biomarkers in young healthy adults.
pmid:33682970.finding: One week of real vs sham HEPA purification lowered diastolic blood pressure, exhaled NO and 8-isoprostane and improved lung function.

pmid:34630006.authors: Hoffmann B, Boogaard H, de Nazelle A, et al.
pmid:34630006.title: WHO Air Quality Guidelines 2021-Aiming for Healthier Air for all: A Joint Statement by Medical, Public Health, Scientific Societies and Patient Representative Organisations.
pmid:34630006.finding: Joint statement endorsing the WHO 2021 Air Quality Guidelines, including annual mean PM2.5 not exceeding 5 ug/m3 and peak-season 8-h ozone not exceeding 60 ug/m3.

pmid:22452928.authors: Forchhammer L, Møller P, Riddervold IS, et al.
pmid:22452928.title: Controlled human wood smoke exposure: oxidative stress, inflammation and microvascular function.
pmid:22452928.finding: Three-hour controlled exposures to 220-354 ug/m3 particles from a modern wood stove had no effect on oxidatively damaged DNA, inflammatory markers or microvascular function.

pmid:17704195.authors: Barregard L, Sällsten G, Andersson L, et al.
pmid:17704195.title: Experimental exposure to wood smoke: effects on airway inflammation and oxidative stress.
pmid:17704195.finding: Four-hour exposure to 240-280 ug/m3 wood smoke raised malondialdehyde in exhaled breath condensate and alveolar NO, indicating airway oxidative stress.

pmid:23962958.authors: Lin W, Brunekreef B, Gehring U
pmid:23962958.title: Meta-analysis of the effects of indoor nitrogen dioxide and gas cooking on asthma and wheeze in children.
pmid:23962958.finding: Gas cooking was associated with higher odds of childhood asthma (OR 1.32) and indoor NO2 with current wheeze (OR 1.15 per 15 ppb).

pmid:37638371.authors: Li W, Long C, Fan T, et al.
pmid:37638371.title: Gas cooking and respiratory outcomes in children: A systematic review.
pmid:37638371.finding: Systematic review concluding the gas-cooking and childhood asthma literature is heterogeneous, mostly cross-sectional and low quality, and insufficient to establish causation.

pmid:25653189.title: Oxidation events and skin aging.
pmid:25653189.finding: Review: UV drives skin photoaging through direct DNA damage and indirect ROS/RNS-mediated oxidation of lipids, proteins and DNA.

pmid:23732711.authors: Hughes MC, Williams GM, Baker P, et al.
pmid:23732711.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial.
pmid:23732711.finding: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years gave 24% less skin aging than discretionary use; 30 mg/day beta-carotene had no overall effect.

pmid:17015167.authors: Hanson KM, Gratton E, Bardeen CJ
pmid:17015167.title: Sunscreen enhancement of UV-induced reactive oxygen species in the skin.
pmid:17015167.finding: Organic UV filters that penetrate into the epidermis increased UV-induced ROS above unprotected skin after about 60 minutes, arguing for reapplication.

pmid:30415629.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
pmid:30415629.title: Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease.
pmid:30415629.finding: Vitamin D3 2000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years did not lower invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events (VITAL).

pmid:15574496.authors: Epel ES, Blackburn EH, Lin J, et al.
pmid:15574496.title: Accelerated telomere shortening in response to life stress.
pmid:15574496.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:15574496.finding: Higher perceived and chronic stress was associated with higher oxidative stress, lower telomerase and telomeres shorter by the equivalent of about a decade of aging.

pmid:25462890.authors: Black CN, Bot M, Scheffer PG, et al.
pmid:25462890.title: Is depression associated with increased oxidative stress? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:25462890.finding: Depression was associated with higher 8-OHdG (g = 0.31) and F2-isoprostanes (g = 0.48).

pmid:28963884.authors: Pascoe MC, Thompson DR, Ski CF
pmid:28963884.title: Yoga, mindfulness-based stress reduction and stress-related physiological measures: A meta-analysis.
pmid:28963884.finding: Yoga-based practices, versus active controls, lowered cortisol, ambulatory blood pressure and resting heart rate; trials were heterogeneous.

pmid:28670311.authors: Buric I, Farias M, Jong J, et al.
pmid:28670311.title: What Is the Molecular Signature of Mind-Body Interventions? A Systematic Review of Gene Expression Changes Induced by Meditation and Related Practices.
pmid:28670311.finding: Meditation, yoga, tai chi and related practices were associated with down-regulation of NF-kB pathway gene expression; studies were small and heterogeneous.

pmid:24280463.authors: Hegde SV, Adhikari P, Shetty S, et al.
pmid:24280463.title: Effect of community-based yoga intervention on oxidative stress and glycemic parameters in prediabetes: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:24280463.finding: Three months of community yoga lowered malondialdehyde versus wait-list control but did not change antioxidant levels; no active control.

pmid:25705824.authors: Laukkanen T, Khan H, Zaccardi F, et al.
pmid:25705824.title: Association between sauna bathing and fatal cardiovascular and all-cause mortality events.
pmid:25705824.finding: Compared with one session/week, 4-7 sauna sessions/week was associated with 63% lower sudden cardiac death and lower CVD and all-cause mortality; sessions >19 min were also associated with lower risk.

pmid:29897261.authors: Kunutsor SK, Laukkanen T, Laukkanen JA
pmid:29897261.title: Longitudinal associations of sauna bathing with inflammation and oxidative stress: the KIHD prospective cohort study.
pmid:29897261.finding: 4-7 sauna sessions/week was associated with lower CRP and leukocyte counts over 11 years, but not with gamma-glutamyltransferase, the oxidative-stress proxy studied.

pmid:30077204.authors: Laukkanen JA, Laukkanen T, Kunutsor SK
pmid:30077204.title: Cardiovascular and Other Health Benefits of Sauna Bathing: A Review of the Evidence.
pmid:30077204.finding: Review of observational and interventional evidence linking Finnish sauna bathing to lower blood pressure, cardiovascular disease and mortality, with proposed vascular and autonomic mechanisms.

pmid:27270841.authors: Brunt VE, Howard MJ, Francisco MA, et al.
pmid:27270841.title: Passive heat therapy improves endothelial function, arterial stiffness and blood pressure in sedentary humans.
pmid:27270841.finding: Eight weeks of 40.5 C hot-water immersion 4-5 times/week (rectal temperature >=38.5 C for 60 min) doubled flow-mediated dilation (5.6 to 10.9%) and lowered blood pressure versus thermoneutral sham.

pmid:23411620.authors: Garolla A, Torino M, Sartini B, et al.
pmid:23411620.title: Seminal and molecular evidence that sauna exposure affects human spermatogenesis.
pmid:23411620.finding: Two sauna sessions/week at 80-90 C, 15 min each, for 3 months impaired sperm count, motility, chromatin condensation and mitochondrial function; fully reversed 6 months after stopping.

pmid:10396606.authors: Siems WG, Brenke R, Sommerburg O, et al.
pmid:10396606.title: Improved antioxidative protection in winter swimmers.
pmid:10396606.finding: Winter swimmers had higher baseline erythrocyte glutathione and higher SOD and catalase activity, interpreted as adaptation to repeated cold-induced oxidative stress.

pmid:36137565.authors: Esperland D, de Weerd L, Mercer JB
pmid:36137565.title: Health effects of voluntary exposure to cold water - a continuing subject of debate.
pmid:36137565.finding: Review of voluntary cold-water immersion: studies are small and heterogeneous; possible benefits on insulin sensitivity and adipose tissue, but no firm conclusions.

pmid:28833689.authors: Tipton MJ, Collier N, Massey H, et al.
pmid:28833689.title: Cold water immersion: kill or cure?
pmid:28833689.finding: Review of cold-water immersion as hazard (cold shock, drowning, cardiac arrest, hypothermia) and treatment; evidence for many claimed benefits ranges from credible to anecdotal.

pmid:26174323.authors: Roberts LA, Raastad T, Markworth JF, et al.
pmid:26174323.title: Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training.
pmid:26174323.finding: Ten minutes of cold-water immersion after each strength session for 12 weeks blunted gains in strength and muscle mass versus active recovery.

pmid:21414382.title: Advances in metal-induced oxidative stress and human disease.
pmid:21414382.finding: Review: redox-active metals (iron, copper, chromium) generate radicals via Fenton chemistry, while cadmium, arsenic and lead act mainly by binding thiols and depleting glutathione.

pmid:35150710.authors: Urbano T, Filippini T, Wise LA, et al.
pmid:35150710.title: Associations of urinary and dietary cadmium with urinary 8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2'-deoxyguanosine and blood biochemical parameters.
pmid:35150710.finding: Urinary and dietary cadmium were positively and linearly correlated with urinary 8-oxodG in non-smoking blood donors.

pmid:31678726.authors: Kim SS, Meeker JD, Keil AP, et al.
pmid:31678726.title: Exposure to 17 trace metals in pregnancy and associations with urinary oxidative stress biomarkers.
pmid:31678726.finding: Among 17 urinary metals, the strongest associations with 8-isoprostane and 8-OHdG were for essential selenium and copper, illustrating confounding in spot-urine biomarker studies.

pmid:25402001.authors: Ferguson KK, McElrath TF, Chen YH, et al.
pmid:25402001.title: Urinary phthalate metabolites and biomarkers of oxidative stress in pregnant women: a repeated measures analysis.
pmid:25402001.finding: Urinary phthalate metabolites were associated with higher urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane across repeated measures in pregnancy.

pmid:37813138.authors: Chen JC, Baumert BO, Li Y, et al.
pmid:37813138.title: Associations of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, polychlorinated biphenyls, organochlorine pesticides, and polybrominated diphenyl ethers with oxidative stress markers: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:37813138.finding: Associations of PFAS, PCBs, organochlorine pesticides and PBDEs with oxidative stress markers were mostly inconsistent; only a few pooled associations (e.g., DDE with malondialdehyde) were significant.

pmid:25477703.authors: Liu Z, Liu Y, Song Y, et al.
pmid:25477703.title: Systemic oxidative stress biomarkers in chronic periodontitis: a meta-analysis.
pmid:25477703.finding: Chronic periodontitis was associated with lower serum total antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde and nitric oxide.

pmid:30076616.authors: da Silva JC, Muniz FWMG, Oballe HJR, et al.
pmid:30076616.title: The effect of periodontal therapy on oxidative stress biomarkers: A systematic review.
pmid:30076616.finding: Mechanical periodontal treatment generally reduced oxidative markers (8-OHdG, total oxidant status) in saliva and gingival fluid, and in serum in most studies.

pmid:17486089.authors: Ohsawa I, Ishikawa M, Takahashi K, et al.
pmid:17486089.title: Hydrogen acts as a therapeutic antioxidant by selectively reducing cytotoxic oxygen radicals.
pmid:17486089.finding: Molecular hydrogen selectively reduced hydroxyl radical and peroxynitrite in cells and, inhaled, limited brain ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats.

pmid:34601077.authors: Zanini D, Todorovic N, Korovljev D, et al.
pmid:34601077.title: The effects of 6-month hydrogen-rich water intake on molecular and phenotypic biomarkers of aging in older adults aged 70 years and over: A randomized controlled pilot trial.
pmid:34601077.finding: Pilot trial of 0.5 L/day hydrogen-rich water for 6 months reported small differences in telomere length and some molecular markers; exploratory, many outcomes.

pmid:37259294.authors: Todorovic N, Fernández-Landa J, Santibañez A, et al.
pmid:37259294.title: The Effects of Hydrogen-Rich Water on Blood Lipid Profiles in Clinical Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:37259294.finding: Hydrogen-rich water modestly lowered total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides in small clinical trials (pooled SMD about -0.2 to -0.4).

pmid:22291721.authors: Chevalier G, Sinatra ST, Oschman JL, et al.
pmid:22291721.title: Earthing: health implications of reconnecting the human body to the Earth's surface electrons.
pmid:22291721.finding: Narrative review by proponents of earthing summarizing small studies claiming better sleep, less pain and other effects from conductive contact with the ground.

pmid:26505864.authors: Liu J, Zhang P, Tian J, et al.
pmid:26505864.title: Ozone therapy for treating foot ulcers in people with diabetes.
pmid:26505864.finding: Cochrane review: three small, high or unclear risk-of-bias trials; no firm conclusions possible on ozone therapy for diabetic foot ulcers.

pmid:1907548.authors: Aebi S, Assereto R, Lauterburg BH
pmid:1907548.title: High-dose intravenous glutathione in man. Pharmacokinetics and effects on cyst(e)ine in plasma and urine.
pmid:1907548.finding: Intravenous glutathione (2 g/m2) had a plasma half-life of about 14 minutes and was rapidly broken down or excreted in urine.

pmid:24791752.authors: Richie JP Jr, Nichenametla S, Neidig W, et al.
pmid:24791752.title: Randomized controlled trial of oral glutathione supplementation on body stores of glutathione.
pmid:24791752.finding: Oral glutathione 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months raised blood glutathione stores by 17-35%, which returned to baseline after a 1-month washout.

pmid:40500991.authors: Luk HY, Jiwan NC, Appell CR, et al.
pmid:40500991.title: Passive dehydration increases oxidative stress and mTOR signalling pathway activation in young men following resistance exercise.
pmid:40500991.finding: Fluid restriction from 24 h before resistance exercise raised muscle H2O2 compared with euhydration.

pmid:19648152.title: On the possible origins of DNA damage in human spermatozoa
pmid:19648152.finding: Proposes the two-step hypothesis: defective chromatin remodelling (poor protamination) during spermiogenesis leaves sperm vulnerable, and oxidative stress then breaks the DNA.

pmid:19494251.authors: De Iuliis GN, Thomson LK, Mitchell LA, et al.
pmid:19494251.title: DNA damage in human spermatozoa is highly correlated with the efficiency of chromatin remodeling and the formation of 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine, a marker of oxidative stress
pmid:19494251.finding: In human sperm, poor protamination correlated strongly with 8-OHdG formation and with DNA fragmentation (P<0.001), supporting the two-step hypothesis.

pmid:18492763.authors: Koppers AJ, De Iuliis GN, Finnie JM, et al.
pmid:18492763.title: Significance of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species in the generation of oxidative stress in spermatozoa
pmid:18492763.finding: Electron leak from mitochondrial complex I in human sperm causes midpiece lipid peroxidation and loss of motility, preventable by alpha-tocopherol in vitro.

pmid:24369131.authors: Aitken RJ, Smith TB, Jobling MS, et al.
pmid:24369131.title: Oxidative stress and male reproductive health
pmid:24369131.finding: Sperm carry only OGG1, the first enzyme of base excision repair; the oocyte must finish repairing oxidised bases before the first S-phase, and errors become mutations in every cell of the embryo.

pmid:27062870.authors: Aitken RJ, Gibb Z, Baker MA, et al.
pmid:27062870.title: Causes and consequences of oxidative stress in spermatozoa
pmid:27062870.finding: Sperm are vulnerable because their membranes are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids and they have almost no cytoplasm for antioxidant enzymes; stressed sperm default to an apoptotic pathway with mitochondrial ROS and oxidative DNA damage.

pmid:36604857.title: DNA damage in testicular germ cells and spermatozoa. When and how is it induced? How should we measure it? What does it mean?
pmid:36604857.finding: In mature sperm, hydrogen peroxide released from the midpiece (not nucleases) penetrates the nucleus and drives DNA damage; reviews what each SDF assay actually measures.

pmid:37568254.title: Male reproductive ageing: a radical road to ruin
pmid:37568254.finding: Paternal ageing brings more sperm DNA damage, epigenetic change in the germ line and a higher mutational load in offspring.

pmid:14285045.title: KINETICS OF THE GERMINAL EPITHELIUM IN MAN
pmid:14285045.finding: Classic radiolabelling study of the kinetics of the human germinal epithelium, the source of the widely quoted ~74-day duration of spermatogenesis.

pmid:16406920.authors: Misell LM, Holochwost D, Boban D, et al.
pmid:16406920.title: A stable isotope-mass spectrometric method for measuring human spermatogenesis kinetics in vivo
pmid:16406920.finding: Deuterium labelling: newly made sperm first appeared in the ejaculate after 64 +/- 8 days (range 42-76).

pmid:34954800.authors: Newman H, Catt S, Vining B, et al.
pmid:34954800.title: DNA repair and response to sperm DNA damage in oocytes and embryos, and the potential consequences in ART: a systematic review
pmid:34954800.finding: Systematic review: oocytes and early embryos can repair paternal DNA damage, but the capacity is limited and likely declines with maternal age.

pmid:33589137.authors: Setti AS, Braga DPAF, Provenza RR, et al.
pmid:33589137.title: Oocyte ability to repair sperm DNA fragmentation: the impact of maternal age on intracytoplasmic sperm injection outcomes
pmid:33589137.finding: Sperm DNA fragmentation >=30% (SCD) harmed ICSI outcomes only when the woman was over 40 (pregnancy 7.7% vs 20.0%); no effect at 40 or younger.

pmid:17681311.authors: Meseguer M, Martínez-Conejero JA, O'Connor JE, et al.
pmid:17681311.title: The significance of sperm DNA oxidation in embryo development and reproductive outcome in an oocyte donation program: a new model to study a male infertility prognostic factor
pmid:17681311.finding: With the same donor's eggs split between couples, higher sperm DNA oxidation was linked to poorer embryo development and blastocyst formation.

pmid:10632410.authors: Spanò M, Bonde JP, Hjøllund HI, et al.
pmid:10632410.title: Sperm chromatin damage impairs human fertility. The Danish First Pregnancy Planner Study Team
pmid:10632410.finding: In first-pregnancy planners, the chance of conceiving per cycle fell as SCSA-abnormal sperm rose and became small above 40%.

pmid:10221239.authors: Evenson DP, Jost LK, Marshall D, et al.
pmid:10221239.title: Utility of the sperm chromatin structure assay as a diagnostic and prognostic tool in the human fertility clinic
pmid:10221239.finding: No couple conceived naturally when the man's SCSA DNA fragmentation was >=30%; 84% of men whose partners conceived in months 1-3 were below 15%.

pmid:16921163.authors: Bungum M, Humaidan P, Axmon A, et al.
pmid:16921163.title: Sperm DNA integrity assessment in prediction of assisted reproduction technology outcome
pmid:16921163.finding: DFI >30% predicted lower pregnancy and delivery after IUI; with DFI >30%, ICSI did better than conventional IVF.

pmid:22791753.authors: Robinson L, Gallos ID, Conner SJ, et al.
pmid:22791753.title: The effect of sperm DNA fragmentation on miscarriage rates: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:22791753.finding: High sperm DNA damage doubled the risk of miscarriage (RR 2.16, 95% CI 1.54-3.03); strongest with TUNEL (RR 3.94).

pmid:31056315.authors: McQueen DB, Zhang J, Robins JC
pmid:31056315.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation and recurrent pregnancy loss: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:31056315.finding: Male partners of women with recurrent pregnancy loss had sperm DNA fragmentation 11.9 points higher than partners of fertile women.

pmid:27345006.authors: Simon L, Zini A, Dyachenko A, et al.
pmid:27345006.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the effect of sperm DNA damage on in vitro fertilization and intracytoplasmic sperm injection outcome
pmid:27345006.finding: Sperm DNA damage was associated with lower clinical pregnancy after IVF and/or ICSI (combined OR 1.68).

pmid:25530036.authors: Osman A, Alsomait H, Seshadri S, et al.
pmid:25530036.title: The effect of sperm DNA fragmentation on live birth rate after IVF or ICSI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:25530036.finding: Low sperm DNA fragmentation was associated with higher live birth after IVF/ICSI (RR 1.17); the ICSI effect was small and not robust in sensitivity analysis.

pmid:23028579.authors: Ribas-Maynou J, García-Peiró A, Fernandez-Encinas A, et al.
pmid:23028579.title: Double stranded sperm DNA breaks, measured by Comet assay, are associated with unexplained recurrent miscarriage in couples without a female factor
pmid:23028579.finding: A high double-strand break profile (neutral Comet) was found in 85% of men from couples with unexplained recurrent miscarriage vs 33% of fertile donors.

pmid:26780327.authors: Sharma R, Ahmad G, Esteves SC, et al.
pmid:26780327.title: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) assay using bench top flow cytometer for evaluation of sperm DNA fragmentation in fertility laboratories: protocol, reference values, and quality control
pmid:26780327.finding: Flow-cytometric TUNEL reference cut-off of 16.8% had 91.6% specificity but only 32.6% sensitivity.

pmid:23391408.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
pmid:23391408.title: The clinical utility of sperm DNA integrity testing: a guideline
pmid:23391408.finding: ASRM 2013: sperm DNA integrity tests do not reliably predict treatment outcomes and cannot be recommended routinely.

pmid:33309062.authors: Schlegel PN, Sigman M, Collura B, et al.
pmid:33309062.title: Diagnosis and treatment of infertility in men: AUA/ASRM guideline part I
pmid:33309062.finding: AUA/ASRM guideline part I (evaluation): do not order SDF in the initial work-up; do evaluate SDF (and karyotype) in the male partner of couples with recurrent pregnancy loss.

pmid:33309061.authors: Schlegel PN, Sigman M, Collura B, et al.
pmid:33309061.title: Diagnosis and treatment of infertility in men: AUA/ASRM guideline part II
pmid:33309061.finding: AUA/ASRM guideline part II (treatment): counsel that supplements are of questionable clinical utility; consider varicocelectomy for palpable varicocele with abnormal semen; do not prescribe testosterone to men wanting fertility.

pmid:39145501.authors: Brannigan RE, Hermanson L, Kaczmarek J, et al.
pmid:39145501.title: Updates to Male Infertility: AUA/ASRM Guideline (2024)
pmid:39145501.finding: 2024 AUA/ASRM amendment, including the statement that clinicians may consider testicular sperm in nonazoospermic men with elevated DNA fragmentation.

pmid:34511305.authors: Minhas S, Bettocchi C, Boeri L, et al.
pmid:34511305.title: European Association of Urology Guidelines on Male Sexual and Reproductive Health: 2021 Update on Male Infertility
pmid:34511305.finding: EAU 2021: SDF is a useful biomarker for ART outcomes; insufficient evidence for widespread empirical antioxidants or surgical sperm retrieval in men without azoospermia.

pmid:33422457.authors: Tharakan T, Bettocchi C, Carvalho J, et al.
pmid:33422457.title: European Association of Urology Guidelines Panel on Male Sexual and Reproductive Health: A Clinical Consultation Guide on the Indications for Performing Sperm DNA Fragmentation Testing in Men with Infertility and Testicular Sperm Extraction in Nonazoospermic Men
pmid:33422457.finding: EAU consultation guide on when to test SDF and on the still-experimental use of testicular sperm for ICSI in nonazoospermic men.

pmid:29082206.authors: Agarwal A, Cho CL, Majzoub A, et al.
pmid:29082206.title: The Society for Translational Medicine: clinical practice guidelines for sperm DNA fragmentation testing in male infertility
pmid:29082206.finding: Society for Translational Medicine guideline: test SDF in clinical varicocele with borderline semen, recurrent pregnancy loss, ART failure, unexplained infertility and men with lifestyle risk factors.

pmid:29082146.authors: Cho CL, Agarwal A, Majzoub A, et al.
pmid:29082146.title: Clinical utility of sperm DNA fragmentation testing: concise practice recommendations
pmid:29082146.finding: Concise expert practice recommendations on the clinical scenarios where SDF testing changes management.

pmid:33988000.authors: Agarwal A, Farkouh A, Parekh N, et al.
pmid:33988000.title: Sperm DNA Fragmentation: A Critical Assessment of Clinical Practice Guidelines
pmid:33988000.finding: Compares the Agarwal and Esteves SDF guidelines; both use thresholds around 20% for TUNEL/SCD/SCSA (about 26% for alkaline Comet) and link values above 20-30% to worse outcomes.

pmid:27260688.authors: Agarwal A, Sharma R, Roychoudhury S, et al.
pmid:27260688.title: MiOXSYS: a novel method of measuring oxidation reduction potential in semen and seminal plasma
pmid:27260688.finding: Introduced MiOXSYS oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) in semen; proposed a cut-off of 1.48 mV/10^6 sperm/mL.

pmid:31006711.authors: Agarwal A, Panner Selvam MK, Arafa M, et al.
pmid:31006711.title: Multi-center evaluation of oxidation-reduction potential by the MiOXSYS in males with abnormal semen
pmid:31006711.finding: ORP normalised to sperm concentration flagged abnormal semen with 98.1% sensitivity but only 40.6% specificity (AUC 0.765).

pmid:31081299.authors: Agarwal A, Parekh N, Panner Selvam MK, et al.
pmid:31081299.title: Male Oxidative Stress Infertility (MOSI): Proposed Terminology and Clinical Practice Guidelines for Management of Idiopathic Male Infertility
pmid:31081299.finding: Proposes the term 'Male Oxidative Stress Infertility'; 30-80% of infertile men have high seminal ROS; current antioxidant use is not evidence-based.

pmid:33831977.authors: Agarwal A, Finelli R, Selvam MKP, et al.
pmid:33831977.title: A Global Survey of Reproductive Specialists to Determine the Clinical Utility of Oxidative Stress Testing and Antioxidant Use in Male Infertility
pmid:33831977.finding: Global survey: 85.6% of reproductive specialists prescribe antioxidants, mostly for 3-6 months, while most do not test for oxidative stress and rate the supporting evidence as modest.

pmid:25527074.authors: Agarwal A, Mulgund A, Alshahrani S, et al.
pmid:25527074.title: Reactive oxygen species and sperm DNA damage in infertile men presenting with low level leukocytospermia
pmid:25527074.finding: Even low-level leukocytospermia (below 1 million WBC/mL) was associated with higher ROS and SDF (26.5% vs 19.9%).

pmid:36653793.authors: Szabó A, Váncsa S, Hegyi P, et al.
pmid:36653793.title: Lifestyle-, environmental-, and additional health factors associated with an increased sperm DNA fragmentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:36653793.finding: Mean SDF increase: varicocele +13.6, impaired glucose tolerance +13.8, age >=50 +12.6, air pollution +9.7, smoking +9.2 percentage points; abstinence length and chlamydia/HPV showed no clear effect.

pmid:41051027.authors: Ragheb A, Abdelbary A, Massoud A, et al.
pmid:41051027.title: Evaluating the effect of smoking and its cessation on semen parameters
pmid:41051027.finding: After quitting smoking, semen improved at 3 and again at 6 months (progressive motility 20.7% -> 35.3% -> 42.3%).

pmid:22809864.authors: Wang YJ, Zhang RQ, Lin YJ, et al.
pmid:22809864.title: Relationship between varicocele and sperm DNA damage and the effect of varicocele repair: a meta-analysis
pmid:22809864.finding: Men with varicocele had 9.8 points more sperm DNA damage than controls; varicocelectomy lowered it by 3.4 points.

pmid:33985792.authors: Lira Neto FT, Roque M, Esteves SC
pmid:33985792.title: Effect of varicocelectomy on sperm deoxyribonucleic acid fragmentation rates in infertile men with clinical varicocele: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:33985792.finding: Varicocelectomy lowered SDF by 7.2 points (95% CI 5.6-8.9), more in men with high pre-operative SDF.

pmid:33890288.authors: Persad E, O'Loughlin CA, Kaur S, et al.
pmid:33890288.title: Surgical or radiological treatment for varicoceles in subfertile men
pmid:33890288.finding: Cochrane: varicocele treatment may raise pregnancy rates (RR 1.55, low certainty); effect on live birth is uncertain.

pmid:31949297.authors: Sepidarkish M, Maleki-Hajiagha A, Maroufizadeh S, et al.
pmid:31949297.title: The effect of body mass index on sperm DNA fragmentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:31949297.finding: Only class I obesity (BMI 30-35) showed a small SDF increase (SMD 0.23); data insufficient for a firm BMI-SDF link.

pmid:26380863.authors: Campbell JM, Lane M, Owens JA, et al.
pmid:26380863.title: Paternal obesity negatively affects male fertility and assisted reproduction outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:26380863.finding: Obese men had more infertility (OR 1.66), lower live birth per ART cycle (OR 0.65) and more sperm DNA fragmentation.

pmid:39344112.authors: Santi D, Greco C, Barbonetti A, et al.
pmid:39344112.title: Weight Loss as Therapeutic Option to Restore Fertility in Obese Men: A Meta-Analytic Study
pmid:39344112.finding: Weight loss in obese men (mean baseline BMI 45) raised concentration and motility and lowered DNA fragmentation index (effect size -0.69).

pmid:41065428.authors: Peel A, Lyons H, Tully CA, et al.
pmid:41065428.title: The effect of obesity interventions on male fertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:41065428.finding: Lifestyle weight-loss programmes improved motility and morphology; bariatric surgery produced no clinically significant semen or DNA damage change; low certainty overall.

pmid:27410176.authors: Rao M, Xia W, Yang J, et al.
pmid:27410176.title: Transient scrotal hyperthermia affects human sperm DNA integrity, sperm apoptosis, and sperm protein expression
pmid:27410176.finding: Scrotal warming in a 43 C bath for 30 min x 10 sessions reversibly increased SCSA chromatin abnormality, apoptosis and mitochondrial damage; recovery by about 16 weeks.

pmid:17335598.authors: Shefi S, Tarapore PE, Walsh TJ, et al.
pmid:17335598.title: Wet heat exposure: a potentially reversible cause of low semen quality in infertile men
pmid:17335598.finding: After infertile men stopped hot tubs/hot baths, 5 of 11 responded with a 491% rise in total motile sperm count (motility 12% -> 34%).

pmid:30102388.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Gaskins AJ, Chiu YH, et al.
pmid:30102388.title: Type of underwear worn and markers of testicular function among men attending a fertility center
pmid:30102388.finding: Men who mainly wore boxers had 25% higher sperm concentration and 17% higher total count than men who did not.

pmid:15591087.authors: Sheynkin Y, Jung M, Yoo P, et al.
pmid:15591087.title: Increase in scrotal temperature in laptop computer users
pmid:15591087.finding: A working laptop on the lap raised scrotal temperature 2.6-2.8 C in 60 minutes (2.1 C from the closed-thigh posture alone).

pmid:21055743.authors: Sheynkin Y, Welliver R, Winer A, et al.
pmid:21055743.title: Protection from scrotal hyperthermia in laptop computer users
pmid:21055743.finding: Scrotal temperature rose 1 C within 11-28 minutes of laptop use; a lap pad did not prevent it; sitting with legs apart reduced it.

pmid:9756281.authors: Thonneau P, Bujan L, Multigner L, et al.
pmid:9756281.title: Occupational heat exposure and male fertility: a review
pmid:9756281.finding: Occupational heat exposure is a significant risk factor for male infertility, worsening morphology and delaying conception.

pmid:16766665.authors: Wyrobek AJ, Eskenazi B, Young S, et al.
pmid:16766665.title: Advancing age has differential effects on DNA damage, chromatin integrity, gene mutations, and aneuploidies in sperm
pmid:16766665.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:16766665.finding: In healthy non-smokers, sperm DNA fragmentation index rose steadily with age, with no threshold.

pmid:25462195.authors: Johnson SL, Dunleavy J, Gemmell NJ, et al.
pmid:25462195.title: Consistent age-dependent declines in human semen quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:25462195.finding: Age was associated with declines in volume, motility, morphology and the share of unfragmented sperm.

pmid:28029592.authors: Ricci E, Al Beitawi S, Cipriani S, et al.
pmid:28029592.title: Semen quality and alcohol intake: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:28029592.finding: Alcohol lowered semen volume and normal morphology, mainly in daily drinkers; occasional drinking did not clearly harm semen.

pmid:25277121.authors: Jensen TK, Gottschau M, Madsen JO, et al.
pmid:25277121.title: Habitual alcohol consumption associated with reduced semen quality and changes in reproductive hormones; a cross-sectional study among 1221 young Danish men
pmid:25277121.finding: Habitual intake above 5 units/week was linked to poorer semen; above 40 units/week, sperm concentration was 33% lower than at 1-5 units.

pmid:32001159.authors: Verhaeghe F, Di Pizio P, Bichara C, et al.
pmid:32001159.title: Cannabis consumption might exert deleterious effects on sperm nuclear quality in infertile men
pmid:32001159.finding: Regular cannabis users had more sperm DNA fragmentation and aneuploidy than non-users (exploratory).

pmid:16650651.authors: Liu PY, Swerdloff RS, Christenson PD, et al.
pmid:16650651.title: Rate, extent, and modifiers of spermatogenic recovery after hormonal male contraception: an integrated analysis
pmid:16650651.finding: After androgen-based suppression, median time for sperm to recover to 20 million/mL was 3.4 months; longer with longer treatment.

pmid:37567343.title: Recovery of spermatogenesis after androgenic anabolic steroids abuse in men. A systematic review of the literature
pmid:37567343.finding: Systematic review: anabolic steroid infertility is often reversible, but sperm production may take over a year to normalise.

pmid:15980006.authors: Rubes J, Selevan SG, Evenson DP, et al.
pmid:15980006.title: Episodic air pollution is associated with increased DNA fragmentation in human sperm without other changes in semen quality
pmid:15980006.finding: Young men in Teplice had more SCSA sperm DNA fragmentation after high-pollution periods, without other semen changes.

pmid:17090632.authors: Hauser R, Meeker JD, Singh NP, et al.
pmid:17090632.title: DNA damage in human sperm is related to urinary levels of phthalate monoester and oxidative metabolites
pmid:17090632.finding: Urinary phthalate metabolites MEP and MEHP were associated with more neutral-Comet sperm DNA damage (about 14-18% per IQR rise in MEHP).

pmid:20656017.authors: Meeker JD, Ehrlich S, Toth TL, et al.
pmid:20656017.title: Semen quality and sperm DNA damage in relation to urinary bisphenol A among men from an infertility clinic
pmid:20656017.finding: An IQR rise in urinary BPA was linked to 10% more Comet tail DNA and lower concentration and morphology.

pmid:23445617.authors: Miranda-Contreras L, Gómez-Pérez R, Rojas G, et al.
pmid:23445617.title: Occupational exposure to organophosphate and carbamate pesticides affects sperm chromatin integrity and reproductive hormone levels among Venezuelan farm workers
pmid:23445617.finding: Farm workers exposed to organophosphate and carbamate pesticides had higher sperm DNA fragmentation index.

pmid:17953955.authors: Gallegos G, Ramos B, Santiso R, et al.
pmid:17953955.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation in infertile men with genitourinary infection by Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycoplasma
pmid:17953955.finding: Chlamydia/Mycoplasma infection: SDF 35% vs 11% in fertile controls; after about 4 months of antibiotics SDF fell from 37.7% to 24.2%.

pmid:17434502.authors: Sergerie M, Mieusset R, Croute F, et al.
pmid:17434502.title: High risk of temporary alteration of semen parameters after recent acute febrile illness
pmid:17434502.finding: After a 2-day fever of 39-40 C, DNA fragmentation index rose by 24-36% at days 15-37 and returned toward baseline by day 79.

pmid:41330355.authors: Coleman CM, Wesselink AK, Yland JJ, et al.
pmid:41330355.title: A North American preconception study of sleep health and semen quality
pmid:41330355.finding: Short (<6 h) or long (>=9 h) sleep and poor sleep quality were associated with roughly 15-20% lower sperm counts, with wide confidence intervals.

pmid:24700791.authors: Liu K, Li Y, Zhang G, et al.
pmid:24700791.title: Association between mobile phone use and semen quality: a systemic review and meta-analysis
pmid:24700791.finding: In human studies, mobile phone use had no significant effect on semen parameters; in vitro RF exposure reduced motility and viability.

pmid:34333014.authors: Kim S, Han D, Ryu J, et al.
pmid:34333014.title: Effects of mobile phone usage on sperm quality - No time-dependent relationship on usage: A systematic review and updated meta-analysis
pmid:34333014.finding: Phone exposure was associated with lower motility, viability and concentration, but with no dose-response by hours of use.

pmid:18804757.authors: Agarwal A, Desai NR, Makker K, et al.
pmid:18804757.title: Effects of radiofrequency electromagnetic waves (RF-EMW) from cellular phones on human ejaculated semen: an in vitro pilot study
pmid:18804757.finding: In vitro, phone RF exposure raised ROS and reduced motility and viability of neat semen, but did not change DNA damage.

pmid:21924714.authors: Gosálvez J, González-Martínez M, López-Fernández C, et al.
pmid:21924714.title: Shorter abstinence decreases sperm deoxyribonucleic acid fragmentation in ejaculate
pmid:21924714.finding: SDF was lower after 24-hour, and especially 3-hour, abstinence than after the standard abstinence period.

pmid:36555920.authors: Barbagallo F, Cannarella R, Crafa A, et al.
pmid:36555920.title: The Impact of a Very Short Abstinence Period on Conventional Sperm Parameters and Sperm DNA Fragmentation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:36555920.finding: A second ejaculate within 4 hours had lower SDF in men with abnormal semen.

pmid:38828413.authors: Lo Giudice A, Asmundo MG, Cimino S, et al.
pmid:38828413.title: Effects of long and short ejaculatory abstinence on sperm parameters: a meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials
pmid:38828413.finding: Abstinence longer than 2 days was associated with SDF 3.5 points higher; each extra day added about 0.65 points.

pmid:38197853.authors: Du C, Li Y, Yin C, et al.
pmid:38197853.title: Association of abstinence time with semen quality and fertility outcomes: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
pmid:38197853.finding: Short versus long abstinence lowered DNA fragmentation index by about 2.4 points in healthy men, at the cost of lower volume and count.

pmid:33179134.authors: Dahan MH, Mills G, Khoudja R, et al.
pmid:33179134.title: Three hour abstinence as a treatment for high sperm DNA fragmentation: a prospective cohort study
pmid:33179134.finding: SDF fell from 34.6% after 3 days of abstinence to 23.7% in a second sample 3 hours later; 55% of men with SDF >35% moved into the normal range.

pmid:23380634.authors: Gaskins AJ, Mendiola J, Afeiche M, et al.
pmid:23380634.title: Physical activity and television watching in relation to semen quality in young men
pmid:23380634.finding: Men with >=15 h/week moderate-vigorous activity had 73% higher sperm concentration; >20 h/week TV was linked to 44% lower concentration.

pmid:21122845.authors: Wise LA, Cramer DW, Hornstein MD, et al.
pmid:21122845.title: Physical activity and semen quality among men attending an infertility clinic
pmid:21122845.finding: Regular exercise overall was unrelated to semen quality, but cycling >=5 h/week was linked to low concentration (OR 1.92) and low total motile count.

pmid:27920258.authors: Hajizadeh Maleki B, Tartibian B, Chehrazi M
pmid:27920258.title: The effects of three different exercise modalities on markers of male reproduction in healthy subjects: a randomized controlled trial
pmid:27920258.finding: 24 weeks of moderate continuous training improved seminal oxidative and inflammatory markers and sperm DNA integrity more than high-intensity training (same group has several retracted trials).

pmid:24977955.title: Long-term Low-to-Intensive Cycling Training: Impact on Semen Parameters and Seminal Cytokines
pmid:24977955.finding: 16 weeks of intensive road-cycling training raised seminal cytokines and worsened semen; some changes persisted 30 days after training.

pmid:22895856.authors: Robbins WA, Xun L, FitzGerald LZ, et al.
pmid:22895856.title: Walnuts improve semen quality in men consuming a Western-style diet: randomized control dietary intervention trial
pmid:22895856.finding: Adding 75 g/day walnuts for 12 weeks improved sperm vitality, motility and morphology (DNA fragmentation not measured).

pmid:30475967.authors: Salas-Huetos A, Moraleda R, Giardina S, et al.
pmid:30475967.title: Effect of nut consumption on semen quality and functionality in healthy men consuming a Western-style diet: a randomized controlled trial
pmid:30475967.finding: Adding 60 g/day mixed nuts for 14 weeks improved count, vitality, motility and morphology and reduced sperm DNA fragmentation.

pmid:27994040.authors: Karayiannis D, Kontogianni MD, Mendorou C, et al.
pmid:27994040.title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and semen quality parameters in male partners of couples attempting fertility
pmid:27994040.finding: Men in the lowest Mediterranean-diet tertile had about 2.6 times the odds of abnormal concentration, count and motility.

pmid:40419219.authors: Agarwal R, Salas-Salvadó J, Davila-Cordova E, et al.
pmid:40419219.title: Mediterranean Diet, Semen Quality, and Medically Assisted Reproductive Outcomes in the Male Population: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:40419219.finding: Mediterranean diet adherence was associated with higher sperm count (+24 million), motility (+8.8 points) and morphology; no data showing better fertility outcomes.

pmid:28333357.authors: Salas-Huetos A, Bulló M, Salas-Salvadó J
pmid:28333357.title: Dietary patterns, foods and nutrients in male fertility parameters and fecundability: a systematic review of observational studies
pmid:28333357.finding: Systematic review of observational studies: diets rich in fish, fruit, vegetables and whole grains go with better semen; processed meat, sugary drinks, alcohol and soy with worse semen in some studies.

pmid:22888168.authors: Gaskins AJ, Colaci DS, Mendiola J, et al.
pmid:22888168.title: Dietary patterns and semen quality in young men
pmid:22888168.finding: Young men in the top quartile of a 'prudent' diet (fish, chicken, fruit, vegetables, legumes, whole grains) had 11.3 points higher progressive motility.

pmid:24850626.authors: Afeiche MC, Gaskins AJ, Williams PL, et al.
pmid:24850626.title: Processed meat intake is unfavorably and fish intake favorably associated with semen quality indicators among men attending a fertility clinic
pmid:24850626.finding: Highest processed-meat quartile had 1.7 points fewer normal forms; total count rose from 102 to 168 million across fish-intake quartiles.

pmid:24812311.authors: Chiu YH, Afeiche MC, Gaskins AJ, et al.
pmid:24812311.title: Sugar-sweetened beverage intake in relation to semen quality and reproductive hormone levels in young men
pmid:24812311.finding: Young men drinking >=1.3 sugar-sweetened beverages/day had 9.8 points lower progressive motility than those drinking <0.2/day.

pmid:27075904.authors: Chiu YH, Gaskins AJ, Williams PL, et al.
pmid:27075904.title: Intake of Fruits and Vegetables with Low-to-Moderate Pesticide Residues Is Positively Associated with Semen-Quality Parameters among Young Healthy Men
pmid:27075904.finding: Eating >=2.8 servings/day of low-to-moderate-pesticide fruit and vegetables was linked to 169% higher total sperm count; high-pesticide produce was not.

pmid:31591650.authors: Williams EA, Parker M, Robinson A, et al.
pmid:31591650.title: A randomized placebo-controlled trial to investigate the effect of lactolycopene on semen quality in healthy males
pmid:31591650.finding: 14 mg/day lactolycopene for 12 weeks improved fast progressive motility and morphology; the primary endpoint was not significant.

pmid:28646871.authors: Ricci E, Viganò P, Cipriani S, et al.
pmid:28646871.title: Coffee and caffeine intake and male infertility: a systematic review
pmid:28646871.finding: Caffeine from coffee and tea was mostly unrelated to semen parameters; caffeinated soft drinks looked harmful; DNA-damage findings inconsistent.

pmid:18650557.authors: Chavarro JE, Toth TL, Sadio SM, et al.
pmid:18650557.title: Soy food and isoflavone intake in relation to semen quality parameters among men from an infertility clinic
pmid:18650557.finding: Men in the highest soy-food category had 41 million/mL lower sperm concentration; no link to motility or morphology.

pmid:26097060.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Afeiche MC, Chiu YH, et al.
pmid:26097060.title: Male soy food intake was not associated with in vitro fertilization outcomes among couples attending a fertility center
pmid:26097060.finding: Male partners' soy intake was unrelated to fertilization, embryo quality or live birth in IVF.

pmid:33383165.authors: Reed KE, Camargo J, Hamilton-Reeves J, et al.
pmid:33383165.title: Neither soy nor isoflavone intake affects male reproductive hormones: An expanded and updated meta-analysis of clinical studies
pmid:33383165.finding: Soy protein and isoflavones did not change testosterone, free testosterone, estrogens or SHBG in men.

pmid:31116515.authors: Falsig AL, Gleerup CS, Knudsen UB
pmid:31116515.title: The influence of omega-3 fatty acids on semen quality markers: a systematic PRISMA review
pmid:31116515.finding: 14 of 16 studies found omega-3 intake or supplements associated with improvement in at least one semen marker; studies too heterogeneous to pool.

pmid:31951274.authors: Jensen TK, Priskorn L, Holmboe SA, et al.
pmid:31951274.title: Associations of Fish Oil Supplement Use With Testicular Function in Young Men
pmid:31951274.finding: Young men using fish oil supplements on >=60 days had 0.64 mL more semen volume, larger testes and lower FSH and LH.

pmid:27792396.authors: Martínez-Soto JC, Domingo JC, Cordobilla B, et al.
pmid:27792396.title: Dietary supplementation with docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) improves seminal antioxidant status and decreases sperm DNA fragmentation
pmid:27792396.finding: 1.5 g/day DHA for 10 weeks improved seminal antioxidant status and lowered sperm DNA fragmentation, without changing standard parameters.

pmid:30866036.authors: Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Yazdani A, et al.
pmid:30866036.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
pmid:30866036.finding: Cochrane 2019: live birth OR 1.79 (7 RCTs, 750 men, low-quality evidence); no significant benefit once high-risk-of-bias trials were removed (Peto OR 1.38, 0.89-2.16).

pmid:35506389.authors: de Ligny W, Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, et al.
pmid:35506389.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
pmid:35506389.finding: Cochrane 2022: live birth OR 1.43 (very low certainty); after removing high-risk-of-bias trials, no significant benefit (OR 1.22, 0.85-1.75).

pmid:32111479.authors: Steiner AZ, Hansen KR, Barnhart KT, et al.
pmid:32111479.title: The effect of antioxidants on male factor infertility: the Males, Antioxidants, and Infertility (MOXI) randomized clinical trial
pmid:32111479.finding: MOXI: a 7-ingredient antioxidant for 3-6 months did not improve semen parameters or DNA fragmentation; live birth 15% vs 24% placebo.

pmid:31910279.authors: Schisterman EF, Sjaarda LA, Clemons T, et al.
pmid:31910279.title: Effect of Folic Acid and Zinc Supplementation in Men on Semen Quality and Live Birth Among Couples Undergoing Infertility Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial
pmid:31910279.finding: FAZST: 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg zinc for 6 months did not improve semen or live birth (34% vs 35%); DNA fragmentation slightly higher (29.7% vs 27.2%).

pmid:15932912.authors: Greco E, Romano S, Iacobelli M, et al.
pmid:15932912.title: ICSI in cases of sperm DNA damage: beneficial effect of oral antioxidant treatment
pmid:15932912.finding: 1 g vitamin C + 1 g vitamin E daily for 2 months lowered SDF in 76% of men; the next ICSI had 48.2% vs 6.9% pregnancy (uncontrolled before-after).

pmid:17425820.authors: Ménézo YJ, Hazout A, Panteix G, et al.
pmid:17425820.title: Antioxidants to reduce sperm DNA fragmentation: an unexpected adverse effect
pmid:17425820.finding: 90 days of antioxidant vitamins with zinc and selenium lowered DFI by 19% but raised sperm decondensation by 23%.

pmid:40015627.authors: Moazamian A, Hug E, Villeneuve P, et al.
pmid:40015627.title: The dual nature of micronutrients on fertility: too much of a good thing?
pmid:40015627.finding: In healthy mice, high doses of vitamin C, zinc, folate or carnitine disturbed redox balance and damaged sperm DNA; high carnitine cut pregnancy rates, but helped oxidatively stressed mice.

pmid:30298673.authors: Stenqvist A, Oleszczuk K, Leijonhufvud I, et al.
pmid:30298673.title: Impact of antioxidant treatment on DNA fragmentation index: a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized trial
pmid:30298673.finding: Six months of combined antioxidants did not lower DNA fragmentation index in men with DFI >=25%.

pmid:17550489.authors: Tremellen K, Miari G, Froiland D, et al.
pmid:17550489.title: A randomised control trial examining the effect of an antioxidant (Menevit) on pregnancy outcome during IVF-ICSI treatment
pmid:17550489.journal: Aust N Z J Obstet Gynaecol
pmid:17550489.finding: Menevit for 3 months before IVF-ICSI: viable pregnancy 38.5% vs 16% per transferred embryo; embryo quality unchanged.

pmid:32330373.authors: Kopets R, Kuibida I, Chernyavska I, et al.
pmid:32330373.title: Dietary supplementation with a novel l-carnitine multi-micronutrient in idiopathic male subfertility involving oligo-, astheno-, teratozoospermia: A randomized clinical study
pmid:32330373.finding: An L-carnitine multi-micronutrient for 6 months raised the share of normal semen analyses (69% vs 22%) and spontaneous pregnancies.

pmid:23912751.authors: Lafuente R, González-Comadrán M, Solà I, et al.
pmid:23912751.title: Coenzyme Q10 and male infertility: a meta-analysis
pmid:23912751.finding: CoQ10 raised sperm concentration and motility, but there was no evidence for higher pregnancy or live birth.

pmid:18395716.authors: Balercia G, Buldreghini E, Vignini A, et al.
pmid:18395716.title: Coenzyme Q10 treatment in infertile men with idiopathic asthenozoospermia: a placebo-controlled, double-blind randomized trial
pmid:18395716.finding: CoQ10 200 mg/day for 6 months increased seminal CoQ10 and motility in idiopathic asthenozoospermia.

pmid:16110353.authors: Comhaire FH, El Garem Y, Mahmoud A, et al.
pmid:16110353.title: Combined conventional/antioxidant "Astaxanthin" treatment for male infertility: a double blind, randomized trial
pmid:16110353.finding: Astaxanthin 16 mg/day for 3 months lowered seminal ROS; pregnancy 54.5% vs 10.5% in a very small trial.

pmid:35128424.authors: Khaw SC, Wong ZZ, Anderson R, et al.
pmid:35128424.title: l-carnitine and l-acetylcarnitine supplementation for idiopathic male infertility
pmid:35128424.finding: Carnitines improved total and progressive motility and morphology, with no demonstrable effect on clinical pregnancy.

pmid:30462179.authors: Salas-Huetos A, Rosique-Esteban N, Becerra-Tomás N, et al.
pmid:30462179.title: The Effect of Nutrients and Dietary Supplements on Sperm Quality Parameters: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
pmid:30462179.finding: Selenium, zinc, omega-3, CoQ10 and carnitines produced modest improvements in sperm parameters; fertility outcomes not assessed.

pmid:30771790.authors: Jannatifar R, Parivar K, Roodbari NH, et al.
pmid:30771790.title: Effects of N-acetyl-cysteine supplementation on sperm quality, chromatin integrity and level of oxidative stress in infertile men
pmid:30771790.finding: NAC 600 mg/day for 3 months lowered SDF and protamine deficiency and improved count and motility (uncontrolled before-after).

pmid:9698665.authors: Scott R, MacPherson A, Yates RW, et al.
pmid:9698665.title: The effect of oral selenium supplementation on human sperm motility
pmid:9698665.finding: Selenium (with or without vitamins A, C, E) for 3 months raised motility in subfertile Scottish men with low selenium; 11% paternity vs 0%.

pmid:29126319.authors: Blomberg Jensen M, Lawaetz JG, Petersen JH, et al.
pmid:29126319.title: Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation on Semen Quality, Reproductive Hormones, and Live Birth Rate: A Randomized Clinical Trial
pmid:29126319.finding: Vitamin D (300,000 IU then 1400 IU/day) plus calcium for 150 days did not improve semen quality in vitamin-D-insufficient infertile men.

pmid:28865546.authors: Esteves SC, Roque M, Bradley CK, et al.
pmid:28865546.title: Reproductive outcomes of testicular versus ejaculated sperm for intracytoplasmic sperm injection among men with high levels of DNA fragmentation in semen: systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:28865546.finding: Testicular sperm had 24.6 points lower SDF than ejaculated sperm; ICSI with testicular sperm gave higher pregnancy and live birth and fewer miscarriages in high-SDF men.
